First, missionary schools have often played a role in colonization and the oppression of Muslim lands. Out of dignity and honor, a believer would generally avoid such institutions if possible.

Second, in some places, these schools are known for offering high-quality education.

Because of this, it is even more important to seek guidance from local scholars who understand your context.

The Cross and the Title “Father”: The Specific Points You Raised

Regarding your specific concerns, your approach is sound:

Openly wearing or displaying the cross is not permissible, as it represents another faith, and the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) stated, “Whoever imitates a people is one of them” [Abu Dawud]. If you cover the cross on your uniform and ID with tape, stitching, or a similar method so it is not visible, the objection is removed.

As for calling priests ‘father,’ if this is simply the usual way people address them in the institution, and you do not mean any religious reverence by it, it is permitted—just as one might say ‘sir.’ If you can use a neutral term, that is better.

Avoid intending any religious veneration in your words.

Attending the College Itself, and Weighing It Against Your Current One

Regarding studying at the institution, attendance is permitted provided you can protect yourself from un-Islamic beliefs and practices, maintain your prayers and religious observance, and avoid participating in the school’s religious activities.

If alternative institutions are available, they are often preferable. When compared to a college that requires you to shave your beard or participate in musical programs, an institution that allows you to cover your head and uphold your religious commitments may represent the lesser harm. However, this assessment depends on your specific circumstances.

Your context matters greatly. Please consult local scholars who can review your full situation and guide you on what best protects your faith. Also, deal with your parents with patience and gentle wisdom.

records.title: What Are the Limits of Male-Female Interaction on Social Media?
records.question: On social media, many men and women interact under religious posts or on live streams—a brother commenting on a sister’s religious post, or sisters asking a brother religious questions on his live—and what of someone who answers religious questions publicly without being qualified?
records.answer:
Interaction between unrelated men and women online is permitted when there is a real need or benefit, kept modest and public rather than private, and free of any softened or flirtatious speech.

A religious purpose does not lift these limits—and it is often the very place where the self hides what it wants. Answering questions in the name of the religion is another matter: that is only for those who have the knowledge to do so.

The Same Modesty Online as in Person

The believer carries the same restraint onto the screen that he keeps in a room. Allah Most High says, “Tell believing men, they lower and restrain their looks, and keep well chaste their private parts,” and likewise the believing women. [Quran 24:30-31; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

And in the address to the Mothers of the Believers — from which the scholars draw the wider manner of speech between the sexes — He says, “So lower not your voices with soft charm, lest he with sickness in his heart should desire; And speak words correct and chaste.” [Quran 33:32; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

In the Hanafi school, speaking with a non-mahram for a genuine need is permitted, on the condition that there is no softening of speech, no private seclusion (khalwa), and no reasonable fear of temptation (fitna). Online, a comment left in the open is public, not secluded.

Still, private messages and prolonged one-to-one exchanges are the digital form of exactly the seclusion the Shariah asks us to avoid. So keep what you write purposeful, brief, and in the open, and ensure there’s a clear benefit.

When a Religious Purpose Becomes a Doorway

Your instinct here is sound. A religious framing can become the doorway through which needless interaction enters, because the lower self (nafs) is skilled at dressing its desires in the clothing of piety.

Habib Umar bin Hafiz (may Allah preserve him) counsels the seeker to examine his intention and to turn away from every prompting that comes from caprice.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) taught that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should say what is good or keep silent. [Bukhari; Muslim]

For a sister who shares beneficial content, this is freeing: you are responsible for your own conduct and intention, not for the hearts of those who comment.

Keep your replies purposeful, public, and unsoftened, and simply disengage when an exchange carries no clear good. Bonds of faith do not erase the ordinary etiquette between unrelated men and women — if anything, they raise it.

Answering in the Name of the Religion

The last part of your question is a separate and serious one. To speak about the religion — to answer questions of Sacred Law and belief — is to speak on behalf of Allah, and that is not permitted without the requisite knowledge.

Allah Most High says, “Ask the people of knowledge if you do not know” [Quran 16:43].

Someone who is not qualified should not set themselves up to give religious answers, whether on a live stream or anywhere else.

The sincere course is to convey only what one has reliably learned, to point questioners to qualified scholars, and never to exceed the bounds of one’s own learning.

Purposeful, Modest, and Within One’s Knowledge

Thus, the open spaces of the internet are still public spaces, where the same modesty, sincerity, and restraint of the tongue apply as anywhere else. Benefit is welcome; guard your heart while you seek it, and stay within your knowledge.

In practice: keep exchanges purposeful and public, avoid private or softened conversation, and refer any religious question beyond your learning to those qualified to answer it.

Whoever leaves a thing for the sake of Allah, Allah gives him better than it — and the heart that guards itself online tastes a sweetness the noise can never give.

records.title: How Should I Respond When Non-Muslims Casually Say “Oh My God”?
records.question: When you hear or read non-Muslims say phrases with a religious meaning, such as the common “Oh my God!” said in surprise, what should you do?
records.answer:
You are not responsible for what others say, and you do not have to correct every casual word you hear. What matters is that your own heart is filled with veneration for Allah, and that this awe shapes how you speak of Him.

This leads to careful respect for the Divine Name, and a quiet dislike of true mockery. At the same time, it is important to recognize that a common phrase, said without intent, is not blasphemy.

Veneration Begins in the Heart

The Sacred Law trains the believer to magnify whatever is joined to Allah. Allah Most High says, “And whoso exalts the things inviolable to Allah, verily it comes of the godfearingness of the very hearts.” [Quran 22:32; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

The great scholars of Quran tafsir note that Allah singled out the hearts because they are the seat of godfearingness:

Imam Nasafi writes that “the hearts were mentioned only because they are the centers of taqwa” [Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil].

Imam Alusi draws the line clearly: “Godfearingness is of two kinds — the taqwa of the hearts, which is the true and sincere taqwa of the believer, and the taqwa of the limbs, the outward, hollow show of the hypocrite.” [Alusi, Ruh al-Maani]

Veneration is a fruit of the heart. Your first concern should be the awe in your own heart, not the words of others.

Careful with the Name of Allah

Awe leads to reverence in how we use the Name of Allah. When you mention His Name, do so with meaning and presence. Let your speech reflect a heart that magnifies Allah, not a tongue that uses His Name without thought.

A Common Idiom Is Not Intrinsically Blameworthy

The phrase itself does not carry sin. Today, “Oh my God” is a common idiom of surprise, and most people do not mean to refer to God, especially if they do not share our reverence. There is no blasphemy in their intent, and you are not responsible for it.

You are also not required to correct the speech of others, especially when there is no benefit or openness to advice. Often, correcting such habits does more harm than good.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or keep silent” [Bukhari; Muslim].

Allah praises the believers as “those who from idle words are invariably turned away” [Quran 23:3], “and when they pass upon idle empty talk, they pass it nobly by” [Quran 25:72].

And where you meet not idle idiom but genuine mockery of Allah or His religion, the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Whoever of you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart — and that is the weakest of faith.” [Muslim]

For the casual phrase you describe, the heart’s quiet turning is enough.

Awe in the Heart, Gentleness on the Tongue

Your responsibility is to venerate Allah yourself, not to police the words of others.

Strive to have awe of Allah, be present and respectful with His Name, dislike true mockery in your heart, and speak only when your words will bring benefit.

Do not let a passing idiom trouble you or lead you to unnecessary correction. Let it remind you to renew your own reverence.

records.title: Is a Quran Chip Treated Like a Physical Mushaf?
records.question: A silicon chip contains the entire Quran, engraved using nanotechnology at a scale invisible to the naked eye and only observable with a microscope.
records.answer:
The chip is not considered a mushaf but is seen as a storage device, like a memory chip or microfilm, because it does not have readable writing. So, you do not need wudu to handle the misbaha, and you can take it into the washroom while it is sealed.

Making or selling it is allowed as long as it is honestly described as a dhikr aid, does not claim to protect, and is treated with respect.

The Chip Is Not a Mushaf

A mushaf, in the language of the jurists, is the written compilation of the Quran, that is, the Book as gathered in legible script upon its pages.

The rulings of reverence that attach to it, such as the prohibition on the one in a state of minor or major ritual impurity touching or carrying it, are built upon this reality of written, readable text. [Nawawi, al-Majmu’; Misri, Reliance of the Traveller, e8]

What the eye and the hand engage as Quranic writing is what the sacred rulings address.

The chip does not have any writing that people can see or read. Its script is invisible to the naked eye and can only be seen with strong laboratory equipment, and it is sealed so it cannot be touched. To most people, it is simply a misbaha bead, not a page with writing.

Islamic law bases its rulings on what people can normally see and use, not on what only special tools can reveal [Suyuti, al-Ashbah wa al-Naza’ir].

This is why the rules for a mushaf do not apply to things like a phone with the Quran stored on it but turned off, to audio recordings, or to writing that has faded away. Scholars agree that the Quran stored but not displayed is not treated as a mushaf. [Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya; Islamweb]

In fact, this chip is even further from being a mushaf than a phone, since a phone can show readable verses, but this chip cannot be read by anyone.

Carrying It into the Washroom

Since this object is not a mushaf, the usual rule against taking a mushaf into the washroom does not apply. It is treated like a phone that stores the Quran, which can be taken into the washroom.

Because the chip is hidden inside the bead, there is no etiquette issue. Carrying it sealed in the misbaha, whether in your pocket or on you, is fine.

Manufacturing and Selling It

By default, things and transactions are allowed unless there is proof otherwise. [Suyuti, al-Ashbah wa al-Naza’ir]

Making a storage device to preserve the Quran is not a new act of worship; it is not considered an innovation but a permitted tool.

However, it must still be treated with respect, since the honor here is about meaning and intention, not about a readable page.

A Necessary Condition on the Whole Ruling

This answer depends on the chip staying sealed and being impossible for people to read.

If a future version allows the script to be seen, either with a lens or a display, then the rulings would change to those for a visible, readable Quran. What matters is whether people can actually read the text, not just that the letters exist.

Allah (Most High) says, “That is so. And whoever honors the symbols of Allah, it is certainly out of the piety of the heart.” [Quran, 22:32]

The respect we owe here is for the words of Allah as we intend them in our hearts. We show this respect by keeping the object from disrespect, not by giving it a ruling it does not deserve.

Principle and Practical Guidance

The main rule is that the rulings for a mushaf apply only to the Quran when it is written in a way people can read and recognize.

What people normally see and use decides how it is treated. The chip should be treated with respect, not as a mushaf.

You do not need wudu to hold the misbaha, you can take it into the washroom while it is sealed, and you can make and sell it as long as it is honestly described as a dhikr aid, does not claim to protect, and is kept respectful.
references: Misri, Reliance of the Traveller, e8

records.title: What Are the Nullifiers of Islam According to Hanafis?
records.question: I am seeking clarification regarding the nullifiers of Islam according to the Hanafi school. For comparison, the Hanbali school enumerates ten principal nullifiers from which others are derived.
records.answer:
The precision of your question demonstrates sincere concern.

First: What is Faith (Iman)?

In the Hanafi tradition, faith (iman) is defined as the firm assent of the heart (tasdiq) to all that the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) conveyed from Allah.

According to the Maturidi imams, verbal affirmation (iqrar) is a necessary condition for the application of outward Islamic rulings, whereas salvation with Allah depends on the heart’s assent. [Nasafi, al-Aqa’id al-Nasafiyya; Taftazani, Sharh al-Aqa’id; Bayadi, Isharat al-Maram]

Second: What is Disbelief (kufr), then?

Disbelief (kufr) is the opposite of assent: it encompasses denial (takdhib), rejection (juhud), or contemptuous dismissal of what the Messenger conveyed.

records.title: Is It Haram to Make AI Images or Advertise an AI Image Generator?
records.question: Does the Shafi’i School say making AI images is haram? Is it also haram to advertise an AI tool that makes images?
records.answer:
Making AI images is not haram on its own. AI is simply a tool, so the ruling depends on what you make with it, not the tool itself. All scholars allow images of non-living things.

For images of living beings, scholars, including those in the Shafi’i School, have different respected opinions. Advertising an AI image generator is allowed as long as the ad is lawful and does not promote anything forbidden.

Image-Making in the Shafi’i School

The scholars agreed that making three-dimensional images of animate life is impermissible, based on the words of the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace): “Indeed, those who make these images will be punished on the Day of Judgment, and it will be said to them: ‘Give life to what you have created.’” [Bukhari; Muslim]

However, scholars disagreed about two-dimensional images. Some Shafi’i scholars, like Khattabi, and Maliki scholars said these images are allowed. Even those with stricter views permit drawing living things without full facial features or just outlining bodies without details.

Everyone agrees that images of non-living things and scenery are allowed. Modern scholars also disagree about photos and digital images, and it is valid to follow either opinion without blame.

For the detailed discussions, please see:

What Is the Ruling on Photographing, Filming, and Drawing Animate Life? What Is the Ruling on Drawing Images on Clothing and the Like? Is It Disbelief to Draw Pictures?

AI Is a Tool, and the Ruling Attaches to the Doer

The ruling on making images does not change based on the tool. What matters in Sacred Law is what you make and how you use it. If someone uses AI to make lawful images, that is allowed.

If someone uses it to make forbidden things, like images showing nakedness, or sexualizing and degrading others, that is not allowed. The tool itself is not the focus here; each person is responsible for their own actions. Allah (Most High) says, “No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another.” [Quran, 35:18]

Advertising an AI Image Generator

Advertising an AI image tool is permissible. These tools have many lawful uses, and the basic rule is that things are allowed unless proven otherwise (al-asl fi al-ashya’ al-ibaha). [Suyuti, al-Ashbah wa al-Naza’ir]

Advertising is a lawful service for a lawful payment. Make sure the ad does not include forbidden images or encourage forbidden uses. If a tool is mainly used for unlawful things, it is better not to promote it out of caution.

Principle and Practical Guidance

The main rule is that rulings are about what people do, not the tools they use. Use AI image generation for good and lawful purposes. Follow the view on images of living things that you and your trusted scholars support.

Make sure your advertising does not include anything forbidden. May Allah (Most High) bless your work and give you from His bounty.

records.title: Does Waswasa (OCD) Excuse a Person from Prayer in the Shafi’i School?
records.question: If a person experiences waswas (obsessive thoughts) or OCD, does the Shafi’i School excuse them from prayer? Does this rule also cover ghusl, istinja, and the removal of impurities?
records.answer:
No, if you have waswasa or OCD and are sane and aware, you are nevertheless required to pray, perform ghusl, do istinja, and remove impurities, etc.

You must fulfill all religious duties, and your worship is valid. Sacred Law teaches not to act on doubts: do each required action once, then stop and ignore any further thoughts.

What Imam Shafi’i Meant

The passage from al-Umm you mentioned does not apply here. Imam Shafi’i (Allah have mercy on him) was referring to someone whose mind is so affected that they are unaware of their actions.

Such a person is not legally responsible, so prayer is not required for them. In this context, waswasa means a loss of intellect, not the obsessive thoughts of someone who is otherwise sane. [Shafi’i, al-Umm]

Since you understand what prayer is, know when you are praying, and can ask clear questions about Islamic law, you are considered sane and responsible.

This means you still need to pray and purify yourself, and God willing, your acts of worship will be accepted.

How the School Actually Helps You

Sacred Law helps people with waswasa by removing doubts, not by completely removing the obligation. You should live by the maxim: “Certainty is not removed by doubt”. [Suyuti, al-Ashbah wa al-Naza’ir]

So, wash once properly for istinja and ghusl, assume you are pure unless you clearly see impurity, pray once, and treat any thought telling you to repeat or check as coming from Shaytan. Ignore it completely.

A Companion once complained about whispers in prayer, and the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “That is a devil called Khinzab; when you sense him, seek refuge in Allah and dry-spit lightly to your left three times.” [Muslim]

Please read these carefully; they address your situation in detail:

A Reader on OCD and Waswasa (Baseless Misgivings) How Do You Deal with Waswasa and OCD in Purification and Prayer Acts? How to Deal With Waswas Regarding Purity According to the Shafi’i School?

Principle and Practical Guidance

The main rule is that obligation depends on sanity, and doubt never outweighs certainty. Keep praying, do only what is required for purification, and do not look for new rulings for every doubt. The answer is always the same: ignore it.

OCD also needs professional care, so please see a qualified therapist in addition to following this guidance. Getting treatment is also a way to draw closer to Allah. (Most High).

records.title: Is It Permissible for Men to Read Women’s Online Forums?
records.question: Many women discuss topics like periods, body, hijab, and navigating Islam on online forums, believing no men are present.
records.answer:
If a forum is intended for sisters only and advertised as such, and a man knowingly enters and joins, it would constitute deception; and if he were to share posts, it would constitute mockery and harm to others.

Also, it is the responsibility of women to ensure there is a reasonable expectation of privacy, given the known infiltration of social media.

If a forum is known to be easily accessible to anyone, it is wise not to assume complete privacy. This falls under taking reasonable means (asbab) to protect oneself.

Abu Hurayra (Allah be pleased with him) reports that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) passed by a man selling food. He put his hand in it and saw something wrong with it.

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “He is not one of us who cheats.” [Ibn Majah]

Allah Most High says, ‘O believers! Do not let some men ridicule others, they may be better than them, nor let some women ridicule other women, they may be better than them.’ [Quran; 49:11]

Abu Huraira ( Allah be pleased with him) reported: The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Verily, a man might speak a word to make those around him laugh, yet by it he plunges farther than the star of Pleiades.” [Hanbal, Musnad Ahmad]

There Should be No Harming or Reciprocating Harm

Abu Sa’id al-Khudri ( Allah be pleased with him) reported: The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Do not cause harm or return harm. Whoever harms others, Allah will harm him. Whoever is harsh with others, Allah will be harsh with him.” [Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra]

Women have a responsibility to ensure there is a reasonable expectation of privacy before sharing sensitive matters online. At the same time, men have an independent responsibility to respect others’ privacy, avoid deception, and refrain from exposing or mocking what they read.

records.title: Is It Permissible to Have a Male Doctor Remove My Gallbladder?
records.question: I am a female patient who needs to have my gallbladder removed. The only surgeon available at the hospital where I have been admitted is a man.
records.answer:
O Allah, Lord of the worlds, remove the harm and grant healing, for You are the Healer. There is no cure except Your cure. We ask You for a cure that leaves behind no illness. [Bukhari]

It is permissible in Islamic Law for a male surgeon to remove your gallbladder. Ibn Hajr says, ‘Cross-gender looking and touching is permissible for blood-letting, cupping, and medical procedures due to the need’. [Ibn Hajar, Tuhfa]

The above is on the condition that no qualified female surgeon is available to perform the procedure. [Ibid]

In addition, the following conditions should be kept in mind:

(1) preference should be given to a male doctor who is a mahram,

(2) females (doctor or patient) should be accompanied by a mahram or another trustworthy female, and

(3) Viewing and touching should be limited to necessity. [Khatib, Mughni al-Muhtaj]

Maintain modesty of your heart and mannerisms at all times. Modesty is a Muslim Woman’s crown. Ibn Qayyim said, ‘The strength of the virtue of modesty is in proportion to the life of the heart.

A deficiency of modesty is a sign of the death of the heart and the soul. Thus, the more alive the heart is, the more complete a person’s modesty becomes. [Ibn al-Qayyim, Madarij al-Salikin]

records.title: How Do I Repent from a Sexual Sin Committed in My Youth?
records.question: How do I repent from a sexual sin committed in my youth?
records.answer:
This was indeed something serious, but seeing as it was an isolated incident and a number of years ago, you should take it as a moment of folly, and you should repent to Allah Most High.

Repent sincerely, keep asking for forgiveness, and ensure nothing like this happens again. If you need to take active steps to prevent such a desire or situation from recurring, do so.

Yes, you don’t disclose this to your brother, as it would be a betrayal of trust and would only harm your relationship with him and, most likely, your family.

Once again, I must stress that nothing like this should happen again. It leads to a lot of psychological harm to a recipient, and the Prophet, Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded that “No harm should be done and there should be no reciprocal harm.” (Ibn Majah)

Pardon Allah our mistakes and protect us from committing acts that would lead to a difficult situation on the day of judgment.

records.title: Can a Menstruating Woman Enter the Masjid for a Hifz Class?
records.question: Can a menstruating woman enter the masjid or touch the Quran for a hifz class?
records.answer:
Your classmates are incorrect on this point. In the Hanafi school, it is not permitted for a menstruating lady to enter the masjid or to touch a copy of the Quran. [Ibn ‘Abidin Radd al-Muhtar]

Speak to your teacher, explain the situation, and try to reach an understanding with her.

There is a position in the Maliki school that permits someone learning and teaching the Quran to touch the Mus’haf and recite the Quran even whilst menstruating, but that is something we should consult with someone trained in the Maliki school for the particular details.

Otherwise, it’s best for you to stay away from the masjid at those times, and intend to honor and revere what Allah has honored. That is best for you.

“And whoever honors the rituals of Allah, it is best for them in the sight of their Lord.” [Quran, 22:30]

records.title: Is It Permissible to Buy a Home in a Complex With a Temple?
records.question: Is it permissible to buy an apartment in a complex that shares facilities with a temple?
records.answer:
It is permissible to purchase an apartment in this complex. You would not be actively assisting in any sin, and even the contribution towards the general maintenance would not be a sin. [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

You can assume your payment goes toward the cleaning and upkeep of the commonly shared areas, not specifically toward the Hindu temple.

Make a general intention of making a payment towards the upkeep of the areas you use. Should also make an intention of contributing towards removing potentially harmful objects and litter from the path, and that could be an application of the hadith:

“…and for you to remove something harmful from the road is an act of charity.” [Bukhari and Muslim]

records.title: What Should I Do if I Received Prize Money by Mistake?
records.question: In 2017, I entered a student essay and speech contest. Although only students from certain universities were eligible, I entered without hiding my college name. I was shortlisted and won 200000 INR, feeling lucky and unaware it might be wrong.
records.answer:
It was impermissible for you to receive the prize money because you misrepresented the eligibility criteria, even though they should have checked and disqualified you. The prize money must be returned.

This will not be considered full deception, as they should also be aware, but it is nonetheless deception from your side, as you were aware. You should now try to return it to the organizers bit by bit, or to the college without letting them know, as a general donation.

Abu Hurayra (Allah be pleased with him) reports that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) passed by a man selling food. He put his hand in it and saw that something was wrong. The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “He is not one of us who cheats.” [Ibn Majah]

Disbursing Unlawful Income

The general rule that applies to any form of unlawful funds is as follows:

Where the rightful owner is known, it must be returned to them.

Where the rightful owner is not known [or if they refuse], the funds must be disposed of in one of two ways:

a) It must either be given towards a charitable cause that benefits the public at large, such as public hospitals, schools, or mosques

b) or it should be given in charity to a person who is entitled by his need to receive charity. [Karaan, Disposal of Riba (Fatwa issued by the MJC)]

Money Has to be Returned to its Original Owner

As a principle, money is always returned to its original owner. [Taqi Usmani, Fiqh al-Buyu’]

Take this as an opportunity to clear matters and move forward. Do it gradually and anonymously, as long as you have the intention to repay, even if it takes time. Islam values honesty, and Allah’s mercy is greater than our shortcomings.
references: Karaan, Disposal of Riba (Fatwa issued by the MJC)

records.title: What Is the Ruling on Dhikr During Masturbation?
records.question: What is the ruling on dhikr during masturbation?
records.answer:
No, it doesn’t necessarily mean that your tasbih and worship are not accepted. Rather, it means you’re a human being with challenges and a path to drawing closer to Allah Most High.

Allah Most High said in the Quran, “Indeed, Allah loves those who frequently repent.” [Quran, 2:222]. Take this as a rule for any sin in life. If you’re struggling with a sin, keep repenting. Keep going back to Allah. Keep trying to be square with Allah.

If you slip up, embrace it as an opportunity to repent. Maybe the sin is there, so you keep repenting to become beloved to Allah. Sins committed out of weakness won’t harm you as long as there’s sincere repentance.

Keep repenting and keep a good opinion of Allah Most High in your mind at all times.

records.title: What Is the Ruling on Acknowledging Another’s Ownership of One’s Wealth?
records.question: Does iqrar occur when a person says that his money is for so-and-so person? Is the person obligated to give all his money to that person?
records.answer:
An Iqrar is an admission of owing a person money. It usually entails a wording that expresses an unambiguous statement of owing another a certain amount of money. [Maydani, Lubab]

If one owes another person money, they are obligated to repay them. Not necessarily because of the statement, but because it is their right.

Safety on the Day of Judgment and precaution against facing a difficult questioning before Allah Most High would entail that one does their best to repay what they owe to others.

The Iqrar itself is a statement that makes repayment legally binding before a court, but what’s more important is the court of Allah on the day of judgment. If you do owe someone something, focus more on that than on any legal details.

records.title: Is It Permissible to Write Fictional Stories About Magic and Free Mixing?
records.question: My question is about fiction. Is it permissible to write stories in which men and women interact?
records.answer:
Writing fictional stories is permissible, and writing about interactions between men and women is also fine as long as the content is permissible.

Do not write about inappropriate physical interactions or themes of love and romance outside of the Shari’a-approved boundaries. This is not too dissimilar to the boundaries scholars have placed on poetry. [Nabulsi, al-Hadiqa al-Nadiyya]

See your writing as a means of sharing good and some elements of the teachings of the Prophet, Allah bless him and grant him peace. He, Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “The best of people are those who are the most beneficial to people.” [Tabarani, al-Awsat]

Make this your intention: whatever you write about, give it a deep moral message, either something that focuses on showing gratitude to God or gratitude to his creation, or making the right choices: morality, kindness, generosity, gentleness, empathy, mercy, etc.

This should be the core of your content and the beating heart of what you write.

Beyond this, it is permissible to write about people having superpowers, and magic would also be permitted as long as it’s not presented as being a malicious tool of harm, and it’s not glorified in any way.

Present it as a tool and make it secondary, but deeply rooted in morality.

An example of this would be Superman. As a child, I read a number of comics about this character, and the key central theme was hope.

He presented hope and the idea of always trying to do what’s best. This is the kind of approach your writing should take: glorifying something worthy of glory.

Avoid using any sort of anti-heroic characters, and make the morality unambiguous in your story. And if you avoid aggrandizing anything indecent or impermissible, you’ll be fine.

Depicting deaths or murder, if it has the purpose of getting the lesson of the story across, would be permissible. Allah knows best.

Allah grant you the best of both worlds.

records.title: How Can I Find Hope Amid Abuse, Depression, and Pregnancy?
records.question: I come from a deeply abusive family and have struggled with depression for three years. I am now seven months pregnant, and although my husband is supportive, I have lost hope.
records.answer:
My dear sister, may Allah make everything easy for you.

It’s clear you’ve had a very difficult life, and I want to offer you some hope through the fact that the people with the most difficult trials are the people who are dearest to Allah Most High.

It may not seem like you’re special or dear to Allah Most High, but that’s only because of our limited human perspective.

What usually happens is that Allah wants to grant a tremendous and special reward to a person that they couldn’t attain through their own works.

This reward may not necessarily be evident in this life, but it’s certainly one that will last forever and is tremendous in the eyes of Allah, who knows all.

The Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Whoever Allah wants tremendous good for, He tries them repeatedly.” [Bukhari]

This is a sign of being dearly beloved to Allah Most High. Some people get tested occasionally, or they have problems that are not as intense as what you may have experienced.

Then there are other people for whom nothing works out. Everything is a challenge, everything is a problem, everything comes with a burden.

This is the category of people we are talking about, and this is the category of people referred to in the hadith.

Clearly, you seem to be one of those people. The Messenger of Allah guaranteed that whatever happens to the believer is the very best thing for the believer. He said, “Allah bless him and grant him peace. I am amazed at the affair of the believer. Everything that happens to him is the very best thing for him.” [Muslim]

With this in mind, look at the challenges in your life and see every one of those challenges and every one of those obstacles and difficulties as a direct proof of Allah’s love for you.

You may not feel this specialness or this love, but I guarantee you will one day. Allah can reward you with such beauty that all of the pain of the past can melt away to the point that none of it matters.

None of the residual difficulty, its effect, its wounds, its bruises has any effect on you whatsoever.

Be patient, expect the best of Allah, and know you’re under the care of Allah. This is exactly what He said to His Messenger, “Patiently await the judgment of your Loving Lord, for you are under our gaze!” (Quran, 52:48). Do this, and you will see a lot of good in your life.

records.title: What Is the Ruler’s Role in Applying the Ruling on Apostasy?
records.question: Will a person still get the hadd of apostasy if they ask the ruler to be on their religion (eg. christianity) but they will stop advertising their disbelief?
records.answer:
It is important to keep two matters distinct here. Much confusion arises when they are mixed together. The first is the ruling itself. The second is the discretion of the ruler or judge in applying it. When we keep these apart, the issue

The Ruling in Itself

In the Hanafi school, a person who willingly abandons Islam after truly entering it is first called back; offering him Islam again, and resolving whatever doubt drove him out, is recommended, and he is given time, typically three days, because “one who leaves Islam usually has a doubt, which is uncovered for him if he raises it in this period.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

If he then persists, the sacred law prescribes the capital penalty, on the basis of the Prophet’s words (Allah bless him and give him peace), “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.” [Bukhari]

It is important to see what this ruling is actually attached to. Our imams make it clear that the penalty is not for a private act of unbelief. Imam Sarakhsi (Allah have mercy on him) explains that unbelief itself is a matter between the servant and Allah, and its true reckoning is in the Hereafter.

What is addressed in this world are matters of public order and benefit for people.

The penalty, he says, is connected to the potential for public harm, not simply a change of belief. The clearest example is the ruling on a female apostate: in the Hanafi school, she is not put to death, because the penalty is linked to the capacity for combat, and women are not killed since they do not fight.

This follows the guidance of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), who forbade the killing of women and children in war.

Ibn Abidin also clarifies that public action, not private belief, is considered. So, in the Hanafi school, the ruling addresses the public and seditious aspect of a public defection, not the private conscience of someone who has quietly changed their faith.

The Discretion in Applying it

This penalty belongs to the public order of the sacred law. Its administration is for the legitimate ruler or judge alone, “the imam or the qadi” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar], never for private individuals; one who takes it upon himself to kill an apostate without the ruler’s authorization is himself disciplined for overstepping. [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

Beyond this, the ruler and judge weigh the context, for a settled maxim is that the fixed punishments are averted by doubt, and the whole practice of calling the person back exists to surface and dissolve his doubt.

The judge asks whether there is any real sedition, whether the person even entered Islam validly to begin with — a conversion under compulsion is no Islam to apostatize from, for the Quran excuses the one coerced to utter unbelief “while his heart is firm and serene in faith” [Quran 16:106; Keller, The Quran Beheld] — and where the public interest truly lies.

This is why, across Islamic history, many who in fact left Islam faced no penalty at all.

A well-known case shows this clearly. Musa ibn Maymun (Maimonides), the Jewish philosopher and physician, was forced to profess Islam during the Almohad persecution in the Muslim West.

Later, he lived openly as a Jew in Egypt. When a jurist accused him of apostasy, the statesman al-Qadi al-Fadil, who served Sultan Salah al-Din, protected him. The reason was clear: a conversion under force is not true Islam, so there was no apostasy to answer for. Ibn al-Qifti records this event.

Instead of being punished, Maimonides served as a physician to the Ayyubid court and was honored for his service. This is an example of how the principles of Sacred Law—such as the role of doubt and the reality of coercion—are applied in real life.

What Does This Mean for the Case You Describe?

The answer is a matter of principle, not a verdict any of us issues about a real person. The classical penalty targets a public, combative defection and is administered by a legitimate authority, with restraint, after calling the person back and clearing his doubts.

A quiet, private matter of conscience is precisely where the school’s stated cause — public harm — is absent, where doubt weighs heavily, and where no individual has standing to act at all.

What is asked of us toward such a person is what was asked of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace): sincere concern, good character, clear knowledge, and the removal of doubts, leaving the reckoning of hearts to Allah and any question of public order to those who legitimately carry it.

records.title: What Should I Do About Doubtful Past Oaths?
records.question: I made many promises in the past, but now I regret them and am unsure if they were made before or after puberty, whether I used Allah’s name, or if I fulfilled them. I don’t remember the exact wording or reasons for these promises.
records.answer:
Since you’re unsure whether you made them before or after puberty and whether you used Allah’s name, along with the exact wording, there’s no need to worry; it won’t be considered an oath. Just leave it as is, avoid overthinking, and stay assured.

One should disregard waswas-related oaths to avoid unnecessary hardship. Allah Most High says in the Quran, “Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship.”[2:185]

“Certainty is not lifted by a doubt.” [Ibn Nujaym, al-Ashbah wa’l Nadha’ir; Majallat al-Ahkam al-‘Adiliyya]

Legal Distinction Between a Promise to Allah and an Oath by Allah

A promise “to Allah” is legally a promise, whereas a promise “by Allah” is legally an oath.

One should avoid unnecessary promises and oaths, as doing so burdens oneself with unnecessary commitments.

I request you not to dwell on the past; your anxiety will spread to other areas as well. Islam does not want you to suffer from constant uncertainty.

Shaytan sometimes causes a person to doubt the basics until life becomes unbearable. So, ignore past oath-related doubts, and don’t let worry and anxiety take over.

records.title: What Is Required During Ghusl if Retracting the Foreskin Is Difficult?
records.question: I’m a 19-year-old Hanafi convert. I learned I must retract my foreskin during ghusl to clean properly. During my last ghusl, I struggled to do so, finding it hard physically and psychologically.
records.answer:
The washing of your inner glans to the best of your ability will be fine. It is not necessary to clean the deeper inner layers. Water can naturally seep in.

As a general ruling, in your case, you don’t need to be circumcised, although you are encouraged to do so. You just need to ensure that you wash reasonably well under the foreskin, so that no impurities remain. When you do this, your wudu or ghusl will be valid.

As it is an area that is sensitive, except with significant difficulty, pain, or the risk of harm, do what is reasonable and leave it at that. Allah Most High says: “Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.” [Qur’an 2:286]

For a ghusl to be valid, the following eleven things must be washed:

[Tahtawi/Shurunbulali, Hashiyat Maraqi al-Falah]

And the basic ruling is that circumcision is a Sunnah, as indicated in the hadith. It is one of the distinguishing symbols (sha’a’ir) of Islam and one of its distinctive characteristics.

If the people of an entire town were to abandon it collectively, the ruler would compel its observance as a public symbol of Islam. Therefore, it should not be left unless there is a valid excuse. The excuse of an elderly man who cannot bear it is an obvious example. [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

One should not feel inferior for not being circumcised due to age. You are as normal as anyone else and can practice and do what others can do. Always avoid excessive scrutiny, especially in matters of purification, because water, due to its natural flow, can reach and wash reasonably well.

records.title: Do Internal Sensations and Noises Invalidate One’s Wudu?
records.question: I suffer from waswas, which are derogatory thoughts that taunt me. As a teen without access to a madrasa or a teacher, I deal with flatulence issues. Sometimes I hear clicks and groans near my backside, but no gas is released.
records.answer:
Your question and writing suggest you often doubted the validity of your prayers because of these sensations. If these were doubts, your prayers were valid, and no makeups (qadas) are needed.

If you were certain that wind existed during certain prayers, you would need to do makeups, which you can estimate in total without going into worry.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said that if someone feels something during prayer, they shouldn’t leave unless they hear a sound or smell.

Abbas ibn Tamim (Allah be pleased with him) reported: My uncle asked the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) about a man who suspects that he passed wind during prayer.

The Prophet said, “He should not leave his prayer unless he hears a sound or finds a smell.” [Bukhari; Muslim]

Based on the important fiqh principle, “Certainty is not lifted by a doubt.” [Ibn Nujaym, al-Ashbah wa’l Nadha’ir; Majallat al-Ahkam al-‘Adiliyya]

Try to continue finding local circles of knowledge to deepen your knowledge, and any circles of remembrance to help your heart practice what you learn.

A Practical Step

Make wudu before prayer, and while in prayer, ignore sensations, clicks, pressures, or movements unless you’re sure the wind has exited. Don’t investigate, clench, check, or replay in your mind afterward. Just finish your prayer.

Allah Most High facilitates the ease of seeking knowledge and opens inspiring paths in your life in the future, amin.

records.title: Did I Commit Disbelief by Making a Sarcastic Comment?
records.question: I deflected a provocative question at work, about male and female equality, by sarcastically saying, “yes, men are superior, haha.” Was this permissible, and did it affect my faith?
records.answer:
Thank you for being mindful of your faith. May Allah reward you and help you support others too.

You don’t need to worry. Your comment did not affect your faith. You used irony to respond to a social stereotype, and nothing sacred was involved. What matters most is the care behind your question, which I’ll explain next.

Why Your Faith Is Intact

A statement only amounts to disbelief (kufr) when a person intentionally says something that they know rejects the religion. Islam, once affirmed with certainty, is never removed by doubt or by an unintended/accidental word. [Ibn Nujaym, al-Bahr al-Raiq]

Your words did not meet any of these conditions. You were clearly being sarcastic about a workplace stereotype, and your colleague did not even know you are Muslim. Mocking religion requires both the right content and intention, and your comment had neither. Your faith remains the same.

A Better Response Next Time

It’s usually better to respond with wisdom and perhaps redirect the conversation to more important matters, like belief in the Oneness of Allah, prophethood, and the hereafter. If you must say something about the issue, then stick to the fundamentals.

Allah tells us to invite others to His way with wisdom and good advice. [Quran 16:125] You could say, “Islam teaches that human worth is based on character and God-consciousness, for both men and women.”

The Quran also says that the most honored people in Allah’s eyes are those who are most mindful of Him. [Quran 49:13] Remember also, you are not obliged or permitted to discuss matters that you have no knowledge of, so be careful.

The Worry Behind the Question

Notice the pattern. After a normal moment, you spend hours worrying about whether you said something wrong or not. This is a sign of baseless doubts (waswasa),and I urge you to ignore them.

Some companions came to the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), upset by thoughts they were afraid to say out loud, and he told them, “That is pure faith.” [Muslim] Feeling this worry actually shows your belief, not the opposite.

The sunna in these situations is to ignore such doubts, ask Allah for help, and move forward. If you focus on these worries, they get stronger. If you ignore them, they usually fade away.

The main rule is that certainty is not removed by doubt. In practice, ignore these worries when they come up. Instead, focus on learning the basics of your faith with real teachers, spend time with good people, and if you keep having the same worry, talk to one trusted scholar instead of questioning yourself every time.

As someone new to Islam, your main goal is to build your faith. Allah loves steady and consistent actions, even if they are small.

records.title: Can We Treat Someone’s Unspoken Wish as a Fact?
records.question: If someone’s actions don’t show any sign that they want something, can we assume they do and treat it as a fact?
records.answer:
No. If someone’s actions do not show any sign of a desire, we cannot treat that desire as real. Assuming otherwise would just be guessing, and guessing is not a valid basis for judgment.

Three principles from Sacred Law support this.

First, we judge by what is outward, and only Allah knows what is inside a person’s heart (nahkumu bil-dhawahir wa-Allahu yatawalla al-sara’ir).

Second, the default is that a person is free from any claim or obligation (bara’at al-dhimma), so nothing is assumed about them, such as desire, consent, or duty, unless there is clear evidence.

Third, we assume things stay the same (istishab), so if there is no sign of a desire, we keep assuming that until something changes. This means anyone who claims a person wants something must prove it.

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “You bring your disputes to me, and perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than the other, so I judge according to what I hear.” [Bukhari; Muslim]

Even the Prophet, who received revelation, judged only by what was shown outwardly. So, we should not treat guesses about someone’s inner thoughts as facts in Sacred Law. Allah also warns believers to avoid too much suspicion, because some suspicion is sinful. [Quran 49:12]

One important point: if the Lawgiver or custom treats a certain sign as an indication, such as a shy bride’s silence when asked for consent, then that sign counts as an outward indicator. So, the rule of judging by outward appearances is still followed.

The main rule is that we need certainty to make a claim against someone, and only outward actions or words count as proof. In practice, treat people based on what they say and do.

If you need to know their wishes, ask them, and leave what is hidden in their hearts to Allah.

records.title: What Is the Ruling on Talfiq During Umra Tawaf?
records.question: I did tawaf with impurity on my sandals, following the Hanafi view. Later, I found out that Hanafis say the middle of the foot should be uncovered in ihram, but my sandals covered it. Did I fall into talfiq, and do I owe a fidya?
records.answer:
You can relax. Your umra is valid, you did not fall into prohibited talfiq, and you do not owe anything.

What is Talfiq?

Scholars prohibit talfiq when someone mixes two schools on the same issue, creating an act that neither school accepts as valid [Saqqaf, Mukhtasar al-Fawaid al-Makkiyya].

For example, if someone uses one school’s rule to excuse something that breaks wudu in their own school, and another school’s rule for something else, they might end up with a prayer that neither school accepts.

Your situation is different. You followed different schools for two separate issues, and each issue was handled in a way that at least one school fully accepts.

Why your Tawaf is Valid

The first issue is purity during tawaf. In the Hanafi school, being free from filth is not required for tawaf to be valid. It is only obligatory for the part of clothing that covers the nakedness (awra), and recommended for the rest.

So, doing tawaf with impurity on your sandals is still valid [Ibn Nujaym, al-Bahr al-Raiq]. Following this view when you realized the impurity was correct and allowed.

The second issue is footwear in ihram. In the Hanafi school, footwear should leave the raised middle part of the foot uncovered. This is a rule for ihram and has its own penalties in that school. It is separate from the validity of tawaf.

So, even if a Hanafi wore your sandals, their tawaf and umrah would still be valid [Ibn ’Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]. You also followed your school’s rules for ihram, which allow sandals. Since you followed each school’s rules for each issue, this is not prohibited talfiq.

Since you met all the tawaf conditions at the school you followed and did not break any ihram rules at your own school, you do not owe any fidya or sacrifice (dam).

Completed Worship is not Undone by Later Doubts

On the day of sacrifice, people came to the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace), worried that they had done the pilgrimage rites out of order. He told each of them, “Do so, and there is no harm.” [Bukhari; Muslim]

The Lawgiver’s approach in pilgrimage is to make things easy, and a completed act of worship is not undone by doubts that come up later.

The main rule is that certainty is not removed by doubt. In practice, consider your umrah accepted, do not repeat anything, and do not pay anything.

In the future, if you want to follow another school’s view, ask a reliable scholar at the time about what that school requires, then act with confidence. Always think well of Allah, because He is as His servant thinks of Him.

records.title: Does an Impurity inside the Stomach Affect the Validity of Prayer?
records.question: If a person swallows something impure, like haram meat, does having it in the stomach affect whether their prayer is valid according to the Hanafi, Shafi’i, and Hanbali schools?
records.answer:
According to the Hanafi, Shafi’i, and Hanbali schools, anything inside the stomach does not affect the prayer. Your prayer is valid, and you do not need to remove anything from your stomach for it to count.

The Shared Principle

For prayer, purity is only required for three things: the outside of the body, your clothes, and the place where you pray. Filth is only considered when it is visible and on the outside; what is inside the body does not count.

Everyone prays while their stomach and intestines contain waste, and no scholar has said this affects the prayer. If someone eats something unlawful, the schools say to sincerely repent and try to eat only halal food in the future. Allah always accepts repentance.

The Hanafis state that the conditions of prayer relate to external purity of body, garment, and place. [Ibn ’Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

The Shafi’is define the condition as freedom from perceivable filth on the person, clothing, and place of prayer. [Shirbini, Mughni al-Muhtaj]

The Hanbalis state the same three domains. [Buhuti, Kashshaf al-Qina] None of the three schools attaches any prayer ruling to what lies within the stomach.

If you find a statement about this issue, check with a qualified Maliki teacher before accepting it. Sometimes, positions found online are misquoted or taken out of context.

Rulings Attach to What Is Manifest

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) taught that a person who doubts whether something exited from him should not leave the prayer “until he hears a sound or finds a smell.” [Muslim]

The Sacred Law ties its rulings on purity to what appears outwardly and is perceived; what is hidden within the body is entirely left out of the reckoning.

The main rule is that filth is only considered when it is on the outside of the body. What is inside does not affect your prayer.

So, pray with peace of mind, continue eating halal food, and learn your religious knowledge from qualified teachers rather than relying on random information online. This is how this knowledge is best learned.

records.title: Is It Permissible to Keep a Snapchat Streak with My Cousin?
records.question: May I send daily snaps to a boy cousin to keep a streak, even if they show no faces and are just random everyday things?
records.answer:
Let the streak end naturally, and try not to worry about it. Since a cousin is not a mahram, you should keep the same boundaries as you would with any unrelated man. Even if the snaps seem harmless, maintaining a streak creates a private, ongoing connection that could go against Sacred Law.

Why the Content Is Secondary

One should only contact a non-mahram when there is a genuine need. In addition, any contact should be public, brief, and without extra friendliness. A daily streak with a cousin of the opposite sex fails these criteria on all three aspects.

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “No man is alone with a woman except that Shaytan is the third of them.” [Tirmidhi]

What to Do

Let the streak end naturally, by going silent, or you can send a polite message like, “I am trying to practice my din better, so I am stepping back from streaks.”

You can still stay in touch with your cousin at family gatherings, in group chats, as you would with other relatives.

If your intentions were innocent, you are not at fault for the past. Just turn to Allah and make a change.

The main idea is that Sacred Law prevents small actions that could lead to bigger problems.

So, end the streak, keep your family bond strong in public settings, and try to use your daily habit to benefit your afterlife, like saying a short dhikr or reading a page of the Quran. Allah will give you something better in return.

records.title: Can Attending a Shia Mourning Gathering Amount to Kufr?
records.question: In my college years, I had a Shia friend whose grandfather died. She invited us to their home on the 40th day. She was upset we hadn’t visited her after his death. They held a majlis that I wasn’t aware of, and we attended to show our respect.
records.answer:
If you went to pay your respects at your friend’s house and ended up standing in honor of the late father or reading some Quran, it would not constitute disbelief (kufr). So, mere attendance under social pressure is not adoption of another creed, as your intention matters.

Actions Are by Their Intentions

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Verily actions are by their intentions, and one shall only have that which one intended.” [Bukhari; Muslim]

The fact that you are concerned shows you are a firm believer. The worry is a sign of faith, just as some of the Companions’ concern about bad thoughts coming to them. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “That is clear faith.” [Muslim]

Your issue concerns matters of disbelief. Focus on healing. Allah knows you are a believer, and so is your family. Kufr is an active choice, not something that happens by accident. Ask Allah for ease and peace of mind.

records.title: Is It Permissible to Mix Rulings Between Madhhabs?
records.question: I follow the Hanafi school, though I only learned what it means to follow fiqh after digging deeper, and many people around me do not know how either. We often mix rulings from different schools and follow whichever we prefer.
records.answer:
Your desire to understand your religion is a sign of Allah’s concern and mercy for you.

Sticking to one sound school, such as the Hanafi school, is a safe and praiseworthy way. Scholars advise against picking rulings from different schools just because they seem easier or more pleasing. Fiqh is not limited to prayer; it covers every part of your life.

Following a School Is Not “Blind Following”

Many people feel uneasy about the word taqlid, which means following qualified scholars. It is important to understand what it means, rather than fear it.

The Quran itself shows that some are able to weigh the evidence directly, while many rely on those with knowledge. Allah Most High says:

وَلَوْ رَدُّوهُ إِلَى الرَّسُولِ وَإِلَىٰ أُولِي الْأَمْرِ مِنْهُمْ لَعَلِمَهُ الَّذِينَ يَسْتَنْبِطُونَهُ مِنْهُمْ

“Had they but referred it to the Messenger and men of true decision among them, those of them who can draw the right conclusions about it would have certainly known how best to proceed with it.” [Quran 4:83; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

records.title: Does Engaging in Oral Sex With the Same Sex Affect Virginity?
records.question: This is hypothetical and was asked of a friend. If a Muslim man has engaged in oral sex with someone of the same sex and no penetration occurred, and he realized it was wrong, repented, and stopped the actions, is he no longer a virgin?
records.answer:
One will still be a virgin, as one’s virginity is only taken away by penetration of the male private part. One should not entertain this type of hypothetical questioning, as it can lead to other things.

A Muslim who engages in sexual acts with someone of the same sex is sinful. He will have to repent sincerely, stop the sin, regret his actions, and resolve not to return to it.

Allah Most High says, “And remember when Lot scolded the men of his people, saying, ‘Do you commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before? “You lust after men instead of women! You are certainly transgressors.” [Quran, 7:80-81]

If someone intends to sin in this way, he should stop thinking this way immediately, repent, feel regret, and make a resolve not to do so again.

records.title: Is It Sinful to Compare My Strength to the Companions or Prophets?
records.question: Is it haram to say I will be the strongest and best fighter of all time, and even stronger than the Sahaba in terms of raw physical strength, as all time includes them, but not in a way that grows contempt for them?
records.answer:
Thank you for a question that already embodies good manners. Your care not to belittle the Companions or the Prophets is itself a sign of a sound heart, so let me begin by setting your worry at rest.

To wish for great physical strength and to train for it is not blameworthy in itself. Strength is one of Allah’s gifts, and He praises it when it is placed in its right setting.

One of the two women of Madyan said of Moses (peace be upon him), “A strong, trustworthy person is definitely the best to hire.” [Quran 28:26] Notice that strength is praised there beside trust, not on its own. Strength is a tool. What matters is the hand that carries it and the heart behind it.

The Rank of the Prophets and Companions Is Not a Matter of Muscle

The greatness of the Prophets and the Companions (Allah be pleased with them) is not bodily power. It is nearness to Allah, faith, and sacrifice.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) placed their rank beyond all reach: “Do not abuse my Companions, for if one of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not reach a handful of one of them, nor even half of it.” [Bukhari]

So a claim about raw physical strength does not touch their true excellence at all. And it is not from good manners (adab) even to weigh ourselves against the Prophets and the Companions in any quality whatsoever. We hold them above such comparison, and we simply keep them where Allah placed them.

Strength Becomes Blameworthy Only When Pride Enters

The danger is never the strength. It is arrogance and boasting. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.” [Muslim]

Imam Ghazali (Allah have mercy on him) draws the line clearly: a person is not blamed for enjoying a gift of Allah; he is blamed only when he joins it with arrogance or forgets that the gift came from Allah. [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din]

This is why Allah warns us against parading our strength: “And do not walk on the earth arrogantly. Surely you can neither crack the earth nor stretch to the height of the mountains.” [Quran 17:37]

A boast like “the strongest of all time” is the part to leave, even when what it describes is real. Hold the aspiration quietly in your heart, as effort and thanks, rather than as a slogan.

How the Strong of the Quran Carried Their Strength

Look at how Allah’s mighty servants held their power. David (peace be upon him) was given strength, iron softened in his hands, and victory in battle, yet the Quran sums him up not by his might but by his returning: “And remember Our servant, David, the man of strength. Indeed, he constantly turned to Allah” [Quran 38:17].

Moses (peace be upon him) lifted a stone that many men together could scarcely move, then withdrew, hungry, to confess his need of his Lord, so that no self-admiration could touch him. [Qushayri, Lataif al-Isharat]

Dhul-Qarnayn was given dominion across the earth, and when he raised his great barrier of iron and copper, he claimed none of it for himself: “This is a mercy from my Lord.” [Quran 18:98]

And Saul was chosen and increased in knowledge and stature, his strength given for the service of his people, not for display. [Quran 2:247; Qurtubi, al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran]. Their strength turned them toward Allah and turned them toward serving others. That is the pattern to follow.

Wanting Strength for the Sake of Good

So want strength for good, and it becomes a door of reward. Want it out of gratitude to the One who gave you your body. Want it so that, if Allah grants you success in a sport or a discipline, you can support your family, serve your community, and stand for what is right. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though in each there is good” [Muslim]. Our scholars explain that the strength most praised there is strength of resolve in Allah’s cause, not muscle alone [Nawawi; Mulla Ali al-Qari, Mirqat al-Mafatih]. And Allah has promised, “If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more” [Quran 14:7]. Whatever strength you carry, remember its source: “Whatever blessings you have are from Allah” [Quran 16:53].

Aspire High, but Rest in Allah, Not in Yourself

There is one more turn of the heart worth learning. Ibn Ata’illah (Allah have mercy on him) wrote, “The precedence of resolute aspirations does not pierce the walls of the divine decrees.” [Ibn Ata’illah, al-Hikam].

However high your ambition, it reaches only what Allah has already written; so aim high, strive fully, and then rest in Him rather than in your own power. He also wrote, “Realize your weakness, and He will support you with His strength.” [Ibn Ata’illah, al-Hikam]

The believer of high aspiration trains hard and leans on Allah, and so his strength never becomes a veil between him and his Lord.

As for the second-guessing, that “of all time” might somehow wrong the Companions or the Prophets, treat it as a passing whisper (waswasa) and turn away from it. These misgivings are not knowledge, and dwelling on them only feeds them. Your heart already honors those Allah honored; let that settle you.

So train, aspire, and grow strong, and do it out of gratitude and for the sake of good. Keep the Prophets and the Companions above all comparison, hold your strength as a trust from Allah, and let it carry you nearer to Him.

records.title: Is Expiation Required if a Convert Was Unaware of the Fasting Rules?
records.question: I reverted [converted] to Islam and fasted my first Ramadan while ignorant of the rulings. I had intercourse during the day, not knowing it breaks the fast, and I broke my fast by estimating sunset. I only learned the ruling in my second Ramadan. Do I owe the expiation?
records.answer:
There is good news for you.

You do not owe the expiation. In the Hanafi school, this expiation is a penalty, and Ibn Abidin states the governing rule in a single line: “this expiation is averted by doubts.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

A penalty falls away wherever there is a genuine excuse, and the school is explicit that where someone had intercourse by mistake, under coercion, or asleep, “he makes up the day only.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

For someone newly entered into Islam, the ground is stated more precisely still: the offense is a deficient one, “the offense of not verifying, not the offense of breaking the fast, because he did not intend that.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

That is your case exactly. You had only just entered Islam, the rulings had not reached you, and you did not intend to break anything.

I should be honest with you about one thing, so that you rest on solid ground rather than on a general feeling. I gnorance of the rulings is not a blanket excuse for a person who has lived long among Muslims with every opportunity to learn.

What lifts the expiation from you is that you had no real opportunity yet — you were months into Islam, fasting because you loved Allah, with no one having taught you.

This is the mercy Allah built into the fast itself: “Allah wants ease for you, and does not want unbearable hardship for you.” [Quran 2:185; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

What remains is light and full of good. Turn to Allah in sincere repentance, for “Verily Allah loves the oft-repentant, and loves those who remain pure from any reproach.” [Quran 2:222]

Then make up the fasts affected, day for day: each day the intercourse occurred, and any day you broke your fast a little before the true sunset because of your estimate.

These need not be consecutive, and you may spread them out. And carry no burden of sin for what you did while you genuinely did not know.

Let This Be the Beginning of Study, Not a Season of Worry

The governing principle is that responsibility follows knowledge, which means the surest way to protect your worship from here is simply to learn its rulings and then live by them.

So take one concrete step: begin The Absolute Essentials of Islam, then The Essentials of Belief, then the Kharida al-Bahiyya, in that order, within the free Islamic Studies Curriculum at https://academy.seekersguidance.org/islamic-studies-curriculum.

Allah asks, “Are those equal who know and those who know not?” [Quran 39:9], and He raises the grateful: “If you show thanks, I swear to increase you.” [Quran 14:7]

You fasted before you knew how; now you will fast knowing, and that is a life moving in one direction. Above all, let this deepen your love of Him, for “those who believe are greatest in love for Allah.” [Quran 2:165]

records.title: Which Number Should I Follow if I Doubt My Prayer Count?
records.question: Baseless misgivings (waswasa) leave me unable to tell how many cycles of prayer (rakats) I have completed. One answer I read says to take the higher number; another says to follow my inclination, and I never have one.
records.answer:
You have read everything you could find, and you still feel lost, and that is not a failure on your part. Here is the whole of it: when uncertain, follow your first inclination. [Tahtawi/Shurunbulali, Hashiyat Maraqi al-Falah]

Act on your first sense, complete your prayer, and do not revisit it. In Sacred Law, a judgment once made is not overturned by a later thought.

You Do Have an Inclination — It Is the First One

You mention that you do not feel an inclination. Often, it comes first, and doubts follow, covering it. By the time you search for it, the sense has faded.

That first impression, before the argument starts, is your inclination, and it is exactly what the school asks you to act on. Imam Shurunbulali (Allah have mercy on him) writes that one whose doubt is frequent acts on his dominant assumption where he has one, and he says the reason is to relieve hardship [Shurunbulali, Maraqi al-Falah].

That relief was written for you.

There is no contradiction between the answers you found. Follow your first inclination, whether it is toward the higher or lower number. Do not question it further or seek a stronger feeling.

The Second Thought Has No Standing

This is a key point to remember. Your first determination is a judgment, and it is not undone by later thoughts.

When doubt returns, it does not change what you have already decided. You are not required to feel certain, but simply to let your decision stand.

This same principle applies after you finish your prayer. Certainty is not removed by doubt. If a doubt comes after you have given salam, it is not considered unless you are sure of an omission.

Certainty means you remember it clearly, not that you fear it may have happened. The same applies to your prostrations: if you feel it is unlikely you rose after only one, that is your inclination, and it stands.

You do not need to rely on recordings or checking. The relief comes from trusting the permission given by the Sacred Law, which you already have.

You Are Not Being Asked to Stop the Whisper

This is where the answers you read left you stranded, because “ignore it” sounded like an instruction to stop feeling something you cannot stop feeling. That is not what is being asked.

Imam Khadimi (Allah have mercy on him), commenting on Imam Birgivi’s al-Tariqa al-Muhammadiyya, puts it in one line: it is not within the servant’s capacity to stop Shaytan from his promptings and his whisperings, and what is within his capacity is only not to mind them and not to comply with them. [Khadimi, Bariqa Mahmudiyya]

So you have not been failing at ignoring it. Ignoring it was never a feeling you had to produce; it is a decision not to investigate.

Ibn ’Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) holds that a person whose whisperings have taken hold of him is not governed by the ordinary rules of doubt at all, but is obliged to cut off the supply of the whispering and give the doubt-making no attention, because it is the work of Shaytan. [Ibn ’Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar].

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) taught the same discipline inside the prayer: “So let him cast off the doubt and build on what he is certain of.” [Muslim] Cast off, not resolve.

One thing needs to change, and only one. Do not break the prayer when the doubt peaks. Stay in it, follow your first lean, and finish — a prayer that feels ruined to you is still a valid prayer, and walking out of it is the only real loss in everything you have described.

When the whisper arrives, say once, inwardly, “I seek refuge in Allah from Shaytan the accursed,” and carry on without answering it.

Allah Most High has already settled what you owe: “Allah does not tax any soul but what it can bear,” and He teaches you to ask of Him, “O Lord, take us not to task if we forget, or make an honest mistake.” [Quran 2:286; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

A Companion Asked for This Exact Relief, and Received It

Uthman ibn Abi al-’As (Allah be pleased with him) came to the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) and said that Shaytan had come between him and his prayer and his recitation, confusing them for him.

He was told, “That is a devil called Khinzab. When you sense him, seek refuge in Allah from him, and spit lightly to your left three times.” He did it and reported, “Allah drove him away from me.” [Muslim]

During the prayer, seeking refuge is done inwardly, without spitting or counting. A Companion of the Messenger of Allah described the same struggle, was given a simple practice, and found relief. Follow your first inclination, complete your prayer, and ask Allah for the same ease.

Your recitation is a separate matter and less urgent. Bring it to a teacher when you are able, but do not worry about it today.

records.title: How Can I Strengthen My Faith When My Supplication Seem Unanswered?
records.question: I feel my faith weakening, and I feel guilty. I have prayed for years: for guidance, for relief from someone harming my family, for my husband, and for what I deserve at work. Yet I see no answer.
records.answer:
What you are experiencing is a real burden. It is important to acknowledge this and not overlook its weight.

Let me clarify something important: a person whose faith has truly left does not grieve over it.

The guilt you feel, and the pain of having asked for years, are signs of faith, not its absence. You are not witnessing your faith depart. Rather, you are feeling your faith tested under a real burden. This is a different matter altogether.

Now hold on to this: not one of those years of asking has been lost.

The Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, said that no Muslim makes a supplication free of sin and of severing kinship “except that Allah gives him by it one of three: either his supplication is hastened for him, or He stores it up for him in the Hereafter, or He turns away from him an evil equal to it.”

When the Companions said, “Then we shall ask much,” he answered, “Allah is more.” [Ahmad; Tirmidhi]

Sit with the arithmetic of that. Every one of your prayers has already done one of three things. Some of what you asked for may be waiting for you in a place where nothing is taken back.

Some of it may have already come to you as a harm you never saw arrive, because it was turned away.

And the one thing he warned against was not asking too long. It was stopping. “Each of you is answered, so long as he is not hasty and does not say, I supplicated and was not answered.” [Bukhari; Muslim]

In Imam Muslim’s fuller wording, he explains that being hasty means saying “I have supplicated and supplicated and I do not see myself answered,” and then growing weary and abandoning supplication.

Imam Nawawi comments that the hadith shows “one should persist in supplication and not deem the answer slow.” [Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim]

So the years are not the problem in this hadith. The years are the thing being praised, and the only failure available to you is the one you have not committed.

Allah has told you where He is while you wait: “And when My servants ask you of Me, truly I am near; I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he calls on Me.” [Quran 2:186; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

He has promised the one who keeps to Him a way through: “And whoever fears Allah, He grants him a way out of every plight, and provides for him whence he could not even guess.” [Quran 65:2-3]

And He has warned us that the reading of our own lives is short: “And it may well be that you hate something, and it is better for you, and may well be that you love something, and it is worse for you; And Allah well knows, and you know not.” [Quran 2:216]

That verse also covers the ease you see in those who reject Him. Whatever this world hands anyone is not the settling of the account, and it is not worth your envy.

In practical terms, keep your efforts manageable and consistent. Maintain your five daily prayers as your foundation, even on days when they feel difficult. A prayer performed, even without feeling, is better than a prayer missed. Make your supplications brief and frequent, and ask with a good opinion of Allah.

Give a little charity for each of the burdens you mentioned. Allow someone you trust to support you. If the sadness persists, seeking help from a counselor is a sign of strength, not weakness.

Your Prayers Are Held, Not Lost

Do remember what the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, taught: a sincere supplication is never lost. It is either granted, stored for you, or used to turn away harm. Nothing you have asked for over these years has been wasted.

Do not give up. Continue to ask, remain steadfast in your prayers, and allow a trusted person to support you. Allah has told you that He is near and that He answers. He has also said, ‘So verily with hardship comes utter ease.’ [Quran 94:5] He repeated this for emphasis.
