records.title: Is Judaism Still a Valid Religion Today?
records.question: Is Judaism a false religion? Was there a revelation at Mount Sinai, and what was revealed there? The Torah itself says it is everlasting, so how can we dispute that, and current Torah scrolls match ancient ones.
records.answer:
Yes, there was a revelation at Mount Sinai. Belief in this is not a courtesy to others, but a part of our own faith. To deny it would be to deny our own creed. Imam Nabulusi expresses this clearly.

We believe in Allah alone, and in all His angels, and in “all His revealed Books, the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Quran, and the remaining scriptures sent down by the revelation of Allah Most High upon the prophets and messengers,” and in all His messengers, “making no distinction in faith between any of His messengers, as the disbelievers did, who believed in some and did not believe in others.” [Nabulusi, Tahrik al-Iqlid fi Fath Bab al-Tawhid]
references: Nabulusi, Tahrik al-Iqlid fi Fath Bab al-Tawhid

records.title: Can I End an Engagement Because I Am Not Attracted to Him?
records.question: Is it permissible to end an engagement before marriage because of a lack of attraction? If someone is engaged or pressured to marry without attraction, is remaining unmarried preferable to marrying while still desiring someone else?
records.answer:
Yes, you may end this engagement. A lack of attraction is a valid and sufficient reason. You are not breaking a contract. You are not sinning. You are under no obligation to marry this man or anyone else.

What is an Engagement, Islamically?

You asked for the ruling, so here it is. An engagement is simply a proposal and a promise. It is not a marriage contract. Ibn Abidin was asked about a case much like yours. A suitor’s agent proposed to a man’s adult daughter before witnesses.

The father agreed, named a dower, and gave conditional consent. The suitor gave some jewelry, which the father had the daughter wear. Then the daughter refused the engagement. Was this allowed? Did the engagement count as a marriage contract?

He answered that, since no valid marriage contract was concluded, the engagement does not count as a marriage contract at all. [Ibn Abidin, Tanqih al-Fatawa al-Hamidiyya]

He gives the same answer when the Fatiha is read without a contract: that alone is not a marriage [ibid.]. So there is nothing here to be released from.

The Engagement is Not Binding, and You Should Not Feel Pressured

No one can force you into marriage. Imam Haskafi states the rule and its reason: “An adult virgin is not compelled to marry, because guardianship is severed by reaching majority” [Haskafi, al-Durr al-Mukhtar]

Ibn Nujaym explains the reason clearly: “because she is free and legally addressed in her own right, so no one else has authority over her” [Ibn Nujaym, al-Nahr al-Faiq]

Mulla Khusraw says it is about consent: an adult virgin “is not married off without her consent” [Mulla Khusraw, Durar al-Hukkam]. If your family says attraction does not matter, that is their opinion. It is not the ruling. The Sacred Law gives you this right.

Your Question and the Question of Attraction

Now to your actual question. Attraction is not a modern indulgence that the Sacred Law merely tolerates. Rather, it is something the Sunna went out of its way to protect.

The Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, told al-Mughira ibn Shu’ba, who had proposed to a woman, “Have you looked at her? Then look at her, for that is more likely to bring about lasting affection between you.” [Tirmidhi]

Shah Waliullah al-Dihlawi lays out why: so that the marriage be entered upon sight, so that it be further from the regret that binds a man who plunged into marriage and found her unsuited to him and did not turn back, so that it be easier to remedy if he does decline, and “so that he marry her with longing and eagerness if she suits him.” [Shah Waliullah al-Dihlawi, Hujjat Allah al-Baligha]

Gangohi says the looking was commanded “lest discord and aversion arise” when she turns out to be other than he had pictured. [Gangohi, Kawkab al-Durri] Read that list again: regret, aversion, discord, eagerness. Those are the very things you are trying to avoid, and the Sunna named them first.

Unmarried or Married Without Attraction?

As for whether staying unmarried is better than marrying without attraction, know that our school does not treat marriage as a flat obligation that you are failing to meet.

Imam Ibrahim al-Halabi grades it by your state — “it is obligatory in the case of strong desire, disliked where injustice is feared, and a stressed sunna in the state of moderation.” [Ibrahim al-Halabi, Multaqa al-Abhur]

Imam Haskafi notes that it becomes disliked where wrongdoing is feared, and forbidden where that is certain. [Haskafi, al-Durr al-Mukhtar]

A marriage entered without attraction and under pressure is exactly where the risk of failing in a spouse’s rights arises. So you are not choosing a lesser path by declining. Rather, you are avoiding the very situation these texts warn against.

Let me address the last part you mentioned. Marrying this man while your heart is attached to someone else would be a wrong to him, regardless of the ruling on the engagement.

This is a reason to end it cleanly, not a reason to go through with it. It is also separate from whether you may decline, which you certainly may.

An Engagement Binds Nothing, and Attraction Is Not a Luxury

The governing principle is that no marital tie exists before offer and acceptance. Withdrawing from an engagement breaks no contract and needs no excuse. Mutual attraction is a consideration that our own Sunna moved to protect. It is not a preference to be talked out of.

So end it, and end it well. Tell them clearly, without blame, and promptly rather than at the last moment. Return any gifts given for the marriage. Do this kindly, and you will have wronged no one.

The One who arranged your affairs before you knew of them has not left you to a poorer life for choosing honestly. Choosing honestly now is what will make the marriage you do enter a place where you can fulfill your obligations.
references: Shah Waliullah al-Dihlawi, Hujjat Allah al-Baligha

records.title: How Can I Be Humble Without Erasing My Own Voice?
records.question: How can a person be genuinely humble without erasing their own voice?
records.answer:
Humility is not about lowering yourself. It is about standing in your true place. Speaking clearly is not a failure in humility. The self-erasure you mention is a different problem, and our tradition gives it its own name.

Imam Ghazali sets this out with the precision the question deserves. Humility, he says, is a trait like any other, with two extremes and a middle: “the extreme that inclines toward excess is called arrogance, and the extreme that inclines toward deficiency is called self-abasement and abjection, and the middle is called humility.”

Then the line that answers you directly: “the praiseworthy course is that one be humble without abjection and without self-abasement, for both extremes of a matter are blameworthy, and the most beloved of matters to Allah are their middles.” [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, with Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin]

So the thing you sense is wrong actually is wrong. It simply is not humility.

His example makes it concrete. A scholar receives a visit from a tradesman, and he vacates his own seat for him, or seats him in it, then goes ahead of him, sets out his sandals for him, and walks behind him to the door of the house to see him off.

Imam Ghazali’s verdict: “he has demeaned and abased himself, and this too is not praiseworthy. Rather, what is praiseworthy in the sight of Allah is justice, which is that every possessor of a right be given his right.” [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din]

What humility toward such a person does look like, he says, is standing to greet him, a bright face, cheerfulness in speech, gentleness in questioning, accepting his invitation, going to trouble over his needs, and above all not seeing oneself as better than him. [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din] Nothing in this is surrendering your place.

The Limits of Humility

Humility has a limit. Imam Ghazali explains that if someone finds it hard to maintain their own standing and begins to seek excessive deference or to put themselves down, they have gone too far. At that point, he says, let the person raise themselves. It is not for a believer to abase themselves. The right way is the middle path.

Shah Abd al-Haqq al-Dihlawi says: humility is the middle between arrogance and self-abasement. Arrogance is raising yourself above your rank. Self-abasement is putting yourself below your rank. Humility is standing in your own place.

Humility Isn’t About Silencing Your Voice

Humility is not about silencing your voice. It is about letting go of the ego’s claim. Imam Ghazali teaches that the cure for pride is to know yourself and to know your Lord. When you know yourself, you see you have nothing to boast about. When you know your Lord, you know that greatness belongs only to Allah.

Any excellence you have is a blessing from Allah. The favor is His, not yours. See it as from Him, and you will not be impressed with yourself. When you are not impressed with yourself, you will not be arrogant. This frees your speech.

If you see your ability as a gift, you do not need to defend or prove yourself. You can speak the truth plainly. The Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, was the most humble of people and the clearest in speaking the truth.

It is important to name what is not humility, because it is easy to fall into. Pretending to be small, putting yourself down so others will praise you, or staying silent about the truth out of fear of people—none of this is humility.

Often, it is just the ego in another form. Imam Ghazali says that being impressed with yourself and despairing of yourself are both harmful. Neither leads to action.

Humility Is Standing in Your Own Station

The key is that humility is justice to yourself. Do not put yourself above your rank, and do not put yourself below it. Stand in your true place. In practice, this means two things. Do not claim to be better than the person in front of you.

Do not let false modesty stop you from saying what is true and needs to be said. If you notice yourself shrinking to please others, bring yourself back to the middle. If you notice yourself becoming proud, remember that every gift is from Allah.

The Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, said, “No charity ever diminished wealth, Allah ever increased no one through pardoning except in honor, and no one ever humbled himself for Allah except that Allah raised him.” [Muslim]

When Allah raises the humble, it is not to a quieter life, but to a life of greater meaning and responsibility.
references: Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, with Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin

records.title: Is It Permissible to Consume Albumin Containing Porridge for Gastric Study?
records.question: A gastric-emptying study I need for diagnosis requires eating porridge containing albumin, which I understand to be a protein found in human blood. My appointment is on 6 August. May I eat it?
records.answer:
You have been facing illness for a long time. You should not have to carry the added worry of a legal ruling into your appointment. Go ahead with the study. You may eat the porridge and have the test done.

There are three points that clarify this, and the first may resolve your concern completely. Albumin is not a single substance, but a group. Albumin from egg white is pure and lawful, with no issue. Recombinant albumin is produced in a laboratory.

Only serum albumin comes from blood. It is best to call the department and ask which type they use. For two of the three, there is no issue at all.

If it is serum albumin, the prohibition is narrower than you think. Allah Most High has made blood unlawful to consume [Quran 5:3; Keller, The Quran Beheld].

But Imam Jassas points out that the general wording is specified by the verse that names “poured-forth blood,” and concludes: “that shows that what is unlawful of blood is the poured-forth blood and not other than it.” [Jassas, Ahkam al-Quran]

Ibn Nujaym then lists ten kinds of blood that are not impure at all. [Ibn Nujaym, al-Ashbah wa’l-Nazair] A purified protein separated from serum does not flow in the blood.

Add to this that our school holds transformation to purify: “substances are purified by transformation, as carrion that becomes salt, filth that becomes earth, and wine that becomes vinegar.” [Mulla Khusraw, Durar al-Hukkam]

And even leaving all of that aside, your medical need settles it.

Our jurists permit treating with the otherwise-unlawful “when it is known that a cure lies in it and no other remedy is known, just as wine was permitted to the man dying of thirst, and this is the position given in fatwa.” [al-Hawi al-Qudsi, cited in Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

Mulla Khusraw states the mechanism: “the necessity lifts the prohibition, so he is not one treating himself with the unlawful.” [Mulla Khusraw, Durar al-Hukkam] Diagnosis is part of treatment, and prolonged weight loss with a BMI in the range. Two limits to keep in mind before proceeding, not a preference.

Two limits, and then Go

The general rule is that what is permitted by necessity is limited to what is needed. First, ask if a non-albumin version of the study is available. If a lawful alternative exists and is reasonably available, you should choose that. Second, the dispensation applies only to this study and does not extend beyond it.

If there is no alternative, attend your appointment on 6 August with a heavy heart. Seeking a diagnosis is an act of gratitude for the body Allah has entrusted to you. There is no sin upon you for eating what is needed for your treatment.
references: al-Hawi al-Qudsi, cited in Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar

records.title: Did My Sister Die a Muslim After Weeks in a Coma?
records.question: My sister spent her last days on her adhkar and repeating the shahada, then fell into a coma for over two weeks before she passed away. Will she be considered the same as someone who died having declared the shahada?
records.answer:
Your sister died as a believer, with the words of faith on her tongue. Be at peace about her. May Allah have mercy on her, illuminate her grave, comfort your heart, and unite you with her in His mercy.

Her ending had the very shape the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) taught us to hope for. He said, “Whoever’s last words are: there is no god but Allah, enters Paradise.” [Abu Dawud]

He instructed us to help a dying person reach those words: “Prompt your dying to say: there is no god but Allah” [Muslim]. And he taught a supplication for bedtime that closes, “and make them the last of your speech, for if you die that night, you die upon the primordial faith.” [Muslim]

Your sister’s last conscious speech was her remembrance of Allah and the testimony of faith. She arrived at all those points.

Faith is Affirmed

Nothing that came after touched it. Our jurists put the rule plainly: “A man does not leave faith except by denying that which brought him into it, and what is certainly apostasy is ruled to be so, while what is doubtfully apostasy is not ruled to be so, since Islam once established is not removed by doubt.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

A coma denies nothing. It is not a change of heart; it is a body giving out while the heart stays alive. Those two weeks were not empty.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) taught us that every pain or hardship a believer faces is a means for Allah to forgive their sins. Every day of her coma was a mercy for her in her favor.

So turn now to what still reaches her, because death did not close the whole account. He said, “Now, focus on what can still benefit her. Death does not end all opportunities for good.

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) told us that ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, and the prayers of a righteous child continue to reach the deceased.

Muslim devotes a chapter of his Sahih to the reward of charity on behalf of the deceased reaching him, and the scholars of all four schools hold that a voluntary good deed may be offered on a deceased person’s behalf.

See that her debts are paid and any bequest carried out. And recite as much of the Quran as you can, and make the reward over to her.

Her Last Words Were the Words of Faith

Remember: once faith is established, it is not undone by what happens to the body. Allah judges by what a person was upon, not by what illness may have taken away at the end. Do not worry about those final weeks.

Focus on what benefits her now. Your sister spent her last conscious moments remembering Allah and declaring the testimony of faith. Few are granted such a blessed ending. Your concern for her is a mercy, and she continues to benefit from your prayers and good deeds.

And Allah knows best.

Faraz Rabbani

Related SeekersGuidance answers

Last Words of the Dying — Why we are encouraged to end life with the testimony of faith, how that sits with the Prophet’s own last words, “the Highest Company,” and the story of Imam Abu Zur’a al-Razi, who died mid-sentence while narrating that very hadith.

How Should a Muslim Deal with Chronic Illness? — Long illness met with patience expiates sins, raises a person’s rank, and continues to earn them the reward of the deeds they used to do in health. Useful for a family grieving the weeks that looked like nothing.

Donating Reward to the Dead: A Detailed Answer — Sets out what may be offered on a deceased person’s behalf and on whose authority, from the consensus on charity through to the position of all four schools on reciting the Quran for the dead.

How Do We Deal With the Death of a Loved One? — The inward and outward duties together: patience and submission, then the estate settled after debts, supplication, and the Quran recited and made over, with Imam al-Haddad’s chapter on how the living may help the dead.

records.title: Is It Permissible to Benefit From Private Recordings Released Posthumously?
records.question: A marketing expert gave two days of private, privately recorded consultations; after his death, his sons published the recordings on YouTube, though he was never known to have agreed to this. May I listen to improve my own product?
records.answer:
The responsibility for this matter lies with those who published the recordings, not with you as the listener.

Those sessions were private, and Allah has drawn a veil over what people keep concealed.

He says, “O you who believe: Shun much of suspicion: Verily some suspicion is heinous sin; Nor pry into the private matters of others. Nor speak any of you ill of another behind his back.” [Quran 49:12; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

The commentators read the prohibition of prying as: “do not track the private faults and defects of the Muslims,” and they carry Mujahid’s summary of the ethic, “Take what is apparent, and leave what Allah has concealed.” [al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil]

Imam Baghawi puts the purpose plainly: Allah forbade searching out what is hidden of people’s affairs, and tracking their private faults, “so that what Allah has concealed of it is not exposed.” [al-Baghawi, Ma’alim al-Tanzil]

And the honor of a believer does not end at death.

Private Gatherings Are a Trust

A private gathering is a trust. Imam Ghazali’s ruling is exact: “Divulging a secret is a betrayal. It is forbidden if there is harm in it, and base if there is no harm in it.” [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din]

He carries with it the Prophetic principle that two who sit together do so by the trust of Allah, so neither may disclose what the other would dislike. Al-Hasan al-Basri once turned to his students and said, “You seem to think that betrayal is only in dinars and dirhams.

The worst betrayal is that a man sits with us, and we are at ease with him, and then he goes off and informs on us.” [al-Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin]

The wrongdoing is with those who released and spread the recordings. It does not fall on those who hear them afterward.

For you, keep a clear boundary. Do not seek out what is private or personal in these recordings, such as the man’s clients or their affairs, or anything he would not have wished to be made public.

Seeking out such matters can become backbiting, especially regarding someone who has passed away. If there is a general, beneficial principle of his craft that is already known and public, it is lighter. There is no harm in benefiting from a sound idea itself, even if one does not approve of how it was made available.

There is another matter to consider: who owned these recordings, and what rights the heirs had to share them. This is a question of property and contract, separate from the issue of privacy.

If you intend to use the material for commercial purposes, it is important to seek clarification on this.

Take the Wisdom, Leave the Trespass

The guiding principle is that what Allah has concealed of a person is not for us to uncover. A private gathering is a trust. Benefit from what is beneficial in the craft, but avoid the man’s private matters. Do not repeat or spread what was exposed.

The Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, said, “Whoever conceals the private fault of a believer, it is as though he brought a newborn girl, buried alive, back to life from her grave.” [Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim]

Guard him as you would wish to be guarded, keep a good opinion of him, and make dua for him. Dhu al-Nun said, “The chests of the free are the graves of secrets” [Abu Nu’aym, Hilyat al-Awliya] — and there is honor in being that kind of person, whatever others do.

records.title: Is Making Dua From the Nafs or From Allah?
records.question: Does making supplication originate from the nafs or from Allah? If the underlying need arises from the nafs, must the act of asking come from Allah, or can the act itself also stem from the nafs?
records.answer:
Both are true together, without contradiction.

(1) the supplication is genuinely your own act, and

(2) It is Allah who creates and enables it in you. May Allah reward you for your thoughtful question.

Beginning With Realities of Belief

Begin with the doctrine, because it dissolves the either-or. Allah Most High says: “And none of you shall will, save if Allah wills; Verily was Allah ever all-knowing, all-wise.” [Quran 76:30; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Your will is real and truly yours, but it is not independent of Allah. Imam Khadimi applies this to supplication directly: “Supplication too is from His decree, so the cause stands together with its cause within His decree, for Allah decreed that supplication be a cause that removes.” [Khadimi, Bariqa Mahmudiyya]

From the Human Self (Nafs)

Now, to the part that concerns you. A need arising in the nafs is not a flaw. The self feels hunger, fear, and loneliness. Bringing these needs to Allah is what makes them worship: “whomever Allah employs in supplicating Him has had a door of worship opened to him.” [Abu Talib al-Makki, Qut al-Qulub]

Ibn Ata’illah reads the impulse itself as the first good news: “When He loosens your tongue with the asking, know that He wants to give to you.” [Ibn Ata’illah, al-Hikam]

Imam Zarruq comments, “His enabling you to supplicate is a proof that He wishes to grant you what you asked.”

As for telling the difference, the tradition does not locate it in where the impulse came from, but in what you are asking for and why.

Imam Qushayri gives the criterion: “What the Muslims have a share in, or in which there is a right belonging to the Real, supplicating for it is better… and what As for how to tell the difference, the tradition does not focus on where the impulse comes from, but rather on what you are asking for and why.

Imam Qushayri gives the criterion: “What the Muslims have a share in, or in which there is a right belonging to the Real, supplicating for it is better… and what your own self has a portion in, silence regarding it is more complete” [Qushayri, al-Risala]. What He asks of you.” [al-Hikam]

The Human Self and Beyond

Can it be both at once? That is the ordinary case: a need felt in the self, carried on an ability granted by Allah.

The practical sign is in what the asking does to you. When it is sound, it leaves you more needy before Him, more humble, and content with whatever He decides.

When the nafs dominates, it shows as entitlement or bitterness when the answer is delayed.

For this, Ibn Ata’illah wrote the remedy: “Let not the delay of the gift, despite persistence in supplication, be a cause for your despair; He has guaranteed you an answer in what He chooses for you, not in what you choose for yourself, and at the time He wills, not at the time you will.” [Ibn Ata’illah, al-Hikam].Hikam]

Ask, and Let the Asking Itself be Worship

And when My servants ask you of Me, truly I am near; I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he calls on Me.” [Quran 2:186]

Take comfort in this: the fact that you are turning to Him at all, and troubling yourself over how to turn to Him well, is already His gift to you and not your own doing.

records.title: What Should I Do if I Can No Longer Care for My Cats?
records.question: We have nine cats at home, three of them females who give birth every three months, and the strain on our family has become serious: financially, in terms of space, and in terms of cleanliness. Local animal rescues have not responded.
records.answer:
Your concern is real, and seeking a solution does not mean you lack mercy. You are permitted to rehome your cats, whether by giving them as gifts or by selling them. You may also have them neutered. The Sharia does not require you to keep every cat born in your home.

What is the Sunna with Cats?

Begin where the Sunna begins. Abu Qatada (Allah be pleased with him) tipped his water vessel for a cat to drink, and said that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) had said, “She is not impure. She is only one of those who go about among you.”

Imam Tirmidhi (Allah have mercy on him) grades it rigorously authenticated. [Tirmidhi] Keeping cats, and keeping them well, is a sunna.

They are not yours, though, the way your furniture is yours.

Allah Most High says: وَمَا مِن دَآبَّةٍ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا طَـٰٓئِرٍ يَطِيرُ بِجَنَاحَيْهِ إِلَّآ أُمَمٌ أَمْثَالُكُم “For not a single creature is there on earth, nor any bird flying on its wings, save they are nations like you.” [Quran 6:38; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Imam Qurtubi (Allah have mercy on him) reads the likeness this way: they are communities like you in that Allah created them, took their provision upon Himself, and dealt justly with them, so you should not wrong them, nor go beyond what you have been commanded regarding them. [Qurtubi, al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran]

Both halves bind: they are Allah’s, so you may not wrong them, and your duty stops where the command stops.

The Seriousness of Animal Rights

What the command contains, Imam Khadimi (Allah have mercy on him) sets out in his commentary on Birgivi’s al-Tariqa al-Muhammadiyya. Relating from Qadikhan that an animal’s claim is graver than one man’s against another, he concludes: “So care is binding. It is not killed, nor struck without cause; and with cause, its face is not struck. It is not loaded or ridden beyond its capacity, and its fodder and its water are not left off.” [Khadimi, al-Bariqa al-Mahmudiyya]

Every duty there is a duty of care. None is a duty to keep.

Weigh what the warning actually names.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) told of a woman punished over a cat: “She confined it until it died, and so entered the Fire because of it, for she neither fed it nor gave it water while she held it, nor let it go to eat from the creatures of the earth.” [Bukhari; Muslim]

Holding and starving. Not letting go.

Selling Them Is Permitted by Agreement, and Gifting Is Faster

Imam Ibn Maza (Allah have mercy on him) holds that selling a useful cat is permitted by the agreement of the Hanafi jurists. [Ibn Maza, al-Muhit al-Burhani] A gift is equally sound and usually quicker.

Satisfy yourself that whoever takes one will look after it; once you have handed a cat over in good faith, its care is that person’s trust before Allah, not yours.

Begin by letting people know about your cats. Do not wait for rescues to respond. Share their need for homes in your masjid’s groups and on its noticeboard, in neighborhood and school parent groups, with local vet clinics and pet shops, and on local classified sites.

Speak directly to family, neighbors, and the parents of your children’s friends. Most cats find homes through personal connections. In many places, there are people who want cats, and some may even pay for a healthy one.

Neutering Is Permitted Where It Averts Real Harm

Ibn Maza explains that neutering a cat is permitted when there is a benefit or harm averted. If there is no benefit, it is not allowed. [Ibn Maza, al-Muhit al-Burhani; Qadikhan, Fatawa Qadikhan]

Having nine cats multiplying every three months is exactly the kind of situation the jurists considered. Arrange for the three females to be seen by a qualified vet. This step, along with rehoming, will help bring the cycle to an end.

Mercy to These Cats Includes Mercy to Your Household

You accepted a mercy that has now grown beyond your means. This is not a failure in your religion. The Shariah does not place your family in opposition to kindness to animals; it calls you to both.

Your family has a true right over you, and caring for them is an act of worship. This week, call the vet and share about the cats in at least three places.

Kindness to an animal, as Imam Qurtubi says and Khadimi relates, erases sins and magnifies rewards, and the Prophetic mention of watering an animal extends to every kindness, including feeding. [Khadimi, al-Bariqa al-Mahmudiyya]

Finding each of these cats a home where it will be fed is that kindness, nine times over.

records.title: Is It Permissible to Imagine Fictional Married Characters?
records.question: Is it wrong to imagine married fictional characters, including non-explicit romance or family scenes?
records.answer:
Allah reward you for your sincerity in pleasing Him and avoiding His displeasure. Your daily actions—praying, reading the Quran, supporting family, and trying hard show you don’t want to displease Allah.

It will not be sinful to imagine a fictional storyline in your mind as long as it does not include any explicit romantic nature. Scenes like family life, resolving disagreements, kindness, and emotional ups and downs.

If these fictional stories enter your thoughts in an uncontrolled manner, this is a mechanism your mind is using to cope with your emotions. So as long as you don’t dwell on these imaginative stories sinfully, you will not be held accountable.

An alternative is to read prophetic stories, especially the life of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), companions, followers, righteous, etc, and the lives of other historical figures, then reflect on how they lived, sacrificed, and led fulfilled lives.

Stories of Prophets Provide Comfort

The stories of the Prophets in the Quran provide deep comfort and quiet strength for troubled hearts, featuring timeless accounts.

Allah Most High says, And all We recount to you of the tidings of the messengers is that with which We strengthen your ardent heart. [Quran,11:120]

Abu Hurayra (Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Verily, Allah has pardoned my nation for stray thoughts that occur within them, as long as they do not speak of them or act upon them.” [Bukhari; Muslim]

If you are overwhelmed and your imagination leads you to these fictional stories, do not think Allah is displeased with you, as it is a way you are coping mentally and is allowing you to live your life. He is fully aware.

I pray that Allah Most High grants you ease in your meltdowns, that you no longer have them, and that you come to cope with stories that are wholesome, especially from the lives of the Prophet, the companions, and the righteous of the ummah.

records.title: Is It Disliked to Sit Partly in the Sun and Partly in the Shade?
records.question: Is it disliked to sit in a place where part of the body is in the sun, and part is in the shade?
records.answer:
It is disliked (makruh) to sit partway in the sun and partway in the shade for long periods of time, and the sunna in this case is to move so as to be entirely in one or the other.

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “When one of you is in the shade, and it recedes from him, so that part of him is in the sun and part in the shade, let him get up.” [Abu Dawud]

In another narration, he forbade sitting between the sun and the shade and described it as “the sitting place of Shaytan.” [Ahmad] Imam Haythami declared its narrators reliable.

Scholars mention two reasons for this guidance. First, sitting with your body in both sun and shade can harm your health.

Second, and more importantly, this way of sitting is said to resemble the way Shaytan sits, so believers are advised to avoid it, just as they are told not to eat with the left hand. [See: Ibn Muflih, al-Adab al-Shar’iyya]

This rule is meant for guidance and personal refinement, not because it is sinful. The main idea is that Sacred Law looks after both your body and your heart, even in small matters like how you sit.

So if you notice the shade has moved, and you are now half in the sun and half in the shade, follow the Prophet’s advice: stand up and choose to sit fully in the sun or fully in the shade.

records.title: Is Brown Spotting Menstruation or Istihada in the Shafi‘i School?
records.question: I’m twelve years old. My first period occurred in April, and my last one lasted from the 9th to the 15th of July.
records.answer:
Regarding the spotting which started on 25 July as chronic vaginal bleeding (istihada), and continue both your prayers and your fasting during this time.

Fifteen clean days must occur between one menstruation and the next, and since your last period finished on 15 July, these fifteen days will end on 30 July.

If coloured discharge is still present from 30 July onwards and lasts for at least twenty-four hours, then treat that day as the start of a new menstruation.

The Color and the Amount Are Not What Decide This

The first point to establish is that brown blood is included. The Shafi’i school considers menstrual blood to be of five kinds: black, red, brown, yellow, and dusky. [Bafadl, al-Nabras fi Ahkam al-Hayd wa al-Istihada wa al-Nifas]

Quantity has no influence either, as there is no minimum flow. Any discharge which reaches the outer opening and causes staining is coloured discharge, even if it only fills a pad or merely marks a liner.

The age in question is nine lunar years at the very least, meaning that at twelve, you come within the scope of menstrual regulations. [Nawawi, Minhaj al-Talibin]

Thus, the solution depends on timing.

The Fifteen Clean Days Decide It

The Shafi’i calendar is based on three figures: the shortest period of menstruation is one day and one night, the longest such period is fifteen days beginning from the first day, and the minimum period of purity between two menstruations is fifteen days. [Nawawi, Minhaj al-Talibin]

If you apply them to your dating period, since your period started on 9 July, the fifteen-day maximum period would end on 23 July, and the spotting that occurred on 25 July lies outside this period and so cannot be included in it.

Start counting the period of purity from the moment your menstruation ceased on 15 July. By 25 July, you would have had ten clean days, which is five short of the fifteen clean days needed for a new menstruation to occur.

If blood appears during that period of required purity, this is known as istihada, and the rules applicable to menstruation are suspended until the fifteen clean days have been fulfilled. [Bafadl, al-Nabras fi Ahkam al-Hayd wa al-Istihada wa al-Nifas]

The period ends on 30 July, which is about the same time that your period finished on 15 July. From that moment on, the school’s rules regarding menstruation apply to you: if there is coloured discharge at that time and it lasts for at least twenty-four hours, it counts as a new period and can continue for up to fifteen days from that day; intermittent dryness during those fifteen days does not end it.

Fatima, the daughter of Abi Hubaysh (may Allah be pleased with her), went to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and give him peace), stating that she had bleeding which she could not understand,

And he replied, “This is a vein and not menstruation; therefore, when your menstruation begins, you should omit your prayer, and when it ends, you should wash the blood off yourself and then pray.” [Sahih al-Bukhari]

The Sunna shows us that if bleeding occurs outside the period of menstruation, then the obligation to pray is not removed.

What to Do Between Now and 30 July

Clean the area and replace the liner or pad, or whatever is used to prevent spotting, then when the prayer time begins, perform wudu and pray as soon as possible, and carry out the entire process again each time you have to offer an obligatory prayer. [Ibn Naqib al-Misri, Umdat al-Salik]

A purificatory bath (ghusl) is not required for istihada, and normal fasting continues.

For the coming several months, make a simple written record of your dates, noting the hour at which each period begins and the hour at which it ends. Since your cycle is still settling after three periods, keeping the dates in writing will make it easy to answer any similar questions in the future.

The Governing Principle

Doubt does not remove certainty; you were in a state of purity, and if blood appears within the fifteen days required by Sacred Law for that purity it does not invalidate it; prayer remains obligatory until menstruation has become established according to its own conditions.
references: Bafadl, al-Nabras fi Ahkam al-Hayd wa al-Istihada wa al-Nifas

records.title: How Many Expiations Do I Owe for Broken Oaths I Cannot Count?
records.question: I have taken several oaths before Allah, promising not to listen to music, and have broken those oaths, but I do not remember how many there were. What is my obligation in this case, and is there a separate expiation for each oath?
records.answer:
Such determination is beloved to Allah.

For each oath you are certain you took and then broke, you must offer one expiation (kaffara). Decide on the smallest number that you are sure of, go with that, and ignore all the rest.

Because you have no income, fulfilling your obligation consists of fasting three days for each expiation, and the fasts may be spread out according to your health.

Count Only What You Are Certain Of

The basic principle of the sacred law is that certainty is not lifted by doubt [Suyuti, al-Ashbah wa al-Naza’ir]. Expiation is only required for what you know happened.

Therefore, sit down and fix the smallest number of oaths which you are certain that you made and then broke, and let that number stand. If, for instance, you are certain about two and only suspect a third, then two expiations are owed.

Two other points make the situation clearer. It is sufficient to offer only one expiation when one breaks the same oath repeatedly; a second expiation is only required if a new oath is taken after violating the first one.

And in the case where it is not certain whether a subsequent oath was a new one or merely a repetition of the first for emphasis, it should be regarded as a repetition, since there is doubt about the additional obligation. [Shirbini, Mughni al-Muhtaj]

Fasting Fulfills the Expiation When You Cannot Feed the Poor

Allah Most High says: “Allah will not call you to account for your thoughtless oaths, but He will hold you accountable for deliberate oaths.” [Quran 5:89]

The verse then sets the expiation as feeding ten poor people, clothing them, or freeing a slave, and for the one unable to do so, fasting for three days.

Since you are unable to feed or clothe the poor, your expiation is to fast. In the Shafi’i school, the three days need not be consecutive. [Nawawi, Minhaj al-Talibin]

Since you have recently recovered from tuberculosis, fast only when you are strong enough. The obligation is a debt to Allah, and spreading the fasts over weeks or months is sound.

Close the Book

When you have decided on your number and started the fasts, this matter is concluded before Allah. Should your mind pull you back to recall or imagine forgotten oaths, treat that as a baseless misgiving (waswasa) and ignore it, for the sacred law itself has instructed you that such doubts carry no weight.

You did the right thing in ceasing to take oaths, so hold to that decision, maintain your resolve regarding music through ordinary determination and supplication (du’a), and place your trust in the vastness of Allah’s mercy.

records.title: Is a Woman’s Prayer Valid if the Area Under the Chin Is Uncovered?
records.question: I read that a woman’s face goes down to her jawbone, so the area under the chin is considered ʿawra.
records.answer:
In the Shafi’i school, a woman’s face is considered ʿawra, as is what is normally seen. The skin under the chin, which faces downward, is not part of the face and must be covered during prayer.

If any ʿawra is deliberately left uncovered, the prayer is invalid, but small accidental exposures are excused in the broader tradition. If a woman did not know this area should be covered and prayed for years without covering it, she does not need to repeat those prayers.

From now on, she should cover it. The final judgment for women who were unaware of this is with Allah (Most High), not us.

How the Shafi’i School Defines the Face

For wudu, the face includes the underside of the chin, so it must be washed. For ʿawra, though, the face is only what is normally seen by others: mā tuḥṣil bihi al-muwājaha.

Ibn Hajar al-Haytami defines the face as extending from the usual hairline of the head to the front tip of the two jaws (muntaha al-laḥyayn), and states that the area beneath the front of the jaw does not form part of the face, together with the hair that grows in that lower region. [Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, Tuhfat al-Muhtaj]

Sayyid Ba’lawi al-Hadrami gives the same boundaries in Bushra al-Karim and bases the definition clearly on muwājaha, since the face is what one meets. [Ba’lawi, Bushra al-Karim]

Sayyid Ba Sudan, in Ghayat al-Muna, gives the practical ruling that a woman is required to cover part of her forehead and part of her jaws so that the covering of her head and of the area beneath the chin is fully carried out. [Ba Sudan, Ghayat al-Muna Sharh Safinat al-Naja]

Imam Nawawi holds that the face is what lies between the ordinary hairline of the head and the chin and the end of the two jaws in length, and from ear to ear in width. He records that this is the position of the Shafi’i companions and what Imam al-Shafi’i stipulated in al-Umm. [Nawawi, al-Majmu’]

Allah (Most High) says: “And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and guard their chastity, and not to reveal their adornments except what normally appears…” [Quran 24:31]

The Standard Ruling on Prayer Validity, and Where Ease Enters

Covering the ʿawra is a condition for the validity of prayer [Ibn Naqib al-Misri, ʿUmdat al-Salik / Reliance of the Traveller, f5.2]. The strict Shafi’i position is that intentional exposure of any part of the ʿawra invalidates the prayer, because the ruling attaches to ʿawra as such and does not distinguish small from large in this respect.

The wider tradition offers some flexibility. The Hanbali school and the majority of jurists excuse a small amount of ʿawra exposure that is not grossly obvious to the eye by ordinary custom (al-yasir min al-ʿawra maʿfu ʿanhu).

Ibn Qudama in al-Mughni records this as the position of Imam Ahmad and Abu Hanifa, and cites the practice of ʿAmr ibn Salama as reported by Abu Dawud and al-Nasa’i, where exposure that would ordinarily be noticed did not draw prophetic censure. [Ibn Qudama, al-Mughni]

Ibn Taymiyya adopts the majority position, stating that if a small amount of a woman’s hair or body becomes exposed, she owes no repetition. [Ibn Taymiyya, Majmu’ al-Fatawa]

Ibn ʿAtiyya, in the Maliki school, holds that whatever a woman exposes by the necessary movement of her body and clothes is overlooked. [Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Muharrar al-Wajiz on Quran 24:31]

In the Shafi’i school, if the ʿawra is briefly exposed during the prayer and is immediately covered afterward, the prayer is not considered invalid.

This point was made clear in a previous answer regarding the exposure of the neck while in sujud: what is important here is the immediacy, and the prayer stays valid as long as the covering is resumed without any delay [see: SeekersGuidance, “What Happens If My ʿAwra Is Briefly Exposed During Prayer?” by Shaykh Irshaad Sedick]

When the Exposure Was Out of Genuine Ignorance

A woman who prayed for years without knowing that the area beneath her chin was ʿawra is not required to repeat those prayers.

In the Hanafi tradition, Shaykh Faraz Rabbani reports the reasoning of Shaykh Adib al-Kallas that because this area is small and little of it is generally visible from the sides, its exposure does not invalidate the prayer, and Mufti Mahmoud Ashraf Usmani’s related reasoning that scholars do not press this ruling due to the widespread difficulty of covering it [see: SeekersGuidance, “Is the Area under the Chin from the Nakedness of a Woman?” by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani].

From now on, she should cover this area with an under-scarf or by pinning her khimar to cover the jawline and the area beneath it. Her previous prayers, done without knowing the rule, are valid and do not need to be repeated.

A Word on Your Underlying Concern

You mentioned that seeing pious women leave this area uncovered and worrying about their prayers has caused you a crisis of faith. Remember what the tradition says: a woman who did not know about the rule is not responsible for it.

If she learns about it now, it is a sign that Allah (Most High) is guiding her rather than abandoning her. Only Allah knows the full story of each person, including what they know, what they do not, and what is in their hearts.

Our tradition warns against judging the eternal fate of others. The Sacred Law gives us rules for actions, but not the person’s fate. Allah (Most High) says in the Quran that He forgives anything short of associating partners with Him for whomever He wills. [Quran 4:48]

Your responsibility starts with your own actions. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) told men to lower their gaze from what is not theirs to see. Focusing on what others do right or wrong is not helpful.

Instead, use that concern to improve your own prayer and knowledge, and trust in Allah’s great mercy for everything else.
references: Ba Sudan, Ghayat al-Muna Sharh Safinat al-Naja
Ibn Naqib al-Misri, ʿUmdat al-Salik / Reliance of the Traveller, f5.2
Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Muharrar al-Wajiz on Quran 24:31
see: SeekersGuidance, “What Happens If My ʿAwra Is Briefly Exposed During Prayer?” by Shaykh Irshaad Sedick
see: SeekersGuidance, “Is the Area under the Chin from the Nakedness of a Woman?” by Shaykh Faraz Rabbani

records.title: How Can I Invest in the Stock Market With Confidence It Is Halal?
records.question: I’m trying to build wealth through the stock market in a way I’m confident is halal. I’ve done extensive research, but I feel lost between two scholarly positions.
records.answer:
Investing in the stock market essentially revolves around allowing what would otherwise be impermissible due to necessity. AAOFI permits investing in such companies, while the Fiqh Academy does not. Most contemporary scholars have adopted this view, and I recommend you do the same.

It justifies its opinion based on the shari`a principle of removal of hardship from the public and the principle of absolute need (AAOIFI, 2015). [Revisiting the AAOIFI Shariah Standard’s Stock Screening Criteria]

Scholars agree that, as a matter of principle, it is not permissible to invest in companies with mixed income. They differ as to whether concessions can be made based on qualitative and quantitative filters that would now allow investors to invest in such companies.

AAOIFI permits investing in mixed-income companies, provided the qualitative and quantitative filters are not breached, and that impermissible income is disposed of.

The Shariah Board of the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) has ruled an exception to this prohibition under certain conditions:

a) The amount borrowed on interest should not exceed 30% of the company’s market value.

b) The amount deposited earning interest should not exceed 30% of the company’s market value.

c) The revenue from unlawful transactions, such as interest earned and money received from forbidden sales, should not exceed 5% of the company’s total revenue.

The Fiqh Academy, on the other hand, prohibits participation in joint-stock companies that may sometimes engage in prohibited transactions, such as Riba-based transactions, even though their main activities may be lawful under shari’a. [ https://iifa-aifi.org ]

Allah Most High says, “Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.” [Quran, 2:185] The Prophet (May Allah bless him and grant him peace) said, ‘Make things easy and do not make them difficult. Give glad tidings and do not drive people away’. [Bukhari]

records.title: What Is the Ruling on Trading CFD Forex and Gold ETFs?
records.question: What is the ruling on trading (1) CFD forex and gold, and (2) gold ETFs?
records.answer:
Contracts for differences in forex and gold are impermissible as you do not own the underlying asset. Mutually taking possession of the commodity and its counter-value (taqabud) does not occur in contracts for differences. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Do not sell what you do not own.” [Tirmidhi]

Trading in a physically backed gold ETF is permitted if it represents actual ownership of gold and the possession requirements are met. Otherwise, if it merely provides price exposure through derivatives, such as a CFD, it is not permissible.

For more on the rules of money commodity exchange (sarf) please click here

Direct your trading and investments toward enterprises that participate meaningfully in the real economy. Avoid speculative trading entirely so that your earnings can acquire blessings and prosperity.

records.title: What Is the Ruling on Fulfilling Late Father’s Bequest?
records.question: We face inheritance issues. My brother threatens to stop donations of verbal bequests (wasiyya) from my late father if we disagree. I’ve asked for the list of supported families, but he refuses, saying we should do our own sadaqa.
records.answer:
Yes, this verbal bequest (wasiyya) should continue to be honored by the heirs and family.

Your late father’s bequest was witnessed and known to all. You should all continue from one-third of the inheritance until it is finished. Additionally, beyond this, one should give charity on his behalf to various projects. This is a right you owe him.

Mu’adh ibn Jabal (Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said: “Indeed, Allah has graciously given you one-third of your wealth (to dispose of) at the time of your death as an increase in your good deeds.” [Dar al-Qutni]

Giving Charity on Behalf of Deceased Parents

Abu Huraira (Allah be pleased with him) reported: A man said to the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), “My father has died, and he left behind some property without drafting a will for it. While his sin be expiated if I give charity on his behalf?” The Prophet said, “Yes.”[Muslim]

After paying burial expenses, paying off debts, and fulfilling bequests totaling up to one-third of the estate, the remaining estate will be distributed among the heirs of your deceased father. [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

I suggest you contact a local, reliable scholar for guidance on resolving the family matter.

records.title: Can I Rent My Property to Someone Who Will Commit a Sin There?
records.question: I’m considering renting my property to a non-Muslim woman for three months. She has disclosed in advance that her boyfriend will be staying with her for one week during that period.
records.answer:
It is permissible for you to enter into the rental agreement outlined above. The disclosed week is subsidiary and thus overlooked. Leniency is afforded to subsidiary matters but not to principal ones. [Suyuti, Ashbah] The rule, ‘Leniency is afforded in subsequent stages but not in the initial stage’, potentially applies to your case as well. [See ibid]

This is similar to the sale of land that has been fertilized with manure. Because the manure is both secondary to the land and necessary, its presence is overlooked. [Dimyati, I’ana]

Rest assured. The above does not constitute assisting in sin and transgression. Aim for what is right and strive to hit the mark. Come as close to perfection as you can when exact attainment is beyond one’s ability.

The Prophet (May Allah bless him and give him peace) said, ‘None of you will be saved by his deeds alone. Rather, strive to do what is right and come as close to perfection as you can.’ They asked, ‘Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?’ He replied, ‘Not even me, unless Allah envelops me in His mercy and grace. [Bukhari]

records.title: Is My Repentance Valid If I Cannot Delete the Messages I Sent?
records.question: I fell into grave sin over the past year and created a social media account where I posted vile things. I turned to Allah in repentance and deleted everything I had posted publicly.
records.answer:
You are carrying a heavy fear. I want to reassure you from the start.

Your repentance is valid. It is not waiting for anything else, and it does not depend on deleting those messages.

The Sacred Law does not ask you to do what you cannot. Your repentance was complete when you felt remorse, stopped, and resolved not to return. What remains on a server you cannot reach is not your responsibility.

Allah Accepts Repentance Until the Very Last Breath

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Allah, Mighty and Majestic, accepts the repentance of the servant so long as he has not begun the death-rattle.” [Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan]

This is the vast mercy of Allah Most High. Reflect on this, and find hope.

And Allah Most High says, “Say, ‘O My servants who have committed excesses against their very selves, despair not of the mercy of Allah: Verily Allah forgives all sins soever: Truly He is the All-forgiving, the All-compassionate.’” [Quran 39:53; Keller, The Quran Beheld] All sins are forgiven. The verse leaves no category outside itself, and it was revealed for someone in your position.

He Is Not Reluctant. He Is Delighted

You wrote that you fear your repentance will not be accepted. Consider how the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) described the One you are repenting to: “Allah is more delighted at the repentance of His servant than one of you who, having lost his mount in a barren land, suddenly finds it again.” [Bukhari and Muslim]

Allah is not seeking reasons to turn you away. He has told us, “I am as My servant thinks of Me.” Think well of Him. Thinking well of Allah is itself worship.

Above His Throne is a writing: “My mercy has outstripped My wrath.” [Bukhari and Muslim]

What You Owe, and What You Do Not

You are responsible for what is within your ability. If the platform allows you to appeal, report, or request removal, do so properly and only once. This is what is asked of you.

You are not responsible for what is beyond your reach. Returning to it, or reopening the wound, is neither caution nor piety. Allah has closed this account for you.

And take the good that Take the good that remains before you. Do not dwell on what Allah has already forgiven. The believer’s gaze is not fixed on yesterday’s failure but on today’s opportunity to return to Allah.

Allah Most High says, “O you who believe: Repent to Allah from the utter depths of your conscience.” [Quran 66:8; Keller, The Quran Beheld] And He tells us plainly, “Verily Allah loves the oft-repentant.” [Quran 2:222]

Allah loves you for turning back to Him. Live as someone who has been forgiven, because you have. If the fear returns, let it remind you to say astaghfirullah once, and then do something good. Do not treat it as a verdict to revisit.

records.title: What Is the Fate of One Who Leaves Islam Over Doubts?
records.question: In the case of someone who was sincerely convinced and genuinely believed in Islam, but upon doing more research, is no longer convinced and doubts the religion, and then decides to leave it due to a perceived lack of evidence, does this person enter the Hellfire?
records.answer:
I am going to answer the question you asked, and then question the frame you asked it in — because the frame is doing you more harm than the question.

Truth Is Not a Matter of How Things Strike Us

You have written the question in the language of perception: what seems evident, what one is convinced by, what one finds persuasive. But the truth is not settled by impression. Truth is knowable, and it is established.

This is the very first thing our theologians say. Imam Nasafi opens his creed with it: “The people of truth hold that the realities of things are established, and knowledge of them is attainable — contrary to the Sophists.” [Nasafi, al-Aqaid al-Nasafiyya]

He begins there deliberately. Before a single article of belief can be stated, it must be settled that things are what they are and that we can know them. A religion cannot be built on impressions, and neither can a rejection of one.

There Is Evidence, and It Is Available to You

So the honest question is not whether you feel convinced. It is whether the evidence is there.

It is. That the world is originated and that what is originated requires an originator is a demonstrative argument, set out by the theologians of this community in careful detail.

That Muhammad (Allah bless him and give him peace) is the Messenger of Allah rests on evidence of its own kind, examined and transmitted across centuries by people who tested it far more rigorously than a season of reading allows.

None of this is hidden. It is written down, taught, and available to you.

Your Two Cases Are Not the Same

Take them apart, because they part company at the decisive point.

The first describes a conviction that has gone. The second describes conviction present at the level of probability, with assent withheld anyway — a man who grants that Islam is likelier true than its alternatives and declines to affirm it.

The second is the harder case, and it is the one you have described most precisely. If a man judges something likelier true and still withholds assent, what is holding him back is not the evidence.

On the Ruling You Are Asking About

Punishment in the next life attaches to rejection after recognition, not to the honest inability of one who has not been shown. But you are not in that position. You have been shown, and you are still asking — which means the door is not closed, and what is now owed is to look properly rather than to conclude early.

I will not pronounce on your state, and you should be wary of anyone who would. That is with Allah.

The Call That Is Being Made to You

Allah Most High says: “O you who believe: wholeheartedly answer Allah and the Messenger when he summons you to what brings you to life.” [Quran 8:24; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Notice what the summons is toward. Not toward a conclusion — toward life. Ibn Ajiba comments that what gives life here is the knowledge of the religion, “for it is the life of the heart, just as ignorance is its death.” [Ibn Ajiba, al-Bahr al-Madid]

And in the inward sense of the verse he writes that in every age Allah has appointed callers who summon people to what their hearts live by, so that they may be fit to enter the presence of the One they love.

Whoever answers them and keeps their company, his heart lives; whoever turns away from them, his spirit dies “in the valleys of stray thoughts and imaginings.” [Ibn Ajiba, al-Bahr al-Madid]

That is a precise description of where doubt goes when it is carried alone.

What I Would Ask of You

Do not settle this by yourself, from reading. Sit with someone who knows the proofs and can take your objections seriously — not to be talked out of anything, but to be shown what you have not yet been shown.

You are asking the right question. Ask it of someone who can answer it properly, and give the answer a fair hearing.

records.title: What Does the Hadith “A Disbeliever and the One Who Killed Him Will Never Be Gathered in the Fire” Mean?
records.question: I came across a hadith which says, “An infidel and the one who killed him will never be brought together in Hell,” and I wanted to ask what it means. Is it speaking about an innocent non-Muslim, or about combatants?
records.answer:
It speaks about a combatant killed in a lawful engagement. It is a statement of reward for the soldier, not a license against anyone else.

The Wording and Where It Sits

Sayyiduna Abu Hurayra (Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “A disbeliever and the one who killed him will never be gathered together in the Fire.” [Muslim]

You had come across it as Abu Dawud 2495, and it is indeed there in his Book of Jihad, under a chapter on the merit of one who killed a combatant. Its strongest attribution, though, is to Sahih Muslim.

What the Commentators Say It Means

The commentary tradition treats the meaning as settled. Qadi Iyad holds that the report concerns one who killed a combatant while fighting an enemy, and that the meaning is that this expiates his sins so that he is not punished for them.

Mulla Ali al-Qari follows him and adds the grammatical point. What is denied is that the two be gathered together; from that follows the denial that they are equal; and from that follows that the soldier does not enter the Fire at all, for were he to enter it, he would be his equal. [Mulla Ali al-Qari, Mirqat al-Mafatih]

So the hadith is praising the fighter. It says nothing whatever about who may be fought.

Who Is Meant by “Disbeliever” Here

The commentators restrict the word, and they do so plainly. It means one at war — not a person under treaty, not a protected non-Muslim, not a civilian. Shaykh Khalil Ahmad Saharanpuri glosses the chapter heading with a single phrase: one not under covenant. [Saharanpuri, Badhl al-Majhud]

This restriction is not a modern softening. It is how the hadith has always been read, and it is why the same tradition holds by agreement that non-combatants may not be killed — women, children, the aged, the monk in his cell.

How to Read Reports of This Kind

A report that promises reward for a lawful act does not license that act in another setting. The permission itself comes from the law of war, with its conditions, its authority, and its restraints. This hadith speaks only to the state of a man who has already acted within it.

If you have seen it used to argue otherwise, you have seen it read backward. Your instinct to ask was the right one, and the answer should settle rather than trouble you.

records.title: How Do I Make Up Seven Years of Missed Prayers?
records.question: I spent about seven years not praying, or praying without meaning it. I am a Muslim, and I want to repent. If I start praying now, do I have to pray all seven years of missed prayers, or can God forgive me?
records.answer:
Read this first, before anything else: Allah has already turned to you. The wanting you are feeling is not you reaching for Him. It is Him reaching for you.

You asked two questions in one breath, and I want to separate them, because you are hearing them as one thing, and they are not.

Can Allah forgive you? Yes. Completely, and already, the moment you turned.

Do you make up the prayers? Yes. And that is not a refusal of the forgiveness. It is what forgiven people do.

He Has Forgiven You

Allah Most High says, “Whoever commits an ill deed or wrongs himself, then even at length asks forgiveness of Allah while there is still time, shall find Allah all-forgiving, all-compassionate” [Quran 4:110; Keller, The Quran Beheld]. Note the words “even at length.” Seven years is inside that.

And He says, “And verily I am ever-forgiving to whoever repents and believes and works righteousness, then ever after remains firmly guided” [Quran 20:82; Keller, The Quran Beheld].

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) reported that Allah Most High says, “O son of Adam, so long as you call upon Me and place your hope in Me, I forgive you for what is in you, and I do not mind.

O son of Adam, were your sins to reach the clouds of the sky and then you sought My forgiveness, I would forgive you and not mind.” [Mishkat al-Masabih, no. 2336]

And he said, “Allah extends His hand by night that the wrongdoer of the day may repent, and extends His hand by day that the wrongdoer of the night may repent — until the sun rises from its place of setting.” [Riyad al-Salihin, no. 16; Muslim] That hand has been out for all seven of your years. It is out now.

And he said, “By the One in Whose hand is my soul — if you were not to sin, Allah Most High would take you away and bring a people who sin and then seek His forgiveness, and He would forgive them.” [Riyad al-Salihin, no. 1871; Muslim]

You are not an exception to His mercy. You are the reason it was described.

“Every son of Adam is prone to error, and the best of those who err are the oft-repentant” [Mishkat al-Masabih, no. 2341; Tirmidhi, Ibn Maja and Darimi, graded good].

Your Repentance Is Not Waiting on a Verdict

You asked whether God can forgive you, as though the answer were still being decided somewhere.

Imam Ghazali settles that. Where repentance meets its conditions, he writes, it is accepted without question — and then, with characteristic bluntness, “one who imagines that repentance can be sound and yet not accepted is like one who imagines that the sun rises and the darkness does not lift.” [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, with Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin]

And there is a story he relates that I want you to have. A young man among the Children of Israel worshipped Allah for twenty years, then disobeyed Him for twenty years. One day, he looked in a mirror, saw grey in his beard, and was grieved.

He said, “My Lord, I obeyed You twenty years, then disobeyed You twenty years. If I return to You, will You accept me?” And he heard a voice, seeing no one: “You loved Us, and We loved you. You left us, and we left you. You disobeyed Us, and We gave you respite. And if you return to Us, We will accept you” [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, with Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin].

Twenty years. And the respite was itself the mercy, not the absence of it.

Do Not Let the Size of It Stop You

Imam Qushayri writes that repentance “is the first station of the wayfarers and the first stage of the seekers” [Qushayri, al-Risala al-Qushayriyya]. His glossator adds that it is “like the ground is to a building — whoever has no ground has no building.” [Arusi, Nata’ij al-Afkar al-Qudsiyya]

You are not behind. You are standing exactly where every traveler starts.

And there is a line in that same commentary I want you to hold: “Five things in a sin are graver than the sin — making light of it, persisting in it, flaunting it, being emboldened by it, and despairing of its forgiveness.” [Arusi, Nata’ij al-Afkar al-Qudsiyya]

Of those five, only the last one is still available to you. Do not take it.

Ibn Ata’illah put it this way: “If a sin occurs from you, let it not be a cause of your despairing of uprightness with your Lord, for it may well be the last sin decreed for you.” [Ibn Ata’illah, al-Hikam, no. 148]

Ibn Abbad al-Rundi explains that what contradicts uprightness is not the lapse but the persisting in it [Ibn Abbad al-Rundi, Ghayth al-Mawahib al-Aliyya]. You have stopped persisting. That is the whole difference.

And he wrote: “Among the signs of success at the end is turning back to Allah at the beginning” [Ibn Ata’illah, al-Hikam, no. 26].

Now the Make-Up

You follow the Shafi’i school, and its position is that the missed prayers are made up. All four schools hold this.

The school itself understands this as a mercy, for two reasons worth knowing. It does not treat a person who left prayer through laziness as having left Islam for those years. And it gives you a definite way to repair what happened, rather than leaving you with a debt and no means of paying it.

Our answer here sets that out: How to Make up Years of Missed Prayers? (Shafi’i), by Shaykh Shuaib Ally.

So hear it as it is meant. You are not being told that forgiveness is withheld until you finish. You are being handed a way back.

A Schedule You Can Actually Keep

Do not calculate the total and stare at it. That number stops people, and it has no religious function.

Start here instead. Pray today’s five prayers on time. Then add one make-up prayer alongside each of them. That is five today’s and five made up, ten prayers, and it is not a hard day. Keep that for a few weeks until it feels ordinary, then add a second if you can.

“The most beloved of deeds to Allah is the most constant of them, even if little.” [Bukhari and Muslim]

And the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Be upright, though you will not be able to encompass it; and know that the best of your deeds is the prayer.” [Malik, Ahmad, Ibn Maja and Darimi] He is telling you that you will not manage it perfectly and to go on anyway.

He also taught, “Make things easy and do not make them hard; give glad tidings and do not drive people away” [Bukhari and Muslim]. If that is how we are told to treat others, do not treat yourself the opposite way.

If you keep to a schedule you can sustain, and Allah takes you before you finish, you go to Him as a man who was praying and repairing. Do not be afraid of that.

You Do Not Need an Exact Number

You will not be able to reconstruct seven years, and you are not required to.

Imam Ghazali gives the method. One looks back over the years since reaching puberty, and “if he is uncertain of the number of prayers he has missed, he reckons from the time of his coming of age, sets aside the amount he is certain he performed, and makes up the rest — and he may proceed in this on the preponderant opinion he arrives at by careful estimation and diligence.” [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, with Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin]

Estimate honestly, round upward a little to be safe, and then stop counting and start praying.

One Thing to Check

You wrote “fake praying,” and I am not sure what you mean. If you were praying but without concentration, those prayers count and are not made up. If you were going through the motions without wudu, or without intending prayer at all, those are made up.

Write back and tell me, and I will tell you exactly which years you are counting.

And About Your Family

You mentioned losing them almost in passing, and I do not think it was a small thing. Whatever the door back to them looks like, ask Allah for it in your prostration. That is where the asking belongs, and He is nearer to you now than He has been in years.

Begin Tonight

Allah Most High says, “And keep well the prayer at the open and close of day, and first reaches of the night: Verily good deeds do away with ill deeds” [Quran 11:114; Keller, The Quran Beheld].

Read that closely. It is a verse about prayer, and the promise attached to it is that the good will wear away the bad. The very thing you are afraid of owing is the thing that clears the account.

Do not wait for the next Ramadan, or for a better week, or for the feeling to be stronger. Pray the next prayer that comes. Then the one after it. That is the whole of it.
references: Tirmidhi, Ibn Maja and Darimi, graded good
Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, with Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin
Ibn Abbad al-Rundi, Ghayth al-Mawahib al-Aliyya
Malik, Ahmad, Ibn Maja and Darimi

records.title: How Do I Revive a Heart That Feels Spiritually Numb?
records.question: This is not me saying I am depressed or apathetic in the sense of illness, but rather asking with the intention to perfect my own character.
records.answer:
What you are describing is not a fault. It has a name in this tradition, and the people who mapped it thought it was often the better of the two states.

Here is the reassurance first, because it is the answer and not a preface to it: worship carried out without sweetness is frequently weightier than worship carried by feeling. When the sweetness is there, something in you is being fed.

When it is gone and you pray anyway, nothing is holding you up but obedience — and that is precisely what servanthood means.

The States Have Names

What you are calling fire and its absence, the masters of this path call bast and qabd — expansion and contraction. They are neither achievements nor failures. They are visitations, and they alternate.

Imam Qushayri places them carefully. Fear and hope look to what is to come, while contraction and expansion concern something present in the moment: the one who fears and hopes has his heart attached to what lies ahead, while the one in contraction or expansion is seized by his moment.

And he adds that these two are states that come after the servant has risen beyond fear and hope — contraction standing to the knower as fear stands to the beginner, and expansion as hope does. [Qushayri, al-Risala al-Qushayriyya]

Read that again, because it bears directly on you. On this reckoning, what you are experiencing may not be a fall from a higher state at all. It may be the mark of having moved past the beginner’s register.

Why the Darker State May Be the Richer One

Ibn Ata’illah writes: “He expanded you so as not to leave you in contraction, and contracted you so as not to leave you in expansion, and took you out of both so that you would not belong to anything besides Him.” [Ibn Ata’illah, al-Hikam]

Both states are His doing, and neither is where you are meant to settle. Then, more directly still: “Perhaps He has given you in the night of contraction what you did not receive in the daylight of expansion.” [Ibn Ata’illah, al-Hikam]

The commentators press the point. Ibn Abbad al-Rundi notes that the knowers actually prefer contraction, because in it the lower self takes no share; what is there instead is brokenness, lowliness, and need before the Lord of the Worlds.

In expansion, he warns, the self takes its portion by way of delight. [Ibn Abbad al-Rundi, Ghayth al-Mawahib al-Aliyya]

He quotes al-Wasiti more bluntly: “Finding acts of obedience sweet is a killing poison.” [Ibn Abbad al-Rundi, Ghayth al-Mawahib al-Aliyya] The meaning is not that sweetness is bad. It is a man who worships for the taste of it, who has already been paid.

Your Heart Is Not Yours to Steady

There is a mercy here that is easy to miss. The state is not in your hands, and it was never meant to be.

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “The hearts of all the children of Adam are between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful, like a single heart; He turns it however He wills.” [Mishkat al-Masabih, no. 89; Muslim]

And he — who did not need it — asked constantly. Umm Salama (Allah be pleased with her) was asked what supplication he made most often when he was with her, and she said it was: “O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion.” [Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan]

If he asked, the asking is the practice. Make that supplication your own.

What to Actually Do

Do not chase the feeling. Chasing it is how people end up performing a state rather than living one.

Keep the practice steady and small. The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “The most beloved of deeds to Allah is the most constant of them, even if little.” [Bukhari and Muslim] Constancy is what is being asked of you. Intensity was never the standard.

And keep going in the dry season without grading yourself. You wrote that a believer becomes firm and then slackens after a month or two. That is not a special weakness in you. It is the shape of the road, and the ones who arrive are simply the ones who kept walking on the days it gave them nothing.
references: Ibn Abbad al-Rundi, Ghayth al-Mawahib al-Aliyya

records.title: What Is the Ruling on Faith Motivated by Fear?
records.question: What is the Islamic stance on Pascal’s Wager? If somebody truly believes in the religion out of fear of Hell, are they really considered a believer?
records.answer:
You have asked two important questions. Let us look at each one separately.

Let us begin with the second question, as it brings reassurance. Yes, someone who believes out of fear of Hell is a believer. Faith is what the heart affirms, regardless of the feelings that may come with it.

The first question needs some explanation, as Pascal’s Wager is often misunderstood.

What Pascal Actually Argued

Pascal held that reason cannot settle whether God exists, so he treated the matter as a bet no one can decline. If God exists, wagering for God gains an infinite reward against a finite stake, and the bet is therefore worth making at any probability above zero.

The decisive point is what he was not arguing. Set against Anselm, Aquinas, and Descartes, whose arguments “purport to prove that God exists,” the Stanford Encyclopedia notes: “Pascal’s project, then, is radically different.

He aims to show that we ought to believe in God, rather than that God exists. And he seeks to provide prudential reasons rather than evidential reasons for believing in God.” [Hajek, “Pascal’s Wager,” Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]

Pascal’s Wager is about whether it is rational to believe, not about whether belief is true. This is an important distinction.

Why a Bet Is Not Faith

Faith, in our tradition, is the heart’s confirmation (tasdiq) of what the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) brought from Allah.

Imam Bajuri defines it as the confirmation to all that the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) brought that is necessarily known of the religion, and he is careful about what that assent means: acceptance and submission, not the bare notion that he spoke truly held without acceptance.

Otherwise, he notes, we would have to call believers those who knew the truth of his prophethood and rejected it out of obstinacy. [Bajuri, Tuhfat al-Murid]

The Maturidi imams say the same. Abu al-Muin al-Nasafi holds that faith is tasdiq, that this confirmation of the heart is the reality of the faith owed to Allah, and that the tongue’s affirmation is what lets the rulings of Islam run upon a person among people. [Abu al-Muin al-Nasafi, Tabsirat al-Adilla]
