“and let not utter hatred for a people make you unjust.” [Quran 5:8; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

records.title: How Much Recitation Is Required for a Valid Prayer?
records.question: Is the obligatory (fard) and minimum recitation for a prayer to be valid — in all prayers, whether fard, wajib, such as witr, sunna, or nafl — only reciting the first verse of Surat al-Fatiha, or one short verse of any surah, in all rakats?
records.answer:
One verse in two rakats makes a fard prayer valid; the full Fatiha with a sura is what it owes. That comes first, or the answer will mislead you.

You have asked about “the obligatory and minimum recitation” as though they were one and the same.

In our school they are two.

There is what makes the prayer valid, the fard, and there is what the prayer owes, the wajib.

A prayer can be valid and still be defective, and sinful to have prayed that way deliberately. Almost all confusion in this area stems from conflating the two.

So let me give you both.

The Fard: One Verse, and Not in Every Rakat

Recitation is one of the four pillars of the prayer. Imam Shurunbulali lists them: “The pillars among what has been mentioned are four: standing, recitation, bowing, and prostration.” [Shurunbulali, Nur al-Idah]

Its obligatory measure is small. The matn says simply: “even a single verse.” [Shurunbulali, Nur al-Idah] The gloss specifies how small: “meaning even if he recites a short verse composed of two words (such as His saying, ‘Then he looked’), according to the apparent narration.” [Iazaz Ali, Hashiyat al-Isbah ala Nur al-Idah]

And here is the part your question misses. The fard is not in every rakat. It is: “in two rakats of the fard prayer, and in all of the nafl and the witr.” [Shurunbulali, Nur al-Idah] Allama Ala al-Din Abidin states it with the measure attached: “and recitation while standing … for one able to do it, in two rakats of the fard prayer, and in all the rakats of the nafl and the witr; and that is the measure of one verse of the Quran.” [Ala al-Din Abidin, al-Hadiyya al-Alaiyya]

So, on the fard alone: one verse in two rakats of an obligatory prayer, and one verse in every rakat of witr, sunna, and nafl. In the last two rakats of a four-unit fard, no recitation is obligatory at all.

The Wajib: The Whole Fatiha, and a Sura With It

Now what the prayer owes, which is what you should actually be reciting.

Imam Shurunbulali lists among the eighteen necessary acts: “reciting al-Fatiha; and joining a sura or three verses to it, in two non-specified rakats of the fard prayer, and in all the rakats of the witr and the nafl; and specifying the recitation in the first two; and putting al-Fatiha before the sura.” [Shurunbulali, Nur al-Idah]

Ala al-Din Abidin gives the same with the measures: “reciting al-Fatiha in its entirety … and joining a short sura to al-Fatiha, or three short verses, or a verse equal in length to three, in two non-specified rakats of the four-unit and three-unit fard prayers, and in all the rakats of the witr and the nafl; and specifying the recitation in the first two of the fard prayer.” [Ala al-Din Abidin, al-Hadiyya al-Alaiyya]

Three short verses is roughly thirty letters: “meaning short ones, such as ‘Then he looked. Then he frowned and scowled. Then he turned away and grew arrogant’; and that is thirty letters. So if he recites one long verse of thirty letters, he has performed the necessary act.” [Iazaz Ali, Hashiyat al-Isbah]

So, in practice:

Fard prayers: Fatiha in full plus a sura in the first two rakats. Fatiha alone in the last one or two, which is sunna rather than necessary.

Witr, sunna, and nafl: Fatiha in full plus a sura in every rakat.

What This Means If You Recite Only One Verse

If a person prayed a fard prayer reciting only a single short verse, the prayer would be valid (the pillar was performed), but a necessary act would have been abandoned. Done forgetfully, that calls for the forgetfulness prostration. Done deliberately, the prayer is sinful and must be repeated.

So the answer to your question, as you asked it, is no. One verse is the floor beneath which the prayer collapses. It is not the standard you may aim at.

There is one genuine exception, and it is worth knowing: “the obligation of this and what precedes it is conditional upon there being time.

If he fears the time will pass where he has to recite al-Fatiha and the surah, or al-Fatiha, or more than a verse, he recites one verse in each rakat throughout the prayer.” [Tahtawi, Hashiya ala Maraqi al-Falah] In genuine time pressure, the necessary acts fall away, and the fard alone remains.

The Two Sittings

Here, the fard and the wajib separate again, and along a different line from the recitation.

The final sitting is itself a pillar: the sitting, not the words. Imam Shurunbulali lists among the obligatory acts: “and the final sitting, for the length of the tashahhud” [Shurunbulali, Nur al-Idah]

And the commentators specify the measure as the shortest time in which the tashahhud can be recited up to “His servant and His Messenger.” So what is obligatory is that you sit for that long. If you sat in silence that long, the prayer would still be valid.

Reciting the tashahhud is necessary, not obligatory, and it is necessary in both sittings. Among the necessary acts: “and the first sitting, and reciting the tashahhud in it according to the sound position, and reciting it in the final sitting.” [Shurunbulali, Nur al-Idah]

The commentator adds the useful generalization: “perhaps the author did not use the dual and say ‘the two tashahhuds’ in order to indicate that every tashahhud in the prayer is necessary, whether there are two or more.” [Iazaz Ali, Hashiyat al-Isbah, from Maraqi al-Falah and Tahtawi]

So, sitting at the end of the prayer is a pillar. Reciting the tashahhud is necessary in every sitting of the prayer, which, for a latecomer, completing three missed rakats of a four-unit prayer can be three sittings.

The first sitting is itself necessary, not obligatory. That is why omitting it forgetfully is repaired by the forgetfulness prostration, whereas omitting the final sitting invalidates the prayer outright.

Valid Is Not the Same as Owed

Valid: one verse, in two rakats of the fard; one verse in every rakat of witr, sunna, and nafl; and sitting at the end for the length of the tashahhud.

Owed: the full Fatiha and a sura in the first two rakats of the fard and in every rakat of witr, sunna, and nafl; the tashahhud recited in every sitting; and the first sitting itself.

Aim at the second. The first is a floor for emergencies, not a target.
references: Iazaz Ali, Hashiyat al-Isbah ala Nur al-Idah
Iazaz Ali, Hashiyat al-Isbah, from Maraqi al-Falah and Tahtawi

records.title: Is the Hanafi Ruling Different From the Shafi‘i Ruling on Purity?
records.question: Over the years, my purity period has shortened to 12-15 days, but my period occurs with normal symptoms. It has been consistent for months, so it’s not istihada.
records.answer:
It can be unsettling if one’s menstrual cycle shifts around like this.

If one sees blood during the 15-day purity (tuhr) period. You will revert to your regular cycle, and only the blood that comes within the cycle is your menstrual blood; the other bleeding within the 15-day period is considered irregular bleeding, during which you must pray and fast as normal.

The minimum period of purity (tuhr) is fifteen days, because it has been reported from the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) that he said: “The minimum duration of menstruation is three days, its maximum is ten days, and the minimum period between two menstrual cycles is fifteen days.” [Ibn al-Jawzi, al-’Ilal al-Mutanahiya]

This is how it is mentioned in al-Ghayah. The Companions unanimously agreed upon this ruling. Since it is a legally fixed period, it is treated as the minimum period required to establish residence (iqama). [Zayla‘i, Tabyin al-Haqa’iq]

Advice

Every woman must record her menses, lochia, and purity habits. The date and time any vaginal blood begins, including the spotting of blood, and the date and time any vaginal blood ends.

I advise contacting a local, reliable female scholar who is well-versed in matters of menstruation. Also, try to attend any on-the-ground and online courses on menstruation. Also, at your earliest convenience, buy books related to the topic; some are linked below.

records.title: How Should a Convert With No Muslim Family Write a Will?
records.question: I am an unmarried convert with no Muslim family — two sisters, a brother, and two parents, all living.
records.answer:
Most people do not, and their families pay for it.

Your plan is close to right, and the correction I have is in your favor rather than against you. Let me set out the pieces in order.

First: Your Family is Not Your Heirs

This is the premise on which everything else rests, and you may not know it.

A Muslim and a non-Muslim do not inherit from one another. This is agreed upon across the four schools. So the fixed shares of the inheritance law (the portions a father, a brother, a sister would ordinarily take) do not attach to your estate at all.

Your family does not stand to inherit from you by operation of the Law.

That sounds like a door closing. It is actually a door opening, as you will see.

Second: A Bequest to Them Is Perfectly Valid

Not inheriting is not the same as not receiving. A bequest is a different instrument from inheritance, and a non-Muslim relative may receive a bequest without difficulty.

In fact, the restriction that trips most people up runs the other way.

The rule is that there is no bequest to an heir: you cannot use a will to enlarge the share of someone who already inherits. Since your family is not an heir, that rule does not apply to them. How much you may leave them is the next question.

Third: The One-Third Limit, and Why It May Not Bind You

This is where I would have you revisit your plan.

The one-third cap exists for a reason: it protects the heirs. A person may not give away so much by will that the shares Allah fixed are hollowed out. That is the whole logic of the limit.

Now ask what it is protecting in your case. You have no Muslim heirs. There are no fixed shares to preserve. The thing the cap was built to guard does not exist in your estate.

This is why I would not have you simply assume the one-third and stop there.

Where a person leaves no heirs at all, there is a real discussion in our books about whether the cap binds, and a well-supported position that the whole estate may be disposed of by bequest.

Given that your entire plan turns on this, settle it with a specialist who can look at your actual circumstances, your jurisdiction, and whether any Muslim relative might exist or come to exist.

What I can say now is this: your instinct to give two-thirds to charity is sound and rewarded, and you may well have more latitude than you thought.

Fourth: Yes, Your Possessions Count

Your second question has a clear answer: the opposite of what you assumed.

Everything you own of value is part of your estate. Electronics, furniture, clothing, a car, a bank balance, a debt owed to you: all of it. There is no category of “possessions” that sits outside the estate and can be left to a family’s discretion.

That does not mean you must itemize and value every shirt. What it means practically is:

Name the significant items specifically in the will: the things of real value, and the things that would cause an argument.

For the rest, ask your lawyer for a residuary clause: whatever remains after debts, funeral expenses, and the named bequests goes to such-and-such. That disposes of the estate without inventorying a wardrobe.

Fifth: Order of Payment

Your order is correct and worth confirming, since you got it right unaided. From the estate: funeral and burial expenses first, then debts in full, then bequests, then whatever remains passes by inheritance, which in your case is the question above.

What I Would Have You Do

Three things.

Write to us again with your country of residence and confirmation that you have no Muslim relatives at all, and ask about the one-third limit where there are no heirs. That is the live question and it deserves a ruling on your own facts rather than a general answer.

Have the will drafted properly under your local law. A fiqh-correct will that is not enforceable where you live will do nothing for anyone. Many communities have lawyers who do exactly this work.

And put a Muslim executor in it if you can: someone who will see that your funeral is done as it should be, and that what you intended actually happens. This matters more than people realize for a convert with no Muslim family, and it is the single provision I would most want you to include.

“Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt.” [Sunan al-Tirmidhi; sound] You have done the doubting part well. Now let us settle it properly.

records.title: What Should I Do if My Husband Insults My Appearance?
records.question: We married only three months ago, and for all three months, I have heard from him that I am old, ugly, and do not meet his expectations.
records.answer:
I am sorry. Three months into a marriage, you should be settling into someone’s kindness, and instead, you are being told daily that you are not enough. That is a real hurt, and I do not want to move past it quickly.

Let me answer plainly, then the harder part underneath.

Yes, You Are Right: This Is Unjust

You asked whether it is unjust to blame you for what he knew before he married you. It is. You are not mistaken, and you are not being oversensitive.

He saw your age. He saw your face. He chose. To choose with open eyes and then reproach you for what he chose is a wrong done to you, and no amount of framing it as disappointment makes it something else.

And the manner of it is its own wrong, separate from the substance. Allah commands: “But rather live with them graciously and reasonably; If you merely dislike them, you may well dislike something, and Allah make tremendous good in it.” [Quran 4:19; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Read the second half. The verse anticipates a husband who does not feel what he hoped to feel, and its instruction to him is not to say so daily. It is to live well with her and leave room for Allah to put good in what he did not choose warmly.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said the same thing in the language of the heart: “Let no believing man hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one of her traits, he will be pleased with another.” [Sahih Muslim]

The instruction is to look for the other trait, not to itemize the first.

And: “The best of you is the one who is best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family.” [Sunan al-Tirmidhi and Sunan al-Darimi; sound] That is the standard he is being measured against, and he is not near it.

About the Things He Reproaches You For

I want to take these one at a time, because if they are left standing, they will keep working on you.

You began wearing hijab two years ago. That is not a defect. It is a person turning toward Allah, exactly what he says he married you for. To reproach someone for the date they began obeying Allah is to reproach them for having a beginning, and every one of us has one.

Your umra without a mahram. Whatever the ruling on the travel (and the schools differ, with real scholarly latitude on a woman traveling in a safe, organized group), it was done, it is past, and it is between you and Allah.

A husband is not an auditor of his wife’s life before him.

Allah says: “Shun much of suspicion: Verily some suspicion is heinous sin; Nor pry into the private matters of others.” [Quran 49:12; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Raking over a spouse’s past is prying, and using it as a weapon in an argument is worse than prying.

He said he married you for your religion and now says it is not enough. Notice what that sentence actually admits: he got what he asked for. That is not a failure on your side.

On What to Do

Here I will not decide for you, because I should not and because you are better placed than I am.

What I can do is name what is true, so that whatever you choose, you choose it clearly.

You are not obliged to accept being demeaned. A woman has rights in marriage that are real and enforceable, and kind treatment is among them. Allah says: “And women possess rights like those they are bound to fulfill, in lawful fairness.” [Quran 2:228; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Three months is early, and early is not the same as hopeless. Some men enter marriage carrying an expectation formed by images rather than by people, and that expectation can break and be replaced by something truer. That does happen. It happens more often when it is named than when it is endured in silence.

And staying is not the only form of piety. Where a marriage is causing real harm and does not change, a woman may seek release, and the Law provides for it. Choosing that is not a failure of patience.

What I Would Have You Do Next

Four things, in order.

Tell him plainly, once, calmly, and outside an argument: this is hurting me, and I need it to stop. Not a plea and not a fight: a statement. Many men do not realize the weight of what they say until it is said back to them.

Bring in someone he respects. His family is the reason he says he will not divorce, so they can move him. An older relative, an imam, a couple you both trust.

Allah has told us to do exactly this: “And should you fear a rift between man and wife, send an arbiter from his kin and an arbiter from hers; And if both truly desire to settle between the couple, Allah will restore harmony between them.” [Quran 4:35; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Give it a defined period, not an open one. Say to yourself: six months, with real effort on both sides, and then I will look again honestly. Open-ended endurance with no review is how people lose years.

And do not carry this alone. Speak with someone regularly: a teacher, a counsellor, a woman of religion you trust. Our Office Hours exist for exactly this, and I would encourage you to book:

Your Worth Is Not His to Set

Do not let him tell you what you are worth. He is describing his expectations, not your value. Allah made you, and He did not make a mistake.

“And of His truly wondrous signs is having created for you, from your own kind, wives to repose in solace to, and made between you tender love and mercy.” [Quran 30:21; Keller, The Quran Beheld] Solace, tenderness, mercy. That is what a marriage is for. Ask for it. You are entitled to ask.

May Allah soften his heart, give you clarity, and grant you a home you are at rest in.
references: Sunan al-Tirmidhi and Sunan al-Darimi; sound

records.title: How Do I Navigate Foods that Contain Aromas Extracted from Alcohol?
records.question: I live in France, and 98% of products contain aromas, which are usually extracted with alcohol (with tiny traces remaining that are undetectable when consumed) or with glycerin, which can be animal- or plant-based. Unspecified ingredients might also come from animals or plants.
records.answer:
Alcohol and its derivatives are widely used in the food industry as ingredients, not as intoxicants, so their use is permitted.

Alcohol is used in global food manufacturing industries. It is found in medicines, food flavorings, aromas, preservatives, and solvents. This is a case of difficulty and widespread predicament (umum al-balwa) across the world. This is the difference between alcohol used as an intoxicant and alcohol used as an ingredient in food.

Allah Most High says, “Allah wants ease for you, and does not want unbearable hardship for you” [Quran 2:185; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, ‘Verily this religion is ease, and none makes this religion difficult except that it overwhelms them.’ [Bukhari]

Trace amounts are often permitted because they’re not used in large amounts, or for pleasure, or intoxication, and they’re chemically transformed or diluted enough to lose their alcohol (khamr) status in the legal sense.[Maydani, al-Lubab fi Sharh al-Kitab; Usmani, Takmilat Fath al-Mulhim]

Follow what you know, not what you suspect. If a product is sold without an indication containing an impermissible ingredient, treat it as permissible.

records.title: How Can We Have Free Will if Allah Guides Whom He Wills?
records.question: I understand Quran 29:69, which says those who strive are guided, but I struggle with Quran 16:93, which says Allah guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills. If Allah guides whom He wills, how does this work with human choice?
records.answer:
You have found the exact place where this question bites, and you have followed it honestly all the way down instead of stopping at the first comfortable answer.

This is the oldest live question in our theology, and the schools of Kalam were founded in part to answer it.

Let me take your three questions in the order you asked them.

The Two Verses Do Not Collide

Read the two verses again side by side.

The first: “And whoever strives their utmost for Our sake: Verily shall We unfailingly guide them the momentous paths to Us.” [Quran 29:69; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

And the second: “Had Allah willed, He had made you of one common faith; But instead lets stray whomever He wills, and guides whomever He wills; And you shall inevitably be asked of what you used to do.” [Quran 16:93; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Notice that the second verse ends by holding you accountable. If the will named in its middle abolished your choice, the clause at its end would be empty. The verse itself refuses the reading you fear.

What the two verses actually state is a promise and a sovereignty, and those are not rivals. The first tells you what Allah has bound Himself to do when you strive. The second tells you whose act the guiding is.

Your Act Is Created by Allah, and It Is Still Yours

Here is the doctrine that resolves this issue, and it is the settled position of both our schools of theology

Imam Taftazani states the first half plainly: “Allah Most High is the creator of all the acts of the servants, of unbelief and faith, obedience and disobedience.” [Taftazani, Sharh al-Aqaid al-Nasafiyya]

And in the same breath he states the second half, refusing the fatalists: “They have voluntary acts for which they are rewarded if obedience, and punished if disobedience, not as the Jabriyya claimed, that the servant has no act at all, and that his movements are like the movements of inanimate objects over which he has no power, no intent, and no choice.

This is false … for if the servant had no act at all, his being held responsible would not be sound, nor would the deserving of reward and punishment follow upon his acts.” [Taftazani, Sharh al-Aqaid al-Nasafiyya]

The Maturidi imams put it in terms of ownership: the servant has the power to acquire, not to create. “Though they are owned servants, owned by a mastery of bringing into existence and creating, they are not compelled in their acts.

Rather, they have the power of acquisition, not the power of creation … and they have choice in what they do and leave, because choice and intellect have been placed within them.

So they are choosers in what they do, not the choice of lordship, but the choice of trial and burden.” [reported by Abu al-Muin al-Nasafi and Abu Hafs al-Ghaznawi, in Maturidi commentaries]

Two Powers: One, Creating–the Other, Acquiring

The technical formula is this. One and the same act falls under two powers from two different angles: under Allah’s power from the angle of creating, and under the servant’s power from the angle of acquiring [Bajuri, Tuhfat al-Murid].

That is what the tradition calls kasb (acquisition).

So take your question as you asked it: “Is it because they chose to strive or because Allah guided them to?” It has an answer: the alternative is false. You chose. He created the choice. Both, and not in competition.

What Guiding and Leading Astray Actually Mean

The next thing that unsettles people is the word “misguides,” because they hear it as “forces into unbelief.” It does not mean that.

“The meaning of our companions’ statement that He guides whom He wills, and their statement that He leads astray whom He wills, is that He creates the act of being guided in whom He wills, and likewise creates the act of straying in whom He wills.

This is the position of the people of truth regarding the guidance ascribed to Allah and the leading astray ascribed to Him.” [Turkistani, Sharh al-Aqida al-Tahawiyya]

And Imam Abu Hanifa states the point that should settle your fear directly: “He did not compel any of His creation to unbelief or to faith,” which can be clarified with a gloss Imam Bajuri in his commentary on the Jawhara: “the meaning is that Allah does not create obedience and disobedience in the servant’s heart by way of compulsion and overpowering; rather He creates them coupled with the servant’s choice and inclination.” [Abu Hanifa, al-Fiqh al-Akbar, with Bajuri, Tuhfat al-Murid]

Coupled with the servant’s choice. Not against it, not instead of it.

Where the Goodness in the Heart Came From

Now your hardest question. I want to answer it, not deflect it.

Yes. The goodness is from Allah. So is the striving. So is the capacity to strive, the moment in which you strove, and the person who said the word that turned you. Everything you have is a gift, all the way down.

There is no layer beneath the gift where you stand on your own.

But look at what follows from that, and what does not. What follows is that you owe thanks. What does not follow is injustice.

What is Injustice (dhulm)? And What is Justice (adl)?

Injustice means putting a thing where it does not belong, in a way that can be objected to by right.

Imam Bajuri defines justice exactly so: it is “placing a thing in its proper place without objection against the doer, the opposite of wrongdoing, which is placing a thing in other than its place with objection against its doer.” [Bajuri, Tuhfat al-Murid]

Objection by what right? A person can be called unjust because he has crossed a limit set over him by another. Allah has no limit set over Him by another, and everything is His to begin with.

The Quran states it as a bare fact: “Never is He asked of what He does, while rather it is they who shall be asked.” [Quran 21:23; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

That is not a door slammed on your question. It is the answer to it.

Fairness, in the sense you are reaching for, is a claim one party has on another. No one has a claim on Allah because no one gave Him anything first. What He gives is bounty, and bounty distributed unequally is not injustice.

A man who gives one beggar a hundred and another ten has wronged neither.

And on the other side, He has bound Himself: “Verily Allah wrongs not men in the slightest, but men only wrong themselves.” [Quran 10:44; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

And: “Allah does not tax any soul but what it can bear.” [Quran 2:286] No one is held to account for a capacity they were not given.

Your Duty: Your Part Is to Work

The Companions of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) asked your question. Not a version of it: your question, and more sharply.

Sayyiduha Ali (Allah be pleased with him) reports that they were at a burial when the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) sat and said, “There is not one of you except that his seat in the Fire and his seat in Paradise have already been written.”

They said, “Messenger of Allah, should we not then simply rely upon what has been written for us?” He said: “Work, for each person is eased toward what he was created for.” [Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim]

That is the whole of the practical answer, and notice its shape. They put the metaphysics to him, and he gave them back a verb.

Not because the question is illegitimate, but because it is not the kind of question a person can stand on.

You cannot see the decree; you can only see the next thing to do.

So, What Should You Do?

So do this. Hold the doctrine: Allah Most High creates, you acquire responsibility, and you are answerable for what you acquire.

Then stop auditing it. The Quran puts your instruction in one clause: “And by lofty Soul, and That which perfected it in matchless nature, And instilled it its sense of evil and of godfearingness:

He has truly succeeded forever who makes it reach full purity in faith and deed! And he has truly failed forever who buries it in evil.” [Quran 91:7–10; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

You were given the sense of both. Purifying is yours to do.

And take the promise of 29:69 as addressed to you, because it is. Strive, and He guides. That verse is not a description of other people. It is a contract you are already inside.

If you want to hold this steadily rather than re-derive it every few months, learn the tenets of faith properly with a teacher, once, in order. Half of what makes this question torment people is meeting it in fragments.
references: reported by Abu al-Muin al-Nasafi and Abu Hafs al-Ghaznawi, in Maturidi commentaries
Abu Hanifa, al-Fiqh al-Akbar, with Bajuri, Tuhfat al-Murid

records.title: Is It Sinful to Aim to Be the Most Physically Dominant of All Time?
records.question: I want to become the most physically dominant and best combatant of all time in raw strength and fighting ability, and although I exclude the Prophets, “all time” would include the Companions.
records.answer:
No, it is not sinful, and the distinction you have already drawn is the right one.

You separated raw bodily strength from rank before Allah, and you did it without a trace of contempt. The Prophets (peace be upon them) and the Companions (Allah be pleased with them) are revered for faith, precedence, virtue, and sacrifice, not for muscle.

Umar and Ali (Allah be pleased with them) are not honored simply because they were strong. They were strong, and they are honored for what they spent that strength on. So an ambition about bodily power does not touch their rank at all, because their rank was never measured in that currency.

Lawful worldly ambition is not blameworthy either.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said: “The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though in each there is good. Be diligent in seeking what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not be helpless.” [Sahih Muslim]

Wanting strength, and wanting a great deal of it, sits comfortably inside that.

Pride Is the Only Thing That Would Make It Sinful

Hold the aspiration quietly, as effort and gratitude rather than as a slogan, because what spoils an ambition like this is pride. And keep the Prophets and the Companions above comparison as a matter of adab, even in a quality that was never the reason for their eminence.

Then train hard, and spend the strength the way Umar (Allah be pleased with him) spent his.

records.title: Is It Sinful to Live Where Wastewater Pollutes a Creek?
records.question: My neighborhood’s wastewater drainage was routed into the creek more than ten years ago, and the rerouting we were promised has not happened.
records.answer:
You have been carrying this for a while, and it is heavier than it needs to be.

You are not sinning: not by using the lavatory in your own home, not by performing ghusl there, not by washing your dishes. And nothing in what you describe obliges your family to leave the house.

Your Own Purity Is Not Affected

In the Hanafi school, impurity entering flowing water does not render it impure unless one of three traits shows.

Imam Ibn Abidin gives the rule and the traits together: “if there were a carcass in it, or men urinated into it, and another performed wudu downstream, it is valid so long as no trace of it is seen in the current, and that is either taste, color, or smell.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

So the creek below your neighborhood is not automatically ruled impure, and in any case, it is not the water you wash with.

Clean water comes into your house; waste leaves it and does not climb back up the pipe to reach you.

Your wudu, your ghusl, your dishes, and your prayer are sound. Use the backyard for wudu if you prefer it, but you are not required to.

The Sin Belongs to Whoever Routed the Drain

What weighs on you is living inside a wrong you did not choose.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said: “Whoever among you sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand; and if he is unable, then with his tongue; and whoever is unable, then with his heart, and that is the weakest of faith.” [Sahih Muslim]

Read the structure of this: Each tier of responsibility in the hadith is conditional on capacity, and the third is still faith: the weakest of faith, not the failure of it.

Imam Jassas draws the ruling straight out of it: “If he rejects the wrong in his heart and is unable to change it upon another, he does not fall under the threat directed at the one who does it.” [Jassas, Ahkam al-Quran]

Allah says: “So fear Allah all you can,” [Quran 64:16; Keller, The Quran Beheld], and the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said: “When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you are able.” [Sahih al-Bukhari]

You did not build the drain, and you cannot move it; you reject it in your heart and cannot change it. That is the third tier, and it is not sin.

You Are Not Obliged to Move

Nothing in our books requires a family to leave their home over a public wrong they neither caused nor can prevent. Uprooting a household is a real hardship, and the Law lifts hardship.

Imam Zarqa gives the Hanafi maxim with its reason: “Hardship brings ease, because constriction is repelled by the revealed text.” [Ahmad al-Zarqa, Sharh al-Qawaid al-Fiqhiyya]

And the revealed text says: “Nor has He laid on you any hardship in religion.” [Quran 22:78; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

If a move one day becomes easy and better for all of you, move. It is not a religious obligation and should not be pressed on your parents as one.

Raise It Once, as a Health Question

Here I want to redirect you gently, because the way you have framed it will not serve you. Our religion does not require your parents to rebuild a neighborhood sewer, and putting it to them as a ruling would land as pressure rather than guidance.

Raise it instead as what it honestly is: a question of the neighborhood’s health and cleanliness, and a promise made and not kept. That is a real thing to care about.

And keep its adab in view. “Never say ‘Faugh!’ to them or rebuff them harshly; But speak to them respectful words of honor.” [Quran 17:23; Keller, The Quran Beheld] Say it once, well, and then leave it.

Set the Question Down

Use your home normally: the lavatory, ghusl, the dishes, with no extra washing and no avoidance. Reject the wrong in your heart; that tier is complete as it stands.

If a lawful civic route is open to you, a letter to the local authority, that is the hand, and one honest attempt is worth making.

If there is none, or it comes to nothing, what was on you is done.

And then set the question down. This is the part I would most like you to take.

Worry over what you cannot control is a thief: it takes the attention that belongs to your prayer and to the people in front of you, and gives nothing back.

records.title: Is It Permissible to Go Out When Haram Is Almost Everywhere I Look?
records.question: I have been staying at home because so much around me is not in line with Islam, and I want to know whether I may go out and take a walk when women are uncovered almost everywhere I look, and whether I may play football with non-Muslims in a city where there are no other Muslims.
records.answer:
There is real sincerity in this question, and real strain behind it. May Allah bless you and grant you facilitation.

You may go out and play football with the men in your city. Neither permission comes with conditions attached.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) settled something close to this. Abu Said al-Khudri (Allah be pleased with him) reports that he said, “Beware of sitting in the roadways.” The Companions (Allah be pleased with them) answered that they could not do without their gatherings.

He said, “If you must have the gathering, then give the road its due right,” and when they asked what that right was, he said, “Lowering the gaze, withholding harm, returning greetings, commanding good (al-amr bil-maruf), and forbidding wrong (al-nahy an al-munkar).” [Sahih al-Bukhari]

The street was not treated as somewhere to flee. It was given duties.

The Command to Lower the Gaze Assumes You Are Outside

Allah Most High says, “Tell believing men, they lower and restrain of their looks, and keep well chaste their private parts: That is purer for their spiritual growth; Verily Allah is well aware of all they work.” [Quran 24:30; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

You cannot lower your gaze in an empty room. The command was built for a man who is among people, and it places your struggle in your eye rather than at your front door.

What is asked of you is the turn of the eye. Jarir ibn Abdallah (Allah be pleased with him) asked the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) about the accidental glance, “and he commanded me to avert my gaze.” [Sahih Muslim]

He was not told he had sinned; he was told what to do next. So walk, and when something comes into view, look elsewhere and keep walking. You are not the judge of the street. You answer for your own eyes and your own limbs.

Playing Football Where You Live Is Permitted

Go and play, without hesitation. Sport is lawful, your body has a right over you, and dealing well with the people among whom you live is a good in itself.

Withdrawal Is Not the Safer Religion

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “The Muslim who mixes with people and bears their harm patiently is better than the one who does not mix with them and does not bear their harm.” [Tirmidhi and Ibn Maja]

Mulla Ali al-Qari (Allah have mercy on him) writes that this hadith carries “the superiority of mixing over seclusion,” and that it is “the strongest indicant of the recommendedness of mixing.”

He adds that the balance shifts with times, places, and the people in them. [Mulla Ali al-Qari, Mirqat al-Mafatih] So seclusion has its hour.

A man shutting his door on a whole city is not taking that hour. He is carrying a weight the religion never handed him.

Judge a Place by What It Is For

There is one real limit, and it is narrow. A gathering assembled around a wrong is not the same thing as a street where some people happen to sin.

In the Shafiʿi school you follow, Ibn Hajar al-Haytami (Allah have mercy on him) holds that at such a gathering one objects, and “if he is unable, he leaves.” [Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, Tuhfat al-Muhtaj]

A bar, a hall built for gambling: those you do not attend. A park, a market, a pitch, an ordinary road: those you enter with a good intention and a guarded eye.

So open the door. Walk, play, greet people, and come home with your gaze and your heart intact. That is the harder religion, and the better one.

records.title: What Actually Constitutes Apostasy in Islam?
records.answer:
Yes. It requires wanting it. That is the answer. I will give you the grounds for it, and then I will tell you what happened to what you read.

What Actually Removes a Person from Islam

A person enters Islam by affirming what the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) brought from Allah. A person leaves it only by denying that same thing: knowingly, deliberately, with the heart’s rejection following the tongue.

Faith is the heart’s assent (tasdiq). Imam Bajuri is careful about what that assent consists of: acceptance and submission to what the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) brought, not the bare notion that he spoke truly held without acceptance. [Bajuri, Tuhfat al-Murid]

What is built by acceptance is undone only by rejection, not by accident, not by a thought that crossed the mind, not by a phrase that escaped in anger or confusion.

The Quran states the condition directly, in the verse on coerced disbelief: unbelief attaches to “whoever opens his whole breast to unbelief.” [Quran 16:106; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Opening the breast. Not being ambushed by a thought.

And the general principle covers the rest: “Allah has overlooked for my Umma honest mistakes, forgetfulness, and what they are coerced to do.” [Sunan Ibn Maja and al-Bayhaqi; sound by its routes]

Allah says the same of the heart’s liability: “Allah will not take you to task for thoughtlessly uttered oaths, but will take you to task for what your hearts intentionally earn.” [Quran 2:225; Keller, The Quran Beheld] What the heart intends. That is the whole hinge.

The Thoughts Themselves Are a Sign of Faith

You are afraid of what you or your family might think one day. Hear this from the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) himself.

Companions came to him and said, “We find within ourselves something that any of us would find too grave to utter.” He asked, “Have you actually found that?” They said yes. He said, “That is pure faith.” [Sahih Muslim]

He did not tell them to renew their Islam. He told them that being appalled by such a thought is what faith feels like from the inside. An empty heart does not flinch.

So the fear you are describing is, from the tradition’s own point of view, evidence in your favor, not a warning sign.

About What You Read

Now to the thing that unsettled you, because you deserve a straight account of it.

Our archive holds hundreds of answers written by different scholars on different madhabs over many years, each addressing a specific person in a specific state. Some address a person who has knowingly and deliberately denied a known tenet, a genuine case which the books do treat.

That answer is correct for that questioner. It is the wrong answer for you, and it should not be read as though it were addressed to you.

You did not misread us. You read something written for a different case and applied it to yourself, which is exactly what a scrupulous person does.

I am raising the matter internally so that answers of that kind carry the qualification that keeps them from landing on readers in your position.

What I Want You to Do

Stop investigating. That is the instruction, and it is a religious one, not merely practical advice.

Do not look up further rulings on kufr. Do not test yourself. Do not re-examine past thoughts to check whether one of them crossed a line.

The scrupulous whispering (waswasa) feeds on exactly that inspection, and every ruling you read gives it new material. You wrote that this is your last question. Let it be, on this topic.

If a thought comes, do not argue with it. Say “I believe in Allah,” turn your attention elsewhere, and carry on.

Do not renew your Islam, do not repeat the shahada as a fix, do not tell your family they are in danger. Nothing has happened.

And put your attention on what builds rather than on what you fear losing.

Learn the tenets of faith properly with a teacher, once, in order, so your creed rests on knowledge rather than on whatever you happen to come across while searching.

You said our answers have been helping you, and you have been feeling better. That is the direction. Keep going in it.
references: Sunan Ibn Maja and al-Bayhaqi; sound by its routes

records.title: Is It Permissible to Eat More Than I Need While Palestinians Are Starving?
records.question: Is it permissible for me to eat more than I need to stand upright while the Palestinians are starving? By that I mean more than one meal a day, really, the minimum of food I need to consume.
records.answer:
Your concern is not a flaw in your faith. It is a sign of mercy. The discomfort you feel while others suffer is a mark of a living heart. May Allah reward you for this compassion.

Please know that what follows is offered with respect for your sincere care.

The Ruling

You are not permitted to reduce your intake to the bare minimum needed to stand. Eating enough to maintain your health and strength is not just allowed; it is required. Your body is a trust from Allah.

We are responsible for caring for it as He has commanded. Deliberately weakening yourself is not sought by the Sacred Law.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) judged, “that there be no harming nor reciprocating of harm.” [Sunan Ibn Maja]

Imam Malik relates the same in al-Muwatta. The scholars built one of the governing maxims of the whole Sacred Law on it.

That maxim does not begin at the edge of your own skin. The harm you inflict on yourself is harm.

What the Tradition Actually Praises

Moderation, not deprivation. Allah Most High says, “And eat and drink, but not in prodigal waste. Verily, He loves not those who exceed the due bounds.” [Quran 7:31; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Reflect on the wording. The command is to eat and drink. The restriction is against waste and excess, not against sufficiency.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “No son of Adam has filled a vessel worse than his stomach.

A few morsels are enough for a man to keep his back straight. But if it must be more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath.” [Sunan al-Tirmidhi; also Sunan Ibn Maja]

Read it carefully. Even the strictest reading of this hadith gives you a third of the stomach for food and a third for drink. It is a warning against filling yourself, not an instruction to empty yourself.

Choosing to eat only one meal a day, at the minimum needed to survive, is not what the guidance above describes.

Over time, this weakens your strength, focus, worship, and ability to benefit others. Please avoid this approach.

Where Does the Mercy You Are Feeling Belong

Your grief is real and deserves a true outlet. However, your hunger does not reach those in Gaza. These actions do:

Give, and give in a way that you feel. This is closest to what your heart seeks. Unlike self-deprivation, this support truly reaches them. If you wish your sacrifice to be meaningful, let it be through your wealth rather than your health.

Pray for them by name, in the depths of the night, in your prostration, and between the adhan and iqama. Do not think this is insignificant. It is a door that no power on earth can close.

Speak and act wherever you have any influence. This may be through advocacy, boycott, writing, or organizing. Do what is within your capacity and entrust the rest to Allah.

Keep yourself strong enough to sustain these actions. A weakened body cannot give, cannot stand in prayer at night, and cannot advocate for others.

A Word on the Guilt Itself

You are not asked to carry the burden of Gaza alone. You are asked to do what is within your capacity. Allah Most High does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Eat properly, then use that strength to act on their behalf.
references: Sunan al-Tirmidhi; also Sunan Ibn Maja

records.title: Why Are There Four Schools of Islamic Law?
records.question: Why are there four schools of Islamic law? Who decided there should be four and not more? Could a qualified scholar produce his own school, and would that be an innovation?
records.answer:
The four schools are not four religions, and no committee voted them into existence.

There are four rigorously recorded accounts of how the Quran and the Sunna were understood by scholars who had mastered both, and preserved, tested, and refined over centuries by specialists.

Following one is not an alternative to following Allah and His Messenger (Allah bless him and give him peace). If you are not yourself a mujtahid, it is precisely how you follow them.

Our Duty Is to Obey, and the Quran Tells Us How

Allah commands us, “O you who believe: wholeheartedly answer Allah and the Messenger when he summons you to what brings you to life.” [Quran 8:24; Keller, The Quran Beheld] That is the whole business of a believer’s life.

And the same Quran tells those of us who are not specialists how to carry it out.

Of news that people spread carelessly, Allah says they should have “referred it to the Messenger and men of true decision among them, those of them who can draw the right conclusions about it.” [Quran 4:83; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Drawing the right conclusions renders istinbat, the technical word for deriving a ruling from the evidence.

Allah also says, “Ask those who recall, if you know not.” Shaykh Nuh Keller (Allah preserve him) explains that the words “those who recall,” ahl al-dhikri, “indicate those with knowledge of the Qur’an and sunna, at their forefront the mujtahid Imams of this Umma.” [Keller, Why Muslims Follow Madhhabs]

And we are told, “obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in true authority of you.” [Quran 4:59; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

So obedience runs along two lawful routes. You derive the ruling yourself if you are qualified, or you ask someone who is.

There is no third route in which an untrained reader supplies his own conclusions and calls them the Sunna.

Notice how much this leaves in your own hands. Most of your religion you take directly from the Quran and hadith: that Allah is one, that you believe in His angels, Books, and messengers, that you do good, avoid evil, and cooperate in what is right.

Only one narrow band of knowledge needs a specialist. Shaykh Nuh describes it as “the specific understanding of particular divine commands and prohibitions that make up the sharia,” where “because of both the nature and the sheer number of the Qur’an and hadith texts involved, people differ in the scholarly capacity to understand and deduce rulings from them.” [Keller, What Is a Madhhab?]

That technical zone is what a school covers. Nothing more.

No Council Chose Four. The Practice of the Umma Settled There

No caliph, council, or scholarly body ever legislated the number. Great mujtahids lived alongside the four Imams: Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Awzai, al-Layth ibn Sad, and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari (Allah have mercy on them all). Their learning is honored.

What they lacked was a school in the working sense: students who recorded the Imam’s rulings, drew out his governing principles, extended them to new cases, and defended them under challenge for generations.

Ibn Rajab (Allah have mercy on him) locates the reason exactly there.

The other schools, he writes, “were not widely known and were not accurately recorded, so things may have been attributed to them that they never said, or understood from them what they never intended, and their positions have no one left to defend them or to point out the flaws that creep into them, unlike these well-known schools.” [Ibn Rajab, al-Radd ala man Ittabaa Ghayr al-Madhahib al-Arbaa]

Follow an unpreserved school, and you may be following a ruling its Imam never gave.

Four, then, is a historical outcome under divine care rather than a decree.

Ibn Rajab reads that outcome as protection: “Allah’s wisdom decreed that He would secure and preserve the religion by appointing for the people Imams whose knowledge, understanding, and attainment of the intended goal in the rank of knowledge of the rulings and of giving fatwa were agreed upon.” [Ibn Rajab, al-Radd ala man Ittabaa Ghayr al-Madhahib al-Arbaa]

Not more, because no fifth school was preserved to that standard. Not fewer, because these four were.

Ijtihad Was Never Closed in Principle, but Its Bar Is High

Could a qualified scholar produce his own school? In principle, yes. A scholar who genuinely reaches the rank of absolute mujtahid is bound to act on what the evidence shows him.

Ibn Rajab says of such a man that “his obligation is to follow what has become clear to him of the truth, while everyone else’s obligation is taqlid.” [Ibn Rajab, al-Radd ala man Ittabaa Ghayr al-Madhahib al-Arbaa]

Two things temper the picture. Nobody sets out to found a school. The four schools formed around their Imams through their students, largely after their deaths: the Imam taught, and the school was the sediment his students left behind.

And the bar is not rhetorical. Shaykh Nuh relays that a man asked Imam Ahmad (Allah have mercy on him), “When a man has memorized 100,000 hadiths, is he a scholar of Sacred Law, a faqih?” And he said, “No.”

The man asked, “200,000 then?” And he said, “No.” The man asked, “Then 300,000?” And he said, “No.” The man asked, “400,000?” And Ahmad gestured with his hand to signify “about that many.” [Keller, Why Muslims Follow Madhhabs, citing Ibn al-Qayyim, Ilam al-Muwaqqiin]

Add to that command of Arabic as the early Arabs possessed it, and full mastery of legal method. Shaykh Nuh’s verdict on those who skip the training is blunt: “Whoever makes ijtihad without this qualification is a criminal.” [Keller, Why Muslims Follow Madhhabs]

The Schools Are Not Innovation: Shopping Between Them Is the Real Danger

Innovation, bidah, means introducing into the religion what is not from it.

A school introduces nothing. It records how trained scholars understood texts already revealed, and the companions and their students differed in exactly this manner (Allah be pleased with them).

Calling that innovation would make the Companions innovators for differing over inheritance and purification.

What the scholars do warn against is the opposite mistake: treating the four schools as a menu. Ibn Nujaym (Allah have mercy on him) gives the Hanafi position.

A non-mujtahid may follow whichever qualified mujtahid he wishes, and may move from his school, “but he does not chase dispensations. And if he does chase them across the schools, does he become a transgressor? Two views.” [Ibn Nujaym, al-Bahr al-Raiq]

The more evident of the two, the commentator adds, is that he does not, so what follows is a matter of discipline rather than a verdict on your standing.

The reason the scholars give is exact. Imam Nawawi (Allah have mercy on him) writes that if a layman were free to follow whichever school he pleased, it “would lead to his picking out the dispensations of the schools, following his desire, and choosing between the lawful and the unlawful, the obligatory and the merely permitted.

And that leads to the untying of the collar of accountability.” [Nawawi, al-Majmu Sharh al-Muhadhdhab] Zakariyya al-Ansari (Allah have mercy on him) gives the same reason in the same words: he does not chase dispensations, “because of what chasing them involves of the untying of the collar of accountability.” [Zakariyya al-Ansari, Asna al-Matalib]

Two harms follow. The first is talfiq in its blameworthy form: combining two acts from different schools so that the result is an act neither school would call valid, as when ablution omits what one school requires, and prayer omits what the other requires.

The second harm is quieter and worse. The self becomes the arbiter. You are no longer asking what Allah wants of you; you are shopping for permission and calling the result fiqh.

Which is why sticking to one school is a discipline and not a sixth pillar. Mufti Taqi Usmani (Allah preserve him) puts it plainly: “We do not hold that personal taqlid is obligatory or binding in itself.

Rather, we say that by personal taqlid the affairs of the religion are ordered, and that in abandoning taqlid there is chaos.” [Usmani, Usul al-Ifta wa Adabuh]

Ibn Rajab saw what a world without the schools would look like: “people would have witnessed the strangest of wonders from every self-impressed fool, taken with his own opinion, brazen toward the people and quick to pounce.” [Ibn Rajab, al-Radd ala man Ittabaa Ghayr al-Madhahib al-Arbaa]

Follow One School Properly, and Ask Someone Who Knows

Choose one of the four, learn it with a qualified teacher, and act on it. When a genuine need or real hardship arises, take another school’s position through a scholar who can tell you whether it is sound and whether your act still holds together, rather than by browsing for it yourself.

Keep respect for all four in your heart. Each is a preserved road to the same revelation, and partisanship toward one is its own disease.

Allah has not asked you to become a mujtahid. He has asked you to obey Him, and He has told you how: ask those who know.
references: Ibn Rajab, al-Radd ala man Ittabaa Ghayr al-Madhahib al-Arbaa
Keller, Why Muslims Follow Madhhabs, citing Ibn al-Qayyim, Ilam al-Muwaqqiin

records.title: How Do I Seek Allah’s Guidance When the Decision Cannot Wait?
records.question: I am passing through a very uncertain phase regarding my academic and career path.
records.answer:
You are terrified, and only part of that is about istikhara. Istikhara is two units of prayer and a supplication; its answer comes after you act, not before.

Istikhara Takes Two Minutes

You have understood istikhara as a process that takes time and yields a hint. Neither is so.

It is two units of prayer outside the obligatory, followed by a supplication.

That is the whole of it. Jabir (Allah be pleased with him) reports that the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) taught it for all matters as he taught a chapter of the Quran: “When one of you intends a matter, let him pray two units other than the obligatory prayer, then say …” [Sahih al-Bukhari]

There is no waiting period. There is no required dream. If the decision is urgent, pray for it now and make a decision today. If you cannot pray at all (you are traveling, you are in the middle of something), say the supplication on its own and proceed.

And It Is Not a Hint

Here is the correction that will change how you use it. Look at what you are asking for in the words: “O Allah, if You know this matter to be good for me in my religion, my livelihood, and the outcome of my affair, then decree it for me, make it easy for me, and bless me in it.

And if You know this matter to be evil for me … then turn it away from me and turn me away from it, and decree for me the good wherever it may be, then make me content with it.” [Sahih al-Bukhari]

You are not asking Him to tell you. You are asking Him to choose and then to arrange matters accordingly.

Which means the answer is not something you receive before you act. It is what unfolds after you act. You pray, you take the soundest decision you can with the information you have, you move. And Allah opens the road or closes it.

So the university that rejected you was not a silent istikhara. That was the answer. You asked Him to turn the matter away if it was not good for you, and He did. You have been treating a granted request as unanswered.

Now the Real Problem

You told me something more important than the istikhara question, almost in passing: you overthink every step, to the point where you hesitate to ask for help because you over-analyze the consequences.

That is what is actually costing you, and no amount of istikhara will fix it, because it is not a knowledge problem. You are trying to be certain before you move. Certainty about the future is not on offer to anyone.

It was not given to the Prophet’s Companions (Allah be pleased with them), and it will not be given to you.

Look at what Allah commanded His Messenger (Allah bless him and give him peace), who had revelation: “Consult with them on matters of weight; And when you decide, then trust wholly to Allah: Verily Allah loves those who trust in Him.” [Quran 3:159; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Consult. Then decide. Then rely. Reliance comes after the decision, not instead of it. You are trying to reach Reliance without ever passing through the decision, which is why you are stuck.

The Whole Method, in Order

Four steps. It takes an evening, not a season.

Consult (mashwara). Two or three people who know you, know the field, and will tell you the truth. This is more than half the guidance, and it is the step you are skipping because you are afraid to ask.

Weigh the ordinary evidence. What is realistic, what is lawful, what serves your religion, your livelihood, and the outcome of your affair (the three things named in the supplication itself).

Pray istikhara. Two units and the supplication. Two minutes.

Decide and move. Then read the answer in what opens and what closes.

Nothing Is Foreclosed

You are terrified that a wrong turn now will foreclose the future you want. It will not.

“It may well be that you hate something, and it is better for you, and may well be that you love something, and it is worse for you; And Allah well knows, and you know not.” [Quran 2:216; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

And: “whoever fears Allah, He grants him a way out of every plight, And provides for him whence he could not even guess.” [Quran 65:2–3]

Whence he could not even guess. The path you cannot see is precisely the one the verse is promising.

“The most beloved of deeds to Allah is the most constant of them, even if little.” [Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim]

A life is built by steady, ordinary steps, most of them taken without certainty. That has been true of everyone who ever built one.

Ask for help this week. That is the single step that will move you furthest.

records.title: Is Working as a University Consultant Permissible?
records.question: Is working as a university consultant (advising students on universities, programs, and fees) permissible, specifically advising a female student who is considering studying abroad? Does the consultant bear responsibility if she goes on to study abroad as a result?
records.answer:
Working as a university consultant is permissible, provided that the courses you recommend are shari’a-compliant.

The consultant is not responsible for unrelated or incidental matters that may arise from their advice. Allah says, ‘And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another’. [Quran, 35:18]

Your advice and the potential of a female student’s travel arrangements that contravene shari’a are mutually exclusive. The responsibility for whether and how she travels, and with whom, sits with her and her guardians.

Your actions do not fall under the ambit of, ‘Do not assist one another in sin and transgression.’ [Quran, 5:2]

May Allah continue to use you as a means of goodness. The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said, “Whoever guides others to goodness will receive a reward like that of the one who does it.” [Tirmidhi]

records.title: Is Using Earned In-Game Currency for Gambling Permissible?
records.question: In football games like FIFA and eFootball, players get packs like ‘Player of the Day’ to draw players using in-game coins, which can be bought or earned through tasks. If I only use earned coins and not real money, is playing considered halal or gambling and haram?
records.answer:
Gambling (maysir) is risking something of value, like money, for an uncertain reward. Free in-game coins do not count as such a stake in this way.

So, if one uses only earned in-game coins, not real money, it will not be considered gambling but rather a waste of time playing these prolonged games.

Allah Most High says, “O you who believe: wine, the feast lottery, the stone sacrifice altars, and divining sticks are but filth of the work of the Devil, so shun it utterly, that haply you may succeed.” [Quran, 5:90]

Abdullah Ibn Abbas (Allah be pleased with him) defined gambling in the following words: “The risk of losing on both sides or putting something at stake from both sides (mukhatara) is gambling.” [Jassas, Ahkam al-Quran]

The great Hanafi jurist (faqih), Ibn ‘Abidin (Allah have mercy on him), defines gambling in the following words:

“Gambling (qimar) is from the word qamar, that which increases at times and decreases at other times.

It has been given the name al-Qimar due to the possibility that each one of the gamblers may lose his wealth to his counterpart, and it is also possible that one may gain from the wealth of the other.” [Ibn ‘Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

Avoid Wasting Time

If you play a game where no real money is risked or won, it is a game, and not gambling.

It is, however, better to avoid, as it trains you to rely on uncertain guesses, wastes time, and, in the future, leads to an interest in paying in-game money and so on. One should always consider practical sports rather than virtual game play.

records.title: Is Vinegar Produced by Additives Impure?
records.question: In the Shafii school, vinegar produced by adding something to it is impermissible to consume. If such vinegar touches clothing, does that part become impure?
records.answer:
Such vinegar is considered impure. If it comes into contact with clothing, the area in contact is considered impure. However, it would be prudent to adopt the Hanafi position on this issue.

According to the relied-upon view, grape vinegar produced by adding something to it is impermissible to consume. Since it is impermissible to consume, it is also considered impure.

Impure substances are defined as: “Any corporeal substance that is unrestrictedly impermissible to consume, not because of its sanctity, filth, or harm.” [Hisni, Kifayat al-Akhyar]

Khatib says, “If vinegar is produced by adding something to it, such as onions or warm bread, even before it becomes wine, it is not considered pure.” [Khatib, Mughni al-Muhtaj]

Although this type of vinegar is deemed impure according to the relied-upon position in the Shafii school, Shafi‘i scholars typically do not adhere to the relied-upon (mu‘tamad) position of the School.

Allah Most High says, “Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.” [Quran, 2:185]

Likewise, our mother Aisha (May Allah be pleased with her) related that whenever the Messenger of Allah (May Allah bless him and grant him peace) was given a choice between two matters, he would choose the easier of the two, so long as it was not sinful. [Bukhari]

We ask Allah to grant us sound understanding of His religion and to make our worship a source of ease, tranquility, and closeness to Him.

records.title: What Should I Do When I Struggle With My Faith?
records.question: I am sixteen, and although I still believe, I have started to wish Islam were not true; everything feels so strict that I feel I am suffocating, and I want to know how to find peace and happiness in my religion again.
records.answer:
What you have written is more honest than most people manage at any age, and I read it carefully.

What you are describing is not the loss of faith. It is the loss of the sweetness of faith, and our tradition has a name for it and a way through it.

You said it yourself with real precision: you believe, and you wish it were not true.

That is no doubt, and I will not treat it as doubt. It is a heart under contraction (qabd), and no one has taken this road seriously without passing through it.

Your Condition Has a Name, and the Masters Wrote About It

Imam Qushayri (Allah have mercy on him) described the kind of contraction whose cause the person cannot even identify: “There can be a contraction whose cause is unclear to the one it comes upon; he finds contraction in his heart and does not know what has brought it on or what has caused it.

The way of the one in this contraction is to surrender until that time passes … and when he surrenders to the ruling of the moment, it soon lifts.” [al-Qushayri, al-Risala al-Qushayriyya]

Read what he does not say. He does not say you have been cast out. He does not say the feeling is your verdict.

He says the state came upon you without your choosing, it will leave without your forcing, and the harder you fight it, the longer it stays. Your heart is in a season.

You Are Right That Supplication and Remembrance Are Not the Whole Answer

Everyone has told you the answer is supplication (du’a) and remembrance (dhikr), and you wrote that you feel it is much more than that.

You are right, and I would rather agree with you than repeat something that has already failed to reach you.

Supplication and remembrance are medicine, and medicine works inside a regimen: the right dose, at a time you can keep, with rest and food, and someone who checks on you. Handed over as a slogan, they stop being medicine and become one more thing you are failing at.

That is what happened to you, and it is not your fault.

You Are Carrying a Weight Nobody Asked You to Carry

You wrote that the thought of living like this your whole life makes it worse. Of course it does.

You are sixteen, and you have picked up every obligation of an entire adult lifetime and tried to carry all of it at once, today, in one armful. Nobody is asked to do that.

Allah Most High says: “Allah does not tax any soul but what it can bear.” [Quran 2:286; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said: “Indeed this religion is ease. No one presses hard against this religion without it overcoming him. So be straight, draw near, and take glad tidings.” [Mishkat al-Masabih]

What you feel as suffocation is the feeling of pressing hard. It is the signal to loosen your grip.

records.title: Can I Shorten My Prayers if I Stay Less Than 15 Days in Each Town?
records.question: I am traveling 2,800 kilometers over seventeen days, spending eight days in one town and then moving 47 kilometers to a second town for nine days, so neither stay reaches fifteen days. May I pray the traveler’s prayer throughout?
records.answer:
You pray the traveler’s prayer for all seventeen days. In the Hanafi school, this is not optional: your four-cycle prayers are two cycles, and praying four cycles would add to the obligation.

As Imam Marghinani (Allah have mercy on him) states, “the traveler’s obligation in the four-cycle prayer is two cycles, and he does not add to them.” [Marghinani, al-Hidaya]

What ends travel status in the Hanafi school is an intention to stay fifteen days or more in one place without initiating a legal journey. The intention has to be limited to a single town. Split across two, it does not take effect.

Imam Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani (Allah have mercy on him) was asked about exactly your case. A man leaves Kufa for Mecca and Mina, intending to stay fifteen days between the two.

Does he pray in full on entering Mecca? “No,” he answered, “because he does not intend to stay in Mecca alone for fifteen days.” Asked whether Mecca and Mina are counted as one town, he answered, “No,” and gave the same ruling for a man intending to travel 15 days between Kufa and Basra. [Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani, al-Asl]

Imam Ayni (Allah have mercy on him) gives the reason: reckoning the intention across two places “would require reckoning it across many places, and that is untenable.” [al-Ayni, al-Binaya Sharh al-Hidaya]

Notice what that does to your 47 kilometers. Mina lies a few kilometers from Mecca, and the ruling still treats the two as separate places. So the distance between your towns does not carry any weight here.

You do not need the move to count as a fresh journey because nothing was ever canceled: you left home on a journey many times the Hanafi minimum, and you remain a traveler until you either intend to spend fifteen days in one town or come home. Neither of those happens on this trip.

What Would Put You Back on Four Cycles

The two must genuinely be separate localities, each its own town with its own name and boundary; a district or suburb inside the built-up area of one town is one place, not two. Forty-seven kilometres puts you well clear of that line.

The intention also has to be real as you go: if you arrive in the second town and then decide to stay fifteen days or more there, you begin praying in full from the moment you form that intention, not from the day you arrived.

Shortening Is Not Cutting a Corner

You may feel that praying two cycles is taking the easy road. It is the opposite of that. Allah Most High says, “And when any of you journey in the earth, there is no fault in your shortening some of the prayers.” [Quran 4:101; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Yala ibn Umayya (Allah be pleased with him) put to Umar ibn al-Khattab (Allah be pleased with him) the same puzzle that occurs to every careful person: the verse mentions fear, and the people are now secure.

Umar answered, “I wondered at the very thing you are wondering at, so I asked the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) about it.” The answer was, “A charity that Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity.” [Sahih Muslim]

So keep it simple on the road. Two cycles for Zuhr, Asr, and Isha from the moment you pass the built-up limits of your hometown until you return to them. Maghrib, Fajr, and Witr are unchanged.

records.title: What If I Prayed the Fajr Sunna Before Its Time?
records.question: I began the Fajr sunna at 4:34 and later found the time for Fajr was 4:36, so I know that the sunna was not valid. I prayed the obligatory Fajr in its time, and now sunrise and the Dhuhr time have both passed.
records.answer:
Two minutes can feel like a long time when you care this much about getting the prayer right. Nothing is owed now, and you have not sinned.

In the Hanafi school, the sunna before Fajr is the one sunna prayer that can be made up outside its own time, but the window is narrow.

Imam Shurunbulali (Allah have mercy on him) writes that it “is not made up except when it is missed along with the obligatory prayer,” meaning up to the sun’s passing its zenith (zawal), and that Imam Muhammad (Allah have mercy on him) held it may be made up on its own after sunrise and before zawal, “so there is no making it up before sunrise, nor after zawal, by agreement.” [Shurunbulali, Maraqi al-Falah]

Imam Tahtawi (Allah have mercy on him) glosses that last clause: the agreement is on the sound position, and the one dissenting report allows it after zawal only as a follower to a missed obligatory prayer, never on its own, which is by consensus. [Tahtawi, Hashiya ala Maraqi al-Falah]

Read that against your own case. You prayed your obligatory Fajr in its time, so there is no missed obligatory prayer for the sunna to follow. Zawal has passed. Every position in the school closes the window, and nothing remains upon you.

As for sin, the times are not incidental to the prayer; they are part of what was prescribed. Allah Most High says, “Verily the prayer is bounden upon believers at an indelibly prescribed time.” [Quran 4:103; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Imam Jassas (Allah have mercy on him) reads the verse as fixing the obligation and its hours in one stroke: the words comprise “the obligating of the obligatory prayer and its appointed times, because His words, ‘a prescription,’ mean an obligation, and His words, ‘at a prescribed time,’ mean that it is made obligatory within known, specified times.” [Jassas, Ahkam al-Quran] So a sunna begun before its time does not count as that sunna, which you had already worked out for yourself.

But invalidity is one ruling, and sin is another. What is blameworthy is deliberately placing a prayer outside its appointed time.

You acted on what you believed the time to be; you were out by two minutes, and you corrected yourself the moment you knew. That is a mistake, not a transgression, and it leaves nothing on your record.

A Reliable Timetable Is Enough

You are not asked for certainty to the second. You are asked for a sound, preponderant belief that the time has entered, and a reliable prayer timetable for your city gives you exactly that. Begin after it, and then stop looking.

Going back over a prayer you have already prayed is not caution; it is the door through which misgiving comes. Close that door, and pray with ease.

records.title: What If Marriage Falls Through After Istikhara?
records.question: Two months ago, I prayed istikhara about a woman who intended to marry me, and I wanted the same.
records.answer:
I am sorry. Nothing went wrong in your prayer, and your istikhara was not refused: it was answered on the branch you least wanted.

Read back the words you actually said. Jabir (Allah be pleased with him) reports that the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) taught the Companions this prayer for their affairs, the way he taught them a chapter of the Quran.

It opens, “O Allah, I seek Your guidance by Your knowledge, and I seek Your empowerment by Your power, and I ask You of Your immense bounty.” Then it puts two branches before Allah.

If the matter is good for you in your religion, your livelihood, and the outcome of your affair, you asked Him to ordain it, make it easy, and bless you in it.

And if it is not, you asked Him, “then turn it away from me and turn me away from it, and ordain for me what is good wherever it may be, then make me pleased.” [Sahih al-Bukhari]

You did not ask to be told the answer. You asked Allah to choose, and then to bring about what He chose. Badr al-Din al-Ayni (Allah have mercy on him) reads the opening word exactly so: you are asking Him for “the good in what I have resolved upon, and that You choose for me the better of the two matters.” [Badr al-Din al-Ayni, Sharh Sunan Abi Dawud]

So the matter was turned away. By the words of your own supplication, that is not a failed istikhara; it is one answered on its second branch: there is a Divine Promise, through the Beloved Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), that this outcome is for your good, if you accept it as such.

The Dream Was Never the Mechanism

You read a good dream, a good feeling, and a settled mind as a promise. Many are taught it that way, and you took it in good faith, so let me correct it gently. There is no dream anywhere in the supplication above.

A settled mind afterward is a mercy and often a good sign, but it was never given to us as the instrument. The instrument is in the words: You choose, and make it easy.

Which is why the answer shows in what happens next. Ease is how a matter decreed for you shows itself; obstruction is how a matter turned away shows itself. That both of you prayed and both felt peace does not overturn it.

It means He granted you both the calm to keep walking, until He closed the door.

You Know What You Lost, and Not What You Were Spared

Allah Most High says, “And it may well be that you hate something, and it is better for you, and may well be that you love something, and it is worse for you; And Allah well knows, and you know not.” [Quran 2:216; Keller, The Quran Beheld] The two are not equally visible to you.

Notice too the clause people skip. Having asked Allah to turn the matter away, you asked Him to ordain the good wherever it may be, and then to make you pleased. You prayed for contentment in the same breath, and that part is still being answered.

Grieve It, Then Move

Do not go looking for what you did to deserve this. A closed door is not always a punishment, and it is often a protection whose shape you will never be shown. “And whoever fears Allah, He grants him a way out of every plight, and provides for him whence he could not even guess.” [Quran 65:2–3; Keller, The Quran Beheld] You are not meant to be able to see it from where you are standing.

Grieve it properly, and give it time. When the next serious matter comes, pray istikhara again with the same trust, then take the ordinary means: consult people who know you well, look honestly at the practicalities, and move. Read the answer in how the road opens or closes, not in how you feel on the night.
references: Badr al-Din al-Ayni, Sharh Sunan Abi Dawud

records.title: What Should I Do if a Class Makes Me Doubt Prayer?
