If you see mold on a quarter of a dish or half a loaf, you can throw the whole thing away. Mold spreads beyond what you can see, so the rest is not safe to eat. You are not sinful for discarding it, and you do not need to search for pieces to save.

Hardship Excuses You From Separating

The same ruling, on a grounded principle: hardship brings ease. That maxim is the Hanafi school’s own, from al-Ashbah wa al-Nazaʾir of Imam Ibn Nujaym (Allah have mercy on him) [Ibn Nujaym, al-Ashbah wa al-Nazaʾir]. Where picking good rice out of spoiled rice would be genuinely tedious, throw out the pot. The Sacred Law does not price your afternoon at the price of a bowl of rice.

Doubt Permits but Does Not Oblige

Certainty is not removed by doubt, so food you know was sound does not become impermissible merely because you suspect a smell. But that maxim tells you what remains lawful to eat, not what you must eat. You are never required to eat food that you reasonably fear has gone bad. If you are worried, you can discard it without sin.

Residue in a Food Processor Is Not Waste

You can simply wash away the bits of food left on the sides of a container. This is not waste, but just part of using kitchen tools. You do not have to scrape every last piece.

Prevention Is the Duty, Not Salvage

The real responsibility is to plan ahead: buy, cook, and store only what you can finish, and give away or feed to animals what you cannot use while it is still good. Once food has spoiled, the chance to save it has passed. Focus on doing better next time, put the care into next week’s shopping, and do not worry about what is already gone.

records.title: May I Tell Doctors I Am Taking Medication I Am Not, to Keep My Benefits?
records.question: I am genuinely mentally ill and unable to work, and my parents care for me all day. My doctors prescribe medication that I do not take because of its side effects, but I tell them I am taking it so that I keep receiving benefits money, which I would use to pay for treatment. Is this permitted?
records.answer:
I do not doubt that you are ill, that you have tried, or that the need is real, and nothing here is a judgment on you.

However, you cannot tell your doctors you are taking medication you are not taking. Reporting falsely to a clinician to keep money coming is a lie told for gain, and that is impermissible, however genuine the underlying need.

Only an aim the Sacred Law itself recognizes as weightier will excuse a falsehood, and money you have not been granted on the true facts is not such an aim. Imam Ghazali (Allah have mercy on him) leaves no room for it [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din].

A Second Reason More Weighty

A second reason may weigh more on you. A false medication record is medically dangerous. Every judgment your team makes about you rests on it: whether a treatment is working, whether to increase the dose, what to try next, and what is safe to give you in an emergency. A doctor who believes you have been on a drug for months is reasoning about a body that does not exist. They could give you something that interacts badly, or write you off as having failed a treatment you never received. The lie does not only cost you before Allah. It makes your care worse.

Now, separate the two things you have joined together. The lie is one thing. The need is another, and the need is legitimate. Islam does not ask you to pretend you are well, to swallow a medication that makes your life harder, or to refuse support you are entitled to.

The Honest Route Is Open, and Stronger Than You Think

Tell your doctors the truth: you took these medications for weeks, the side effects made things worse, and you stopped. That is an ordinary clinical fact, not a confession, and clinicians hear it constantly. Then ask what else there is. A different medication, a different class, a lower dose, or a treatment that is not medication at all. Declining one drug is not declining care, and services do not discharge people who stay engaged and are honest about what they cannot tolerate.

Then let the claim be assessed on the truth. You describe severe mental illness, physical illness, self-harm, near-arrest, and parents who care for you all day. Those are the grounds on which support is assessed, not whether you swallow a particular tablet.

Ask your doctor to set out your real functioning in writing. Get a free welfare adviser to help with the forms, and if you are refused, appeal, which is your lawful right and often succeeds. And if the honest award turns out smaller than you hoped, the smaller amount is the one that is lawful for you.

Allah says of the God-fearing, “And whoever fears Allah, He grants him a way out of every plight, and provides for him whence he could not even guess; And whoever trusts in Allah, He always suffices.” [Quran 65:2–3; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Do Not Carry the Worst of It Alone

You mentioned that you have harmed yourself. One thing about that: when that pressure comes, tell someone qualified the same day, and let your parents know while you are struggling, rather than after. You are worth the trouble of asking, and asking is obedience, not weakness. Staying in qualified mental health care is itself something Allah rewards you for, not time taken away from Him.

Truthfulness Is the Way Out, Not the Obstacle

A real need never makes a falsehood lawful, and Allah has tied relief to God-consciousness, not to cleverness. The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt, for truthfulness is tranquility and lying is disquiet.” [Tirmidhi]

You already know the disquiet; it is why you wrote. So have one honest conversation with your doctor this week, and let the claim go in on the truth of your condition. You have been ill a long time, and you have never lied about this before. Do not start now, when you are this close to having your real case heard properly.

records.title: How Do We Reconcile Allah’s Preserving the Religion With the Hadith on Scholars Being Taken Away?
records.question: How can we reconcile our belief that Allah Most High will preserve the religion with the hadith indicating that He will take knowledge away by taking away the scholars, until none remain, and that people will then take ignorant men as their leaders?
records.answer:
There is no contradiction between the two, and the way to see that is not to harmonize them after the fact but to ask the hadith commentators what each text actually says. Once you have their definitions, the reconciliation is already inside them: what is seized in the hadith is the men who carry knowledge, and what is preserved in the verse is the Book, along with a group Allah keeps upon the truth until the Hour.

The First Hadith: Knowledge Is Seized by the Death of Scholars

Take the first hadith. Abdullah ibn Amr (Allah be pleased with him) heard the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) say, “Allah does not seize knowledge by snatching it away from the servants. Rather, He seizes knowledge by taking the scholars, until, when He has left no scholar, people take ignorant men as their heads. They are asked, and they give rulings without knowledge, so they stray and lead others astray.” [Sahih al-Bukhari 100]

Imam Nawawi defines seizing plainly. It “is not its erasure from the breasts of those who have memorized it. Rather, its meaning is that its bearers die, and people take ignorant men who judge by their ignorance, so they lead astray and are led astray.” [al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-‘Ilm: Bab Raf’ al-‘Ilm] Ibn Hajar reaches the same place from the other side, reporting Ibn al-Munayyir on the phrase “by snatching it away”: “The erasure of knowledge from the breasts is possible within Allah’s power, except that this hadith indicates that it does not occur.” [Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, on Bukhari 100] The wiping of knowledge out of hearts is precisely what the hadith denies.

Imam Qastallani names both halves. The mode ruled out is “that He raise it up to the sky or erase it from their breasts,” [al-Qastallani, Irshad al-Sari], and the mode affirmed is the taking of the scholars’ souls and the death of those who bear it. Badr al-Din al-Ayni then supplies the mechanism, following Ibn Battal: knowledge is not taken back from those it was given to; “rather its removal comes about through their squandering of knowledge, so that no one is found to succeed those who have passed.” [al-Ayni, Umdat al-Qari, on Bukhari 100] On the ignorant heads, he says the ignorance meant covers the simple kind and the compound kind alike, and that the warning falls on unqualified judges as much as on unqualified muftis (scholars authorized to issue formal religious rulings).

The Second Hadith: A Group Remains Upon the Truth

Now the second hadith. Thawban (Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “A group of my umma will remain manifest upon the truth. Those who fail them will not harm them, until the command of Allah comes while they are in that state.” [Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Imara]

Imam Bukhari defines that group in his own chapter title: “Chapter: the saying of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), ‘A group of my umma will remain manifest upon the truth, fighting,’ and they are the people of knowledge.” [Sahih al-Bukhari 7311] Ibn Hajar notes that the closing words there are al-Bukhari’s own, and reports Ali ibn al-Madini and Imam Ahmad identifying the group with the scholars of hadith. Imam Nawawi widens the definition without loosening it: “It is possible that this group is distributed among the kinds of believers. Among them are brave fighters, among them jurists, among them hadith scholars, among them ascetics and those who enjoin the good and forbid the wrong, and among them are people of other kinds of good. It is not necessary that they be gathered together; they may well be scattered across the regions of the earth.” [al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim] The saved group is defined as the bearers of knowledge and those who live by it, wherever they happen to be.

Reconciling the Two Hadiths

The commentators then face your question directly. Ibn Hajar raises it in the Book of Holding Fast to the Book and the Sunna, where the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr is used to argue that an age may be empty of a mujtahid (a scholar qualified to derive rulings directly from the revealed sources). He records the objection from the hadith of the remaining group and answers it: “The answer given, first, is that it is explicit about there being no such emptiness, not about denying that it is possible; and second, that the evidence for the first position is clearer, since it states plainly the seizing of knowledge at one point and its being raised at another, unlike the second.” [Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, Vol. 13, on Bukhari 7311] He then puts the two texts on one timeline: the absolute mujtahids are taken first, then those of restricted ijtihad (independent legal reasoning from the revealed sources), then those with any attachment to knowledge at all, and only at the very end, near the wind that takes the soul of every believer, is the earth empty of a scholar.

Badr al-Din al-Ayni reports the same resolution from Dawudi: “This hadith came out in the form of a general statement, but what is meant by it is particular, on account of his saying (Allah bless him and give him peace), ‘A group of my umma will remain manifest upon the truth until the command of Allah comes.'” [Ayni, Umdat al-Qari] The general wording is read in the light of the specific promise.

See what those definitions entail. If seizing knowledge means the death of its bearers, then Imam Munawi’s summary follows on its own: “the seizing of knowledge is the death of those who carry it, not its erasure from them.” [Munawi, Fayd al-Qadir] Nothing in that touches the revealed text, and nothing in it touches the men Allah raises up in the generation after. And if the saved group is defined as the people of knowledge, then its survival is a statement about who is present in the world, not about whether the Quran is safe.

What the Verse Guarantees

The verse settles that second half. Allah Most High says, “Verily We Ourselves have sent down the Remindance; And verily it We shall ever preserve.” [Quran 15:9; Keller, The Quran Beheld] Imam Nasafi writes that Allah “sent it down guarded from the devils, and He preserves it at every moment from addition, subtraction, distortion, and substitution, unlike the earlier scriptures, whose safekeeping He did not undertake Himself but entrusted to the rabbis and the learned, who then differed among themselves out of transgression, so distortion occurred; and He did not consign the Quran to the keeping of any other than Himself.” [Abu al-Barakat al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil] The guarantee is on the revealed Book. It was never a guarantee that every century and every land would be full of scholars.

So the two were never in competition. One tells you how the Quran is kept. The other tells you how knowledge leaves a people: by the deaths of those who carry it and by the failure of the living to take it from them while they are here. The hadith describes the far end of that arc, and, in smaller form, what happens wherever a generation lets its scholarship die and then asks the unqualified for answers.

The Remedy Within the Warning

The warning has its remedy inside it. Attach yourself to one qualified teacher you can actually study with, in person or online, and stay with him for years rather than months, taking texts in a real order: the essentials of belief, then the personal fiqh you are accountable for. And before you accept a ruling from anyone, ask who his teachers were and what he read with them. A hadith about knowledge departing is not given to us so that we watch it happen.
references: al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-‘Ilm: Bab Raf’ al-‘Ilm
Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, on Bukhari 100
Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, Vol. 13, on Bukhari 7311

records.title: Is It Sinful to Say “God Forbid” About Something Allah Has Actually Forbidden?
records.question: My friend said, “God forbid, we don’t want to date anyone,” about something Allah has genuinely prohibited, and she seemed to be using it loosely as a complaint; is that permissible for her, and am I in sin for not correcting her on the spot?
records.answer:
Your friend has not sinned, and neither have you.

“God forbid” is an idiom of aversion in English. It means, “May this never come near me,” and that is how everyone in the conversation understood her. She was expressing her own dislike of dating, not asking Allah to withdraw a prohibition He has placed. What governs here is meaning and register, not the bare shape of the words. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Actions are but by their intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended.” [Agreed upon]

A Noteworthy Observation You Made

You have noticed something real, though, and it deserves to be named rather than waved away. If someone genuinely meant “I wish Allah had not forbidden this,” and was content to hold that wish, the matter would be grave: that is, objecting to a known ruling of the religion, not merely careless speech. But that requires meaning it. A loose idiom is not that, and we do not assign to a Muslim a meaning she did not hold.

So the counsel is only this: prefer wording that says what you mean. “Allah protect us from it,” or simply “I want nothing to do with it,” carries no ambiguity at all. Formulas that invoke Allah lightly are worth dropping from habitual speech, even where they carry no legal consequence.

You are not sinful for staying quiet. Correcting a wrong becomes incumbent only when several conditions hold together: that you know the ruling with certainty, that the wrong is actual and evident, that speaking is likely to benefit, and that it will not bring about greater harm [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din]. Here, there was no established wrong to correct, and you were not certain one existed.

And yes, you are excused for not having known. Innocent ignorance is excused where a person has not been negligent about learning; culpable ignorance, where one had access and did not bother, is not. You were unsure in the moment, and you went and asked. That is the whole of what was asked of you.

Intent and Register Govern, Not the Wording

An idiom of aversion is not an objection to Allah’s ruling, and there is nothing here for you to undo. So, if the friendship allows it, offer her a better phrase in passing another time, rather than a correction. And take some ease from the care itself. Noticing how ordinary words brush against Allah’s rulings is the beginning of guarding the tongue, not a sign that you have failed at it.

records.title: Have My Broken Promises to Allah Made Me a Hypocrite Forever?
records.question: Since I was twelve, I have gone through repeated cycles of praying, then abandoning prayer, each time promising Allah I would change, and breaking every promise. After a difficult period that included a death in my family, a hatred toward Allah, the Prophet, and Islam entered my heart that I never chose and do not want. Having then read the verse about hypocrisy settling in the heart until the Day one meets Him, I am terrified that this makes me a permanent hypocrite, and I do not know whether what I was doing all these years was simply ignorance. I am also struggling with depression.
records.answer:
This is a heavy burden to carry. May Allah bless you for reaching out and asking.

What you describe is not the hypocrisy the Quran is speaking of. Hypocrisy (nifaq) in that sense is a settled inward rejection of faith worn behind an outward profession of it, which is a different thing from weakness, laziness, and broken resolve.

The Marks of a Hypocrite

Imam Nawawi (Allah have mercy on him), explaining the Prophet’s words about the marks of a hypocrite, draws the line where you need it drawn: such a person’s hypocrisy is toward those he has dealt with, “not that he is a hypocrite in Islam, professing it outwardly while concealing disbelief within; and the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) did not mean by this that he is a hypocrite with the hypocrisy of the disbelievers who abide forever in the lowest depth of the Fire.” [Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim]

Missed prayers, broken vows, and the private sins of a boy sent to a hostel at twelve are matters that call for sincere repentance. But these aren’t acts of disbelief—nor do they alone make you a hypocrite.

The Verse That Frightened You Has a Companion Verse

The verse you read describes people who made a covenant with Allah, broke it, and hardened into concealment: “So He repaid them with deep-rooted sick hypocrisy in their hearts till the very day they meet Him, for breaking faith with Allah to do what they promised Him, and that they ever lied and lied.” [Quran 9:77; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Read a little further in the same sura, and you meet a different man: “And there are others from both of these who have admitted their sins: They have added righteous deed to ill; Allah may well soon relent towards them; Verily Allah is all-forgiving, all-compassionate.” [Quran 9:102; Keller, The Quran Beheld] One man hides what he is and persists; the other admits it, has good mixed in with the bad, and is met with mercy rather than a sentence. You have just written out your failures in full to a stranger because they grieve you. You are the second man.

Hatred That Visits the Heart Is Not Disbelief Nor Hypocrisy

Now, the thing that frightens you most. Companions came to the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) and told him they had found within themselves things that any of them would find too terrible to say aloud. He asked, “Have you found that?” They said yes. He said, “That is pure faith.” [Sahih Muslim]

Imam Khattabi (Allah have mercy on him) explains the meaning: what was called pure faith is not the whispering itself, but the thing in you that finds such a thought enormous and refuses what the devil throws into your heart, and without it you would not have recoiled at all [Khattabi, Gharib al-Hadith]. So do not argue with the thought, do not test yourself against it, and do not renew your Islam over it. Leave this, and let it go. May Allah bless you.

Fear of Hypocrisy Is the Believer’s Own Mark

Notice what your fear is telling you. Imam Bukhari (Allah have mercy on him) opens a chapter of his Sahih on the believer’s fear that his deeds may come to nothing, and records there the words of Ibn Abi Mulayka (Allah have mercy on him): “I met thirty of the Companions of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), every one of them fearing hypocrisy for himself.” He then mentions from Imam al-Hasan al-Basri (Allah have mercy on him): “None fears it but a believer, and none feels safe from it but a hypocrite.” [Sahih al-Bukhari]

A hypocrite is not the man lying awake at twenty-one, terrified of hypocrisy. He is comfortable. Your terror is the wrong evidence for the case you have built against yourself.

Begin With the Next Prayer

The way back is not another grand promise. You have made those; they broke under you, and each break cost you more than the one before, so stop promising. Pray the next prayer that comes, then the one after it, and when you fall, get up without a new vow. Find one teacher or imam you can speak to and tell him what you told me.

Since you say you are depressed, speak to a doctor as well; a mind and body that are unwell make worship feel like a heavy burden, and treating that is part of caring for what Allah entrusted to you.

That sura does not end in hypocrisy. It ends with three men left in the narrowness of the earth until they turned back, and “He has truly forgiven the three men whose judgement was deferred.” [Quran 9:118; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Turn to Allah Most Merciful at the next call to prayer, and do not decide about yourself what your Lord has not decided about you.

records.title: May I Sell Replica Branded Goods Online?
records.question: I sell replica, or “first copy,” branded products—shipped directly from the manufacturer to the customer—and I openly tell every buyer that the item is a copy. Most already know this and buy it precisely because they cannot afford the original, so there is no deception in the sale itself. Given that transparency, is this business permissible? Does infringing the brand’s trademark make it impermissible on its own? And does it matter that local law treats the sale of such goods as illegal?
records.answer:
Selling a replica is lawful in itself, but selling goods that carry another company’s trademark is not, and your transparency with the buyer does not change that. If the item you ship bears a specific business mark, such as Nike or Gucci, this is impermissible. If it is an unbranded item of similar cut and quality, sold as what it is, you may sell it freely.

You are right that there is no deception between you and your customer, and it is to your credit that you looked at this closely. That closes one door of objection. The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Whoever deceives is not of us.” [Sahih Muslim] He said it of a seller who had hidden wet grain beneath dry, so its force is deception of the one you deal with, and your buyer is not deceived. My own reading is that the mark keeps speaking after he takes delivery, telling everyone who sees the bag that Nike made it. That is my reasoning rather than the scope of the hadith, so the ruling does not rest on it.

The heavier matter is the mark itself, and you should know where the ruling comes from. Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) gives the Hanafi definition of wealth: “What is meant by wealth is what the natural disposition inclines towards and what can be stored against time of need, and the character of wealth is established by people treating a thing as wealth, whether all of them or some of them.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar] That clause about storing is why the school has generally held that a bare right is not wealth at all, and a trademark is a bare right before it is anything else. What settles it is a considered contemporary judgment resting on that last clause, the one about what people in fact treat as wealth.

Mufti Taqi Usmani (Allah preserve him) makes that judgment in Buhuth fi Qadaya Fiqhiyya Muasira. He grants that the right in a trade name or a mark is in origin a bare right, not settled in any standing object, then holds that registration alters its standing: “it is also true of it that it is stored against time of need, so the elements that confer on a thing the character of wealth are present in it, save that it is not an object standing by itself.” [Taqi Usmani, Buhuth fi Qadaya Fiqhiyya Muasira] He allows dealing in a registered mark on two conditions, the second being that it must not mislead consumers. The Fiqh Academy of the Organization of the Islamic Conference reached the same place at its fifth session in Kuwait, holding that trade names and marks have come to carry a recognized monetary value in contemporary custom because people treat them as wealth, and that “these rights are recognized in the Shariah, so it is not lawful to infringe them.” [Wahba al-Zuhayli, al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuhu]

Take the mark as the holder’s property, and the settled Hanafi rule follows: “No one may dispose of another’s property without his permission.” [Majallat al-Ahkam al-Adliyya] Reproducing the swoosh without Nike’s leave is taking what is not yours, and full disclosure to your customer does not cure it, because the wrong is not against him. That step is my own, and I would rather you saw it as a judgment than as a line lifted out of an old book.

The law of your country weighs on its own as well. Allah Most High says, “O you who believe, fulfill your binding obligations” [Quran 5:1; Keller, The Quran Beheld], and a Muslim living under a country’s protection has undertaken to keep its laws. Where counterfeit goods are unlawful to sell, you are exposing yourself to seizure and prosecution, and your customers to losing their parcels at the border. That the manufacturer ships directly and you never handle the goods does not lift liability from you.

You may have seen two answers on our site that seem to pull in opposite directions. Mawlana Ilyas Patel (Allah preserve him) permits acknowledged replicas; my own answer on placing a brand logo without authorization forbids it. Read his second condition, and they meet: he permits the replica so long as “one does not falsely hold the original trademark.” A generic garment of the same make, sold as itself, is what he is allowing. A “first copy” bearing the brand’s mark is what I was referring to, and that one stays closed.

The way forward is wide. Source unbranded goods of the same quality from the same factories, price them honestly, and put your own name on them. Many of these manufacturers will ship without any markings at all if you ask. You would be serving the same customer, at the same price, with the same product, and nothing would be hanging over the earnings.
references: Taqi Usmani, Buhuth fi Qadaya Fiqhiyya Muasira
Wahba al-Zuhayli, al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuhu

records.title: Does the Bracketed Note in the Hilali-Khan Rendering of Quran 47:4 Reflect the Verse?
records.question: The Hilali-Khan translation brackets a note at Quran 47:4, after “until the war lays down its burdens,” saying one must fight the disbelievers until they accept Islam or submit to Muslim rule—seemingly glossing the word “dhalika,” though Tabari, Ibn Kathir, and Ma’ariful Quran read it no such way. Is the bracket sound, or does it import 9:29’s ruling into 47:4? Does 47:4 impose a standing duty to fight, or only govern a war already underway? Does the perpetual-war reading rest on 9:5 having abrogated 8:61, 60:8, and 2:256? And is Hilali-Khan the right translation for a non-Muslim reader who cannot tell a bracket from the text?
records.answer:
The bracketed sentence is not a translation of the word it sits beside, and no classical commentator reads that word as the bracket does. They take dhalika as standing in for an omitted subject: the matter is as has just been stated. Imam Qurtubi (Allah have mercy on him) gives three constructions of it, all to that effect, and adds that it is a word an eloquent speaker uses when moving from one stretch of speech to the next [Imam Qurtubi, al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, on Q. 47:4].

Imam Nasafi (Allah have mercy on him) glosses it the same way in his Hanafi commentary: the matter is thus, subject and predicate, or else do that to them [Imam Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on Q. 47:4].

There is an English witness too. Shaykh Nuh Keller’s (Allah preserve him) certified translation gives the word as “Even thus,” and adds nothing [Quran 47:4; Keller, The Quran Beheld].

Your survey is accurate. Ibn Kathir (Allah have mercy on him) does not comment on dhalika at all, and neither he nor Imam Tabari (Allah have mercy on him) hangs a war aim on it.

That bracket’s content does exist in the tradition, but not here. Part of it belongs to the clause before it, whose terminus the commentators debate: “until the war lays down its burdensome plate and arms.” [Quran 47:4; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

The rest, the alternative of paying the poll tax (jizya), belongs to the verse that mentions it: “until they pay the poll-tax in place of armed duty out of hand, meekly humbled.” [Quran 9:29; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Carrying one verse’s ruling into another’s brackets, with nothing to mark the move, is the fault you have put your finger on.

Does 47:4 Impose a Standing Obligation to Fight?

As for whether 47:4 imposes a continuing obligation to fight until people accept Islam or pay the poll-tax, it does not, and the grammar settles much of it. Abu Hayyan (Allah have mercy on him) holds that the apparent sense attaches the terminus to the command to bind the captives firmly [Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit, on Q. 47:4].

Imam Razi (Allah have mercy on him) attaches it instead to the command to fight, so the syntax is disputed. The subject matter is not. On either reading, the passage governs conduct inside an engagement already underway, and Ibn Kathir puts its end plainly: once the war has run its course and the battle has broken off, you may free the captives or take a ransom [Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, on Q. 47:4].

Imam Tabari gives his verdict in as many words: the sound view is that the verse is operative and unabrogated (muhkam) [Imam Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, on Q. 47:4].

Read that verdict narrowly. He is ruling on the clause of release and ransom, and he goes on to say that there is nothing objectionable in the choice between release, ransom and execution resting with the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) and those who lead the community after him, permission to kill having been given in another verse [Imam Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, on Q. 47:4].

Where the early authorities did claim abrogation in 47:4, that clause is what they meant: the question was what an imam may do with a prisoner in hand. Ibn al-Jawzi (Allah have mercy on him) and Imam Qurtubi both report the well-known Hanafi position that the verse of the sword abrogated it. The dispute is about prisoners, not a standing aim of fighting.

Imam Bayhaqi (Allah have mercy on him) puts one side sharply. He records that al-Hajjaj handed a captive to Ibn Umar (Allah be pleased with him) to be executed, and Ibn Umar refused, saying that this is not what Allah commanded us, then recited this verse. Bayhaqi takes that to show the verse was muhkam in his view, and asks how it could be abrogated when Allah tied it to a terminus [Imam Bayhaqi, Ma’rifat al-Sunan wa’l-Athar].

The other side sits on the same page. Imam Qurtubi carries Ibn al-Arabi’s (Allah have mercy on him) objection: the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) both said this and did it, and Allah’s naming of release and ransom forbids nothing He did not name, just as He set out the lashing for fornication while the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) set out the stoning. Perhaps Ibn Umar disliked the business coming from al-Hajjaj’s hand [Imam Qurtubi, al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, on Q. 47:4].

The commentators also differed over what the terminus refers to: the idolaters abandoning their idolatry, which is Imam Tabari’s gloss; the descent of Sayyiduna Isa (upon him be peace), which he transmits from Mujahid (Allah have mercy on him); and Ibn Atiyya’s (Allah have mercy on him) reading of it as a figure for the duration of the war. Each answers when the fighting ends, and none makes poll tax the point at which it stops.

The Abrogation Claim Behind the Perpetual-War Reading

Now to the abrogation claim, where the real weight of your question lies. That one verse canceled the verses of peace and of no compulsion was held by some early authorities, but it was never settled, and rarely means what a modern reader hears in it.

Take 8:61 first. Imam Tabari, whom you have read, met this claim and rejected it. A text abrogates, he argues, only where it negates the other’s ruling in every respect, and that is not met here: one verse concerns a people with whom peace was permitted, the other those from whom no tribute was accepted, so each is operative in the matter it was revealed about [Imam Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, on Q. 8:61].

The verse he was defending reads: “And if they turn toward peace, then turn towards it and trust to Allah; Verily He is the All-hearing, the All-knowing.” [Quran 8:61; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

On 2:256, Imam Qurtubi lists six positions, with abrogation not being the settled one. The second is that the verse is not abrogated at all, held by al-Sha’bi (Allah have mercy on him), al-Hasan al-Basri (Allah have mercy on him), Qatada (Allah have mercy on him), and al-Dahhak (Allah have mercy on him), and supported by Umar (Allah be pleased with him), inviting an elderly Christian woman to Islam and accepting her refusal [Imam Qurtubi, al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, on Q. 2:256].

Ibn Kathir reports the same split and calls the non-abrogation side the majority [Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, on Q. 2:256].

The verse opens as plainly as it sounds: “There is no compelling anyone to enter the faith: The right is plain from the wrong.” [Quran 2:256; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Nor does 60:8 need rescuing. Allah Most High says, “Allah does not forbid you from those who have not fought against you in religion or expelled you from your homes to be good and kind to them and show them justice: Verily Allah loves the thoroughly just.” [Quran 60:8; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Underneath this sits a point of legal theory that dissolves much of the conflict. Imam Shatibi (Allah have mercy on him) states it plainly: abrogation (naskh) in the usage of the early authorities is more general than in the language of the legal theorists, who keep the word for the lifting of a ruling by a later text, whereas the early would also call it abrogation to restrict an unrestricted text, to specify a general one, or to clarify one that was ambiguous or undetailed [Imam Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat].

So when an early authority says the sword verse abrogated a verse of peace, he may mean only that a general expression was specified, or a situation distinguished. Tallies of a hundred and twenty abrogated verses or more rest on that usage, and cannot carry the weight a perpetual-war reading puts on them.

Which Translation to Give Him

On the translation, give him the Saheeh International. Your reason for asking is the right reason to decide it. The Noble Qur’an sets its interpolations in brackets that a reader with no Arabic cannot tell from the text, and some, as you have found, carry claims the verse does not make. What he takes away from 47:4 will be the bracket. Keep your own copy if its notes serve you, since you can check a bracket against the Arabic; it is the wrong book for a reader who cannot.

Your instinct here was sound.
references: Imam Qurtubi, al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, on Q. 47:4
Imam Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on Q. 47:4
Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit, on Q. 47:4
Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, on Q. 47:4
Imam Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, on Q. 47:4
Imam Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, on Q. 8:61
Imam Qurtubi, al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, on Q. 2:256
Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, on Q. 2:256

records.title: Is It Disbelief to Rate a Film Highly When It Contains Kufr?
records.question: I rate films publicly, and some of them contain disbelief (kufr), such as references to Greek gods or a blasphemous line from a character. If I rate one highly for its story, acting, and direction while rejecting its disbelief, is that itself disbelief? Would a low rating be disbelief, too?
records.answer:
Rating a film highly for its craft is not disbelief, and neither is rating it low. Contentment with disbelief (al-rida bi-l-kufr) attaches to the disbelief itself. The Kuwaiti Fiqh Encyclopedia gives the case of a man who refuses to teach the word of Divine Oneness (Tawhid) to a non-Muslim seeking Islam: he “is a disbeliever, because he was content with disbelief.” [al-Mawsua al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 42:307] A score for story, acting, and direction says the work is well made. It says nothing about the truth of what a character says inside it.

Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) records what the Hanafi muftis work by, citing the Tatarkhaniyya: no one is declared a disbeliever on what is merely possible, “because disbelief is the utmost punishment, so it demands the utmost crime, and where there is only possibility there is no utmost.” What is settled is “that no verdict of disbelief is issued against a Muslim whose speech can bear a sound construal.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar] You supplied that construal yourself, twice. What you intend by a score is what that score counts for. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Actions are but by their intentions.” [Nawawi, Riyad al-Salihin]

Two Things Worth Your Care

Neither touches your faith. Your score is public, and a high one sends people to the film. Keep that in mind. The other is a matter of company, not of creed. Imam Qurtubi (Allah have mercy on him) is speaking about sitting where the sacred is mocked, not about your verdict on a film’s craft. He held that avoiding open sinners becomes obligatory “when a wrong appears from them, because whoever does not avoid them has been content with their act.” [al-Mawsua al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 42:176] Where blasphemy is an incident, that is one thing; where mockery is the substance, leave the film unwatched and unrated.

Your Faith Was Never in the Rating

Your second question, whether a low rating would also be kufr, is the useful one. A fear that follows the number up and down is fastened to the rating, not to what you believe. So appraise the craft, and let this question rest. The heart that recoiled at that line is the heart Allah gave you.

records.title: Must a Man Learn the Rulings of Menstruation?
records.question: As a man, am I obliged to learn the rulings of menstruation (hayd) taught in Level One of Ascent to Felicity, and do I need all of it for the Level One certificate?
records.answer:
No, you are not obliged to learn the whole chapter as Level One teaches it. In the Hanafi school, what binds you personally is what your own state requires, and if you are married or heading there, part of this chapter is genuinely yours. In practice, that is a short list: when intimacy becomes unlawful and when it becomes lawful again, how to tell menstruation from irregular bleeding (istihada) when your wife is unsure, and what to do if you get it wrong. The rest is hers to learn, and you are not answerable for it.

The Kuwaiti Encyclopedia of Fiqh (al-Mawsua al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya) states it in a line: “Learning is sometimes a personal obligation (fard ayn), and that is the learning of what one cannot do without.” [al-Mawsua al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 13:6] This is the knowledge of one’s own state (ilm al-hal), and it moves as your life moves.

The Encyclopedia puts the learning of this chapter on the woman, and on her husband the duty to teach her if he knows, or to let her ask the scholars. You may not stand between your wife and the answer. Ibn Nujaym (Allah have mercy on him) adds that knowing its questions “is among the most important matters, for the countless rulings that rest upon it, such as purity, prayer, the recitation of the Quran, fasting, spiritual retreat, hajj, and the coming of legal majority.” [al-Mawsua al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 18:293]

The Quran puts your share in front of men:

(وَيَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الْمَحِيضِ قُلْ هُوَ أَذًى فَاعْتَزِلُوا النِّسَاءَ فِي الْمَحِيضِ)

“And they ask you about menstruation; Say: It is foul, so leave off from women while in their menses.” [Quran 2:222; Keller, The Quran Beheld] Men asked, and the command came down addressed to men. When intimacy becomes lawful again, it turns on how her bleeding ended, and the cost of guessing falls on you.

Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) warns: “Know that the chapter of menstruation is among the most intricate of chapters.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar 1:282] A chapter of that kind is not one you pick up on the night you first need it, from a search engine or from a spouse who may be unsure herself.

For the certificate, you complete the whole of Level One, including this chapter. That is a course requirement, not a ruling on you: a course may teach more than binds any student in the room, and what binds you does not shrink a syllabus. Write to the Academy team for the exact requirements; I would sooner send you than guess.

Take the Lessons Now

Your state will change, and what you owe changes with it. Learn it now, while someone is explaining it to you. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Whomever Allah wishes well for, He gives understanding of the religion.” [Bukhari; Muslim] Nothing you learn in Level One will be wasted on you.

records.title: Why Have I Relapsed into Pornography and What Do I Do Now?
records.question: I am nineteen. I left pornography and masturbation for three or four months, and my prayers and my life were in order. For the past three weeks, I have relapsed. It feels as though something has taken control of me, and I have no one to talk to about it.
records.answer:
I hear the fear in your question, and fear like that is not the sound of ruin; it is the sound of a heart still alive. What has taken hold of you these three weeks is a habit and not a possession; it has not taken you out of your religion, and it is undone the way habits are undone, by cutting off the means that feed it rather than by testing your will against them. Repentance is open to you tonight, and open again every time you fall, so the work in front of you is to close the doors that stand between you and Allah.

Imam Zabidi (Allah have mercy on him) carries in his commentary on the Ihya the words of Imam Abu Talib al-Makki (Allah have mercy on him): “then let the repentant not take on from a sin a habit that makes repenting from it hard for him, for habit is one of the armies of Allah Most High; were it not for habit all people would be repentant, and were it not for trial all people would be upright.” [Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin, Kitab al-Tawba] Three or four good months did not make you invulnerable. They quieted the habit while the means were out of reach, and when the means came back, the old road opened in a single evening. That is the ordinary working of the self, and our tradition has a plan for it.

What Repentance Asks of You, and Where Relapse Is Won

Imam Ghazali (Allah have mercy on him) writes that among the meanings of repentance are “leaving acts of disobedience in the present, resolving to leave them in the future, and making up for what was neglected in past states, and there is no doubt as to the obligation of that,” and he adds that “as for remorse over what has passed and grief over it, that is obligatory, and it is the spirit of repentance, and by it the making good is complete.” [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din 4:5] He is naming meanings rather than counting parts, and notice where that leaves you. The sorrow you already carry is the spirit of the thing, so you are not starting from nothing. What decides the next three weeks is the resolve, and resolve here is not a feeling. It is a set of doors you close.

Block the Means Before You Test Your Strength

This is where most sincere young men lose the ground they gained. Imam Ghazali warns that a person still weak in resolve should not walk into the situation where appetite is stirred and the means are at hand, and then hope to hold himself back at the edge: “Rather, the way is to flee from the very beginnings of the causes that make it easy for him, until he blocks off its roads against himself, striving meanwhile to break his appetite as much as he can. By this, his repentance is kept safe at the outset.” [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din 4:44] The same passage in Zabidi’s commentary states the rule in a line worth memorizing: “… and every cause that invites to disobedience or calls disobedience to mind is itself disobedience, and every cause that ends in a sin and leads to it is itself a sin; and if it is permitted in itself, cutting it off is an act of obedience. This is among the subtleties of works.” [Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin, Kitab al-Tawba]

Read that as a practical instruction. The phone that carries you there does not sleep in your room, and the hour before bed is not spent alone with a screen. Install a filter you cannot remove by yourself, and give the password to someone older whom you respect. Leave the accounts and feeds that put images in front of you, even ones lawful in themselves, because for you, they are the road. None of this is weakness; cutting the cause is itself worship.

Heedlessness Is the Door: What You Watch and What You Scroll

You wrote that it felt as though something overtook you. Something did, and it has a name in our books: heedlessness (ghafla), the state in which the eye wanders and the heart follows without a decision ever being made. Imam Khadimi (Allah have mercy on him), in his commentary on Imam Birgivi’s al-Tariqa al-Muhammadiyya, presses the discipline of the eye to this point: “… so that leaving a mote of what Allah has forbidden is better than the worship of men and jinn together, especially at the moment of craving and of opportunity.” [Khadimi, al-Bariqa al-Mahmudiyya 4:57] That moment, craving plus opportunity, is the whole battle. Mindless scrolling is how you arrive there without noticing that you were walking.

(وَأَمَّا مَنْ خَافَ مَقَامَ رَبِّهِ وَنَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَى﴾ ﴿فَإِنَّ الْجَنَّةَ هِيَ الْمَأْوَى)

“And as for him who feared to stand in judgement before his Lord, and forbade his self its willful folly; Verily the lush grove of paradise shall be the refuge.” [Quran 79:40-41; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Your fear sits in the same verse as the forbidding of the self. Use it while it is fresh. And do not leave the emptied hour empty: the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Be mindful of Allah wherever you are, follow a wrong deed with a good one and it will wipe it out, and meet people with beautiful character.” [Tirmidhi] Give that hour to the Quran, to sleep, to the gym, to your studies. An hour with nothing in it will be filled by the habit.

Company Does What Willpower Cannot

You said you have no one to discuss this with, and that is the most dangerous fact in your letter. The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “The likeness of the righteous companion and the evil companion is but as the carrier of musk and the blower of the bellows: as for the carrier of musk, either he gives you some, or you buy from him, or you catch a pleasant scent from him; and as for the blower of the bellows, either he burns your clothes, or you catch a foul smell from him.” [Bukhari; Muslim] Imam Khadimi relays the saying that “sitting in a gathering of knowledge is better than keeping vigil for a whole night.” [Khadimi, al-Bariqa al-Mahmudiyya 4:163] Company is the setting in which a habit either starves or is fed.

So put company on a schedule: one weekly circle of knowledge at a fixed hour, in the masjid or online, and one older brother or teacher you tell the truth to, before the fall and after it. If the compulsion keeps feeling beyond your control, there is no shame in adding a qualified counselor. Seeking treatment is no retreat from repentance; it is part of blocking the means.

Two Rakas Tonight, and the Shame You Feel Is the Beginning of the Cure

Do not wait for a better version of yourself before you turn back. Sayyiduna Abu Bakr (Allah be pleased with him) related that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “There is no man who commits a sin, then rises and purifies himself, then prays, then seeks Allah’s forgiveness, except that Allah forgives him,” and he then recited the verse of Al Imran, “… those who when they commit a heinous deed or wrong themselves, remember Allah and ask forgiveness for their sins …” [Tirmidhi] That is the prayer of repentance: make wudu, pray two rakas, ask. Pray it tonight. Pray it again every time you fall, without argument and without delay, so that no sin is ever left standing between you and Allah.

And take this from Ibn Ata’illah (Allah have mercy on him), who put your case in a single line: “The root of every act of disobedience, of heedlessness, and of appetite is being pleased with oneself; and the root of every act of obedience, of wakefulness, and of chastity is your not being pleased with the self.” [Ibn Ata’illah, al-Hikam al-Ataiyya] You are not pleased with yourself tonight. Keep that, and do not let it curdle into despair, because it is the ground in which obedience, wakefulness, and chastity grow. Close the doors, keep the company, pray your two rakas, and let Allah do with your nineteen years what He does with soil that has been turned over.
references: Zabidi, Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin, Kitab al-Tawba

records.title: Do My Sunna Rak’as Count Toward a Vow to Pray Two Extra Rak’as Daily?
records.question: I made a vow to pray two extra rak’as daily for thirty days. By “extra,” I meant two in addition to the obligatory prayers, not necessarily in addition to the regular sunnas. When I made the vow, I intended in my heart that I could fulfill it either by praying two separate voluntary rak’as or by praying the regular two-rak’a sunna, though I did not say this aloud. So far, I have been praying the regular sunna with the intention that those same rak’as fulfill the vow while also being the sunna, and I have not prayed separate rak’as for the vow. Is this valid? Do the sunna rak’as I have already prayed count toward the thirty days? If not, must I repeat all thirty?
records.answer:
What you have been doing is valid, and the days you have already prayed count toward your vow. You do not have to repeat the thirty days.

A Vow Binds You to What You Meant, Not to Every Possible Reading

A vow binds you to what you actually meant, not to the widest sense your words could carry. Where the wording admits more than one reading, the Hanafi jurists give effect to the intention of the one who vowed: “This is where he had no intention; but where there was an intention, what he intended is binding on him.” [Shaykhizada, Majma’a al-Anhur] You meant the word extra to mean extra to the fard, and you had it in mind at the time that the regular sunna could serve. That is the vow you made, and you are not held to a stricter one than you never intended.

A Vowed Prayer That Coincides With the Sunna Is Covered by the Same Rak’as

The school also treats a vowed prayer that coincides with the sunna as covered by a single performance. The Fatawa al-Hindiyya records: “If he vows the sunnas and performs what he vowed, it is the sunna. And Taj al-Din, the father of the author of al-Muhit, said he is not thereby performing the sunna, because once he bound himself to it, it became another prayer, and so it does not stand in place of the sunna.” [al-Fatawa al-Hindiyya] The Hindiyya gives the first ruling plainly and names the second as the view of a single jurist, so what you have prayed so far stands.

For What’s Left, Take the Safer Road Without Restarting the Count

Because there is a real difference of view here, and because this is an obligation you placed on yourself, take the safer road for what is left. For the remaining days, pray your regular two-rak’a sunna as you always do, and then pray two separate rak’as with the intention of the vow alone. That is a few extra minutes a day, and it puts the matter beyond dispute. Do not restart the count.

Be Sparing With Vows Going Forward

After these thirty days are done, be sparing with vows. What you are already doing for the sake of Allah is better left as a gift than turned into a debt.

records.title: May I Accept a Discount Shopkeepers Give Me Because of My Government Uniform?
records.question: I am a government employee. Sometimes when I am in uniform and use a shopkeeper’s services, he reduces the bill or refuses to take my money at all. Is this unlawful?
records.answer:
The discount is not yours to take. A benefit that reaches you because of your post belongs to the office you serve and not to you, so unless your department has authorized its staff to accept such reductions, pay the bill in full.

The Discount Belongs to Your Office, Not to You

That is the reasoning the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) gave himself. He appointed a man to oversee the zakat of Banu Sulaym, and upon his return, the man said, “This is what belongs to you, and this is a gift given to me.” He answered, “Why did you not sit in your father’s house and your mother’s house until your gift came to you, if you were truthful?” [Bukhari] Ibn al-Humam (Allah have mercy on him) reads that reply as a statement of cause: “the reasoning of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) is proof of the prohibition of a gift whose cause is the office.” [Ibn al-Humam, Fath al-Qadir] On the same page, he carries it past the judge: anyone who does work on behalf of the Muslims stands where the judge stands in the matter of gifts. Your post is such work. The shopkeeper is not reducing the bill for you but for the uniform, and the uniform is your department’s.

Your Department Can Lift the Bar, but You Cannot Decide That Yourself

Then comes the exception, and it is where your question sits. Because the benefit belongs to the office, only the office can release it. Ibn Hajar (Allah have mercy on him) says as much in his commentary on this hadith, noting that it bars officials from taking a gift from anyone who has a matter before them, then adding: “and that holds where the authority has not given him leave in the matter.” [Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari] So, where your department has authorized the benefit for its staff, by a written policy or by a settled practice your superiors know of and allow, the bar is lifted. What you may not do is settle the question yourself, so ask your line manager or read the service rules.

Let me be plain about how our Hanafi school reaches that. Its books do not take up staff discounts in the chapter on gifts to officeholders. What they give is the general rule of property, in Imam Haskafi’s (Allah have mercy on him) words: “it is not permitted to dispose of another man’s property without his leave, nor without authority over it, except in cases mentioned in al-Ashbah.” [Haskafi, al-Durr al-Mukhtar] Read that closing clause, because it is the half that helps you. Ibn Abidin’s (Allah have mercy on him) commentary gathers there the cases in which a man may deal with another’s property without express leave, and ends on the rule that leave found by indication counts even where none was given in words. Applying it to your case is reasoning from a principle rather than a ruling written for you. It is the right principle, and it lands where Ibn Hajar lands.

A Discount From Someone With Business Before Your Office Is Never Clean

One thing no policy can settle. A discount offered to all staff by a trader who has nothing to do with your office is one matter. A discount from a man who needs something from your department now or may need it next month is another. Imam Zayla’i (Allah have mercy on him), writing of the judge, permits the gift of a close relative and of a man whose habit of giving was established beforehand, then closes even that door: “even if the two of them have a matter in dispute, or he gave beyond the custom, he returns it, because it is then for the sake of the judgeship, so it is of misappropriation.” [Zayla’i, Tabyin al-Haqa’iq] His word is ghulul, taking for yourself what belongs to the Muslims at large. Where the giver may be affected by how you do your job, the benefit is not clean, no matter what the rulebook says.

Two Tests, and What to Do When You’re Offered One

Two tests will keep you right. Would this shopkeeper give the same discount to a stranger in ordinary clothes? Does he have any business before your office, now or likely soon? If the first answer is no, or the second is yes, pay in full.

When you pay, put the money down before he can wave you off. If he presses, tell him warmly that your work does not permit it, and that you would gladly be his guest at home, where the uniform counts for nothing. As for what you took before you knew, Ibn al-Humam’s page directs that it be returned to the people it came from, where they are known; so return what you can and turn to Allah for the rest.

For the wider question of what counts as a bribe and where a narrow allowance exists, see What Are the Ruling Regarding Bribes?

Find out what your department actually permits, and let your salary be the only thing your uniform earns you.

records.title: Is a Marriage in a Church to a Christian Woman Valid, and What of Intimacy Within It?
records.question: Can a Muslim man be married in a church to a Christian woman if the conditions of the nikah are met, such as two male witnesses, given that he will obviously not take part in the Christian prayers? If that marriage is valid, does oral sex become clearly permissible, since part of the reason some hold it impermissible is that seminal fluid is unlawful to ingest, and it would not be unlawful from the woman’s standpoint, because a Christian is not bound to follow Islamic law? I am sorry if the questions seem inappropriate, but they have been stuck in my head.
records.answer:
There is nothing improper in either question, and you did well to ask rather than to guess.

Marrying a Chaste Christian Woman Is Valid, Even With Christian Witnesses

A Muslim man may marry a chaste Christian woman, and a marriage that meets its conditions is valid, whatever building it is contracted in. The place of the contract is not one of the conditions. Allah Most High says, “And lawful too are chaste freewomen from those who believe, and chaste freewomen of those given the scripture no great while before you, when you give them their due wages in marriage payment, seeking chaste wedlock, not as open fornicators, or private takers of lovers.” [Quran 5:5; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Imam Quduri (Allah have mercy on him) gives the conditions, and the very next line of his text gives your own case. “The marriage of Muslims is not contracted except in the presence of two witnesses, free, adult, sane, and Muslim, or one man and two women, whether they be upright or not upright or punished for slander. If a Muslim marries a dhimmi woman with two dhimmi witnesses, it is valid according to Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said it is not valid.” [Quduri, Mukhtasar al-Quduri] Ibn Qutlubugha (Allah have mercy on him) wrote over this same text to mark which view the school relies on, and here he records that Imam Isbijabi said, “The correct view is theirs,” and that Imam Nasafi and Sadr al-Sharia, among others, went by it. [Ibn Qutlubugha, al-Tashih wa al-Tarjih]

So two Muslim witnesses are the norm, and arranging them is the safer and better course. But if the witnesses who sit at your nikah are Christian, your marriage is valid on the position our school relies upon, and Imam Muhammad’s dissent does not undo it. Nobody should be telling you that such a marriage is void.

Entering a Church Is Still Disliked, and the Nikah Should Be Held Elsewhere

Validity is not the whole of the answer. Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) transmits, “It is disliked for a Muslim to enter a synagogue or a church, and it is disliked only from the standpoint that it is a gathering place of devils, not from the standpoint that he has no right to enter. He said in al-Bahr: the apparent position is that the dislike is prohibitive, since that is what is meant when they use the word without qualification, and I have given a fatwa that a Muslim who keeps attending the church with the Jews should be disciplined. So if entering is unlawful, praying there is more so, and by this the ignorance of anyone who enters one to pray in it is plain.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

That is heavier than a mild caution. The later authorities take the dislike of entering a church to be the prohibitive kind, and Ibn Nujaym (Allah have mercy on him), whose words those are, disciplined a man for making a habit of it.

You told me you would not take part in the Christian prayers, and that matters. It is not the whole of it, though: the dislike in these texts attaches to going in, and taking part would be graver still. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Whoever imitates a people is one of them.” [Abu Dawud]

The practical course is clear. Do not hold the nikah in the church, and do not sit through a service there. Have it conducted properly somewhere else, with your witnesses present. Whatever the civil registration requires can be done on its own terms, and a meal or a gathering with her family afterward is a fine thing and no difficulty at all.

Oral Sex Remains Disliked Regardless of Her Faith

Now the second question. Your wife not being addressed by the Shariah has no bearing on you. The ruling attaches to your act, and what you do with your own body is weighed by your law rather than hers. Nor does the discussion in our books rest on swallowing in the first place. Ibn Mazah al-Bukhari (Allah have mercy on him) records, “If a man puts his male organ in his wife’s mouth, it has been said that it is disliked, because it is the place of the recitation of the Quran, so it is not fitting that the organ be put into it; and the contrary has also been said.” [Ibn Mazah al-Bukhari, al-Muhit al-Burhani] The Hindiyya carries the same pair of views out of the fatwa literature, “In al-Nawazil: if a man puts his male organ in his wife’s mouth, it has been said that it is disliked, and it has been said otherwise. So it is in al-Dhakhira.” [al-Fatawa al-Hindiyya]

So the position is that this is disliked, with the scholars differing over how strongly and on what grounds the severity is the impurity that may be emitted. If filth is swallowed or is likely to be, it is prohibitively disliked and sinful; short of that, with every precaution taken, it remains disliked and improper, and even where there is no fear of it at all, it falls short of what is best. The clean permission you were hoping for is not in the school.

What is beyond question is broad enough. A husband and wife may look at one another and touch one another freely, and what passes between them is a good thing before Allah. Keep the modesty our people have always kept in these matters, and hold her comfort and her right as weighty as your own. That will serve you better than a list.

records.title: If Dry Ablution Is Permitted, Must Impurity Beyond the Excused Amount Still Be Removed?
records.question: If I am permitted to use dry ablution (tayammum) but have impurity on me beyond the excused amount, must I remove it before praying?
records.answer:
Yes. If you can remove it, do so before praying. Dry ablution stands in for washing the limbs; it does nothing to physical filth on your body, your clothes, or the place where you pray. Purification from the ritual state and purification from filth are two separate conditions of a valid prayer in the Hanafi school, and being excused from the first does not touch the second.

The Excused Amount Is a Dirham of Heavy Filth

Within that amount, you may pray; beyond it, you may not. Imam Shurunbulali (Allah have mercy on him) states it plainly: “The amount of a dirham of heavy filth is excused.” [Shurunbulali, Maraqi al-Falah, 1.65] So the question is not whether you are praying with earth or with water. It is whether what is on you exceeds that amount, and whether you have the means to wash it.

If Your Water Is Enough for Only One Purpose, Spend It on the Filth

Imam Kasani (Allah have mercy on him) gives the case directly: “A traveler in a state of ritual impurity, on whose garment is filth greater than the measure of a dirham, and who has with him water enough for only one of the two, washes the garment with it and performs dry ablution for the ritual state, according to the generality of the scholars.” [Kasani, Badaʾiʿ al-Sanaʾiʿ, 1.57] His reason: “directing it to the filth makes him one who prays with two purifications, the actual and the legal, so that is better than praying with a single purification.” [Kasani, Badaʾiʿ al-Sanaʾiʿ, 1.57]

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “The clean earth is the ablution of the Muslim, even for ten pilgrimage seasons …” [Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra, 1.326] Notice what the earth replaces: the ablution. Filth is washed off instead, and not with water only. Imam Quduri (Allah have mercy on him) writes, “It is permitted to purify filth with water and with every pure liquid by which its removal is possible, such as vinegar and rose water.” [Quduri, Mukhtasar al-Quduri, 1.21]

That washing is meant to be unburdensome. When a bedouin urinated in the mosque, the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) told the people, “Leave him, and pour over his urine a bucket of water, or a pail of water, for you were sent only to make things easy, not to make them hard.” [Bukhari]

If You Genuinely Cannot Remove It, Pray as You Are

No water, nothing else that would lift it, no clean garment to change into: then you pray with the filth, your prayer is valid, and you owe no repetition. Imam Shurunbulali writes: “One who lacks the means to remove filth prays with it and owes no repetition, and neither does one who lacks what would cover his nakedness.” [Shurunbulali, Maraqi al-Falah, 1.90] Imam Tahtawi (Allah have mercy on him) glosses it: “One who lacks the means to remove preventive filth prays with it and owes no repetition, because accountability is according to capacity.” [Tahtawi, Hashiyat al-Tahtawi, 1.238] Do not let the prayer leave its time while you look for a remedy.

Water Goes First to the Filth, Earth Stands In for the Ablution

Hold the two purifications apart, and the matter settles: earth substitutes for the ablution, filth is washed off wherever you have something that lifts it, and where you have no means to remove it, you pray as you are and owe no repetition. Since these situations arrive without warning, study the chapter of purification with a teacher, or take a structured SeekersGuidance course in Hanafi worship, so the rulings are in your hands before the day you need them.

records.title: Is My Repentance From Acts of Disbelief Valid, and Am I Still Muslim?
records.question: I went through a period of baseless misgivings about disbelief, and I am convinced that in my desperation, I committed certain acts of disbelief. I am very sad. If someone commits such an act, repents, and later becomes convinced it never happened, though it did, is the repentance and the faith nullified? If a Muslim later realizes a past act was disbelief, must the testification of faith be renewed, and was he a Muslim in the meantime? Is a general repentance enough, covering what is known, what is forgotten, and what one did not recognize as disbelief? If a person repents but feels no remorse and wishes he did, is the repentance valid, and must remorse remain for life? And as someone who reads and wants to keep learning, should I worry that studying more will expose me to further danger?
records.answer:
You have carried this fear for a long time, and you do not owe anyone an apology for asking about it.

You are a Muslim. Nothing you have described has taken you out of Islam, and none of it asks you to go back and investigate your past. Our tradition has already answered every one of these questions in your favor. Here they are in order, as you asked.

A Mistaken Memory Does Not Undo a Repentance Already Made

One. No, on both counts. A repentance that was made is made, and a later mistake about the facts does not reach back and undo it. Faith does not lapse whenever the memory of it goes unclear. Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) gives the Hanafi rule: “What is known with certainty to be apostasy is ruled to be so, and what is only doubted to be apostasy is not ruled to be so, since established Islam does not depart through doubt.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar] Read that slowly, because it is about you. Your Islam is the established thing. Your fear is the doubt. The doubt does not win.

You Were a Muslim the Whole Time, and Nothing Here Needs Renewing

Two. You do not need to renew the testimony of faith (shahada), and you were a Muslim throughout that interval. The Hanafis begin from the principle that nothing takes a person out of faith but a denial of what brought him into it, and a suspicion arriving years later about something long past denies nothing. Ibn Nujaym (Allah have mercy on him) records the standing instruction to every scholar who is asked such a question: “If a matter admits of several aspects that require a verdict of disbelief and one single aspect that prevents it, the mufti must incline to the aspect that prevents the verdict of disbelief, thinking well of the Muslim.” [Ibn Nujaym, al-Bahr al-Raiq] The jurists set aside only the man who says outright that he intends the disbelieving sense, and nothing in your letter resembles him. A scholar is bound to read your case charitably. You are not entitled to a harsher verdict on yourself than a scholar is permitted to give. So leave your shahada alone, and leave that interval alone.

One General Repentance Covers What You Forgot and What You Never Recognized

Three. Yes, and a general repentance is exactly what you should make, once. Repentance never required you to itemize anything. Imam Nawawi (Allah have mercy on him) writes that one “must repent from all sins, and if he repents from some of them, his repentance is sound, in the view of the people of truth, from that sin, and the remainder stays upon him.” [Nawawi, Riyad al-Salihin] If repenting from a single sin is sound for that sin, a repentance that intends everything is sound for everything, the forgotten and the unrecognized, along with the rest.

Then there is everything that was never written against you to begin with. The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Allah has passed over, for my sake, what my community’s breasts have whispered to them, so long as they do not act on it or speak it.” [Bukhari] What stayed inside your chest was never recorded. What did not stay there, your repentance has already covered. Between the two, there is nothing left over for you to look for. He also said, “Do you not know that Islam demolishes what came before it, that the emigration demolishes what came before it, and that the pilgrimage demolishes what came before it?” [Muslim]

Grief Is Enough; You Are Not Required to Keep Manufacturing Remorse

Four. The repentance is valid, and the feeling does not have to stay with you for the rest of your life. Remorse is not an emotion you are asked to produce on demand. Imam Ghazali (Allah have mercy on him) defines it plainly: “If the loss came about through his own act, he grieves over the act that caused it, and this pain of his, on account of his act that lost him what he loves, is called remorse.” [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din] You wrote that you are very sad, and that you wish you felt remorse. That grief and that wish are the thing itself. You have been searching for something you were holding the whole time. What comes after it is turning away and meaning not to go back, and you have done both. A sin repented from is as though it had never been. You are not asked to keep feeling it, and you are certainly not asked to keep checking whether you feel it.

The Threshold for Disbelief Is Public Knowledge, Not a Private Fear

Five. No. And the rule as it reached you is not the rule. A verdict of disbelief by denial attaches to what is known of the religion by necessity, and Ibn Hajar al-Haytami (Allah have mercy on him) sets that threshold as something “definitive and well known, such that it is not hidden from ordinary people who keep the company of scholars.” [Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya] He adds that such people know it straight off, without having to reason their way to it. That is a public standard, not a specialist one, and study does not add to it. Learning more about your religion only fastens you more firmly to what is already on that list. So keep reading and keep studying, and let this fear go with the others.

Think Well of Yourself, the Way a Scholar Is Bound To

Six. Yes to both. A Muslim who loves Islam and wants to remain a Muslim should never call himself a disbeliever, and should read his own case in the best light it admits. Calling yourself a disbeliever is not humility, and it is not caution. It is a verdict, and you are no more entitled to pass it on yourself than a scholar would be entitled to pass it on you. Nor is there anything here left for you to worry about. Thinking well of yourself in this is not a leniency you are inventing for your own comfort. It is the ruling.

What to Do Now

What to do now is short. Make one general repentance, in your own words, for everything known and unknown, and then treat the matter as closed. Do not renew your shahada. Do not compile a list. Do not test yourself. When the thought arrives, and it will, say “la ilaha illa Allah” once, without arguing with it, and go back to whatever you were doing. Keep your prayers, and keep learning as you have been.

This has weighed on you for a long time, and it is worth speaking to a qualified doctor or counselor about the distress itself. That is care for your well-being, and it says nothing about your faith.

Allah says: “Say, ‘O My servants who have committed excesses against their very selves, despair not of the mercy of Allah: Verily Allah forgives all sins soever: Truly He is the All-forgiving, the All-compassionate.'” [Quran 39:53; Keller, The Quran Beheld] That verse came down for people who were certain they had gone too far. They had not. Neither have you.

records.title: What Did Islamic Law Actually Permit in the Treatment of Enslaved Women?
records.question: I know slavery is over, but I want to understand it properly: did Muslim men through history treat enslaved women the way ISIS treats its captives, and was force, or dismissing a woman’s fear and pain as beside the point because she was property, ever actually permitted?
records.answer:
Nothing ISIS did was lawful, and none of it can be reconstructed as law: their captives were not lawfully taken, their war was not a lawful war, the authority that claimed to distribute those women was not a lawful authority, and no one alive today can bring a human being into slavery at all. That is not a technicality about paperwork. It is the whole answer to your first question. Shaykh Wahba al-Zuhayli (Allah have mercy on him), writing on the zakat share set aside for freeing slaves, states that no slave exists in the world today, and that whatever may be found of it has no permitted path in the Sacred Law. [Wahba al-Zuhayli, al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuhu 3:1956]

Your real question sits underneath that one: had the acquisition somehow been valid, would the cruelty have been licensed? Honesty serves you better here than defense. Jurists working inside an institution that the whole pre-modern world took for granted did permit, within it, things we would now name coercion, and I will not pretend otherwise. That we now name them coercion is a moral gain, and I hold it a real one. So do not defend the tradition by claiming its law criminalized every coercion. It did not.

What the law did do was bind the owner and press steadily toward the exit. Cruelty was sin, and kindness was commanded. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said: “They are your brethren whom Allah has placed under your hands. So whoever has his brother under his hand, let him feed him from what he eats, clothe him from what he wears, and not burden him with work that overwhelms him; and if he does burden him with what overwhelms him, let him help him with it.” [al-Khatib al-Tabrizi, Mishkat al-Masabih 3345]

Revelation then pressed on the exit rather than the entrance. Where a bondsman sought to purchase himself and his good was known in him, his owner was to write him that contract and help him meet it from the wealth Allah had given him. The jurists read that directive as a recommendation rather than a binding order, with the purpose of freeing necks. [Wahba al-Zuhayli, al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuhu 3:1956] The same verse forbids the owner to force his bondwomen into prostitution, and it closes by turning to the woman who was forced, declaring Allah forgiving and compassionate toward her after she has been forced:

“And let those who find no means to marry keep themselves wholly chaste till Allah enriches them of His bounty; And those who want to purchase themselves from their masters, of bond servants your right hands own, write them a contract to do so if you know in them good, and give them to help them do so of the wealth of Allah which He has bestowed you. Nor force any of your bondmaids to prostitution when they full well want to remain chaste … And whoso may force them, Allah is to them after their having been forced all-forgiving, all-compassionate.” [Quran 24:33; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

As for the graphic particulars in your second and third questions, I will not treat them as live questions of Shariah, because they are not: no ruling waits on them, and there is no lawful slavery left to regulate.

A Structure Built to Empty Itself

The law was built to end slavery, and it has. What is left to you is not a hypothetical to litigate but a faith to hold: the revelation that regulated the world it inherited taught that world to feed the one under its hand from its own plate and to write out his freedom. The answers below work this ground at length.
references: Wahba al-Zuhayli, al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuhu 3:1956

records.title: Is It Permissible to Resell Sealed Trading Card Boxes?
records.question: I am considering starting a business reselling trading cards and want to inform myself before I start. On sealed products, the customer pays a fixed, known price for a sealed box.
