The general contents are stated on the packaging, but which cards are inside is unknown until it is opened, to me as well as to him, and there is a possible gap in value between a disappointing box and one holding a rare card. Is that sales model permissible, and under what conditions? The cards also depict fictional creatures, some with supernatural powers, and I have seen opinions diverge sharply on selling them. Is that permissible? And if I proceed on the most favourable opinion I can find, would the earnings be lawful?
records.answer:
Selling Sealed Boxes Is a Valid Sale, Not a Game of Chance

The sales model you describe is sound in the Hanafi school. Buying sealed trading card products at a known price and reselling them is ordinary trade in a tangible good, and income from such trade is lawful. The pictures on the cards are the harder matter, and scholars differ over them, so take the model as settled and the illustrations as the cautious side of this venture.

The condition for a valid sale is not that the buyer know every particular of what he is buying. Imam Kasani (Allah have mercy on him) puts it as “that the object of sale and its price be known with a knowledge that prevents dispute. If one of the two is unknown with an unknowingness that leads to dispute, the sale is invalid; and if it is unknown with an unknowingness that does not lead to dispute, it is not invalid.” [Kasani, Badaʾiʿ al-Sanaʾiʿ] The school goes further and validates the purchase of a thing the buyer has not yet examined at all, which it treats under the option of inspection (khiyar al-ruʾya).

A sealed box states its product line, the number of packs, the number of cards, and the price, which is fixed before any money changes hands. The buyer knows the class of goods he is receiving, and he receives exactly that quantity. What he does not know is which particular cards fall inside, and that is a variation of quality within a known class, not ignorance of what he bought. The uncertainty (gharar) that voids a sale is not the same as this.

The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) forbade “the sale of the pebble and the sale of uncertainty.” [Muslim] The sale of the pebble was that a stone was thrown, and whatever it landed on was the thing sold, so chance settled the contract rather than the two parties. Paying for a virtual pack is close to that, because the money buys a draw. A physical box is not, because the money buys a determinate quantity of a manufactured good that arrives, regardless of what is printed inside it.

Sell factory-sealed product with its contents printed on the packaging, at a stated price, and describe your stock exactly as it is. Do not sell resealed or tampered boxes, and keep your advertising off the rare card a customer might chance upon.

The Pictures Are the Cautious Part of This Trade

In the illustrations, the Hanafi discussion concerns making images, keeping them in the home, and praying towards them, and it turns on whether the image is being honored. Imam Kasani writes that “images are disliked in houses… because keeping them is a resemblance to the worshippers of idols, except when they are on rugs or on the small cushions that are laid on the ground to be sat upon, in which case they are not disliked, because treading them underfoot is a degradation of them, so keeping them in a place of degradation is not a resemblance to the worshippers of idols,” and that they are disliked “on curtains, on the cloths hung upon the wall, on large cushions, and on the ceiling, for the honouring of them that this involves.” [Kasani, Badaʾiʿ al-Sanaʾiʿ]

You may fairly object that these creatures are animate forms, and that the school’s default is to dislike keeping such pictures at all. That is so, and the exception in the passage turns on where the image sits rather than on what it shows: a picture in a place of degradation is not the resemblance the school is guarding against. A card that is handled, shuffled, sleeved, and boxed is a long way from an image raised up to be revered, and you neither draw these pictures nor open the packs. But the passage speaks of images kept and displayed, not of trading in flat printed pictures of animate beings, so carrying it across to a card is a considered extension of the school’s reasoning rather than something the text itself states. Some scholars, including those in answers published on our own site, decline this trade on account of the pictures.

Earnings Are Sound When You Have Genuinely Consulted a Scholar

As for your third question, earnings from a valid sale are lawful earnings, and a man who acts on a ruling he received from a qualified scholar has done what was asked of him. Should that scholar prove to have been mistaken, the income is not thereby tainted, and you carry no sin for it. What matters is why you hold the position: hold it because a scholar you trust holds it and you have put your case to him, not because it was the lightest answer you could find.

Begin small while you learn the trade, and keep a scholar you can return to as the business grows.

records.title: Is My Income Lawful as a Risk Methodology Analyst at an Investment Bank?
records.question: I work at an investment bank on a methodology team. The company’s main income comes from wealth management and other financial services, which may involve interest-bearing products. My own work is to build and maintain a model that enables the firm to identify the maximum possible loss it could incur on its current investments, which are positions in bonds, equities, and similar securities. I have no advisory role in those investments and am not directly involved in any interest-bearing transaction; the model simply takes the existing positions as inputs. Is my income lawful?
records.answer:
Your Work Measures Risk; It Does Not Create the Contract

The work you have described is lawful, and the salary you take for it is lawful. Building and maintaining a model that measures the maximum loss your firm could suffer on positions it already holds is a permissible service, and you are neither a party to an interest-bearing contract nor bringing one into existence for anyone else.

In the Hanafi school, hiring out one’s labor (ijara) is sound whenever the work contracted for is itself permissible, and the wage is owed for that work. Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him), citing al-Khaniyya, gives the case of a man who hires himself out to labor on a church and repair it. There is no harm in it, “because there is no disobedience in the substance of the work itself.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar]

Allah has commanded us to help one another to righteousness and God-consciousness and not to help one another to sin and enmity [Quran 5:2]. The school takes that seriously, and it does not treat every connection to wrongdoing as one thing. Its measure is whether the wrong subsists in the very substance of what one does. Ibn Abidin sets it out in the law of sales: “whatever the disobedience subsists in by its own substance, selling it is disliked to the degree of prohibition, and otherwise the dislike is one of mere impropriety.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar] Applied to employment, that is, the line between doing the unlawful thing and standing near it.

See where the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) drew that line. He cursed “the one who consumes interest (riba), the one who pays it, the one who records it, and its two witnesses,” and he said, “They are the same.” [Muslim] Those are the two contracting parties and the two roles that bring the contract into legal being. The scribe writes it, the witnesses make it stand. Your model does neither. It reads existing positions and reports a number to your own management.

This Differs from the Risk Assessment That Underwrites a Loan

You may have come across the ruling that assessing risk at a bank is impermissible. What is meant there is the assessment that goes into making the loan, the underwriting that decides whether it is written at all and on what terms. That work is one of the causes of the contract. Measuring what a portfolio already stands to lose sits downstream of contracts concluded without you.

Mixed Income at This Scale Does Not Taint Your Wage

As for your firm’s income being mixed, the Hanafis look to what predominates rather than to the presence of anything unlawful at all. Ibn Mazah al-Bukhari (Allah have mercy on him) gives the reason plainly: “because people’s wealth is not free of a little that is unlawful, though it is free of much of it, so what predominates is what is taken into account, and the ruling is built upon it.” [Ibn Mazah al-Bukhari, al-Muhit al-Burhani] A bank of that size draws revenue from a wide range of activities, and you are paid for your labor, not out of an identified unlawful sum.

Two Changes That Would Move Your Work Closer to the Wrong

Two things would change this answer. If you were moved into structuring, pricing, marketing, or advising on interest-bearing products, or asked to draw up, record, or sign such contracts, your work would become a cause of the wrong rather than a measurement of its consequences. And if the model were built to enable interest-based deals rather than reporting exposure, the same would follow. Ask again if either comes near you.

So take your salary without unease. If a door opens to work further from all of this, walk through it and thank Allah. Until then, do your work well, give what you can in charity, and let this scruple remain what it is, a sign of a living heart and not a source of fear.

records.title: Is the Variant Reading of Ghalabat al-Rum Soundly Transmitted?
records.question: A teacher discussing the readings of the Quran cited the variant ghalabati l-Rum at Quran 30:2, attributed to Ali and other Companions, and rejected it as anomalous for want of mass transmission. This confused me. If the only defect is a lack of mass transmission rather than a broken chain, the reading would still accord with Arabic and with one of the Uthmanic codices, so it could, in principle, be the Quran. Yet it also contradicts what happened in history and what the other readings say. Does this reading have an authentic chain at all?
records.answer:
No, the reading ghalabati l-Rum does not have an authentic chain, and your teacher’s conclusion is right, though his reason is not the one the qurraʾ rely on. Only one chain for it appears in the major commentaries, and the man at its center was graded weak by the very critics whose standards you are asking about. Even a sound chain would not have made it the Quran, because Ibn al-Jazari’s third condition means something narrower in the science of readings than it means in hadith. And the collision you noticed with history is real; the commentators had raised it before us as well.

The Third Condition Means Something Narrower Than a Hadith Scholar’s Chain

Ibn al-Jazari (Allah have mercy on him) sets the three conditions out at the opening of al-Nashr: “Every reading that accords with Arabic in some manner, and accords with one of the Uthmanic codices even by implication, and whose chain is sound, is the sound reading, which it is not permitted to reject and not lawful to deny.” [Ibn al-Jazari, al-Nashr fi al-Qiraʾat al-Ashr] He then adds, “Whenever one of these three pillars fails, it is called weak, or anomalous, or baseless, whether it comes from the seven or from someone greater than them.” [Ibn al-Jazari, al-Nashr fi al-Qiraʾat al-Ashr]

You have read that third condition, as almost everyone does, as the ordinary criterion of the hadith scholars. Ibn al-Jazari glosses his own words: “By our saying ‘and its chain is sound,’ we mean that an upright and precise transmitter narrates that reading from one like him, and so on until the chain ends, and that along with this it is well known among the imams of this discipline who have mastered it, not counted by them among the errors or among what one or another of them read anomalously.” [Ibn al-Jazari, al-Nashr fi al-Qiraʾat al-Ashr]

Two clauses sit on top of the chain there: that the reading is well known among the masters of recitation, and that they have not classed it a slip. A report can pass every test a hadith scholar applies and still fail that, because the readings came down not as reports but as a recitation taught mouth-to-mouth. A chain in a book of tafsir shows that a Companion said something. It does not show that the qurraʾ received it and taught it as the Quran.

Mass Transmission Was Never the Requirement, and a Sound Chain Alone Is Not Enough

Your instinct that the appeal to mass transmission (tawatur) is doing suspicious work is sound, too. Some later scholars made mass transmission a condition of this third pillar, and Ibn al-Jazari rejects it: if every point of difference among the readers had to be mass-transmitted, much of what is firmly established from the seven imams would fall away. He says of himself: “I used to incline to this view, then its unsoundness became clear to me, as did the agreement of the imams of the earlier and later generations.” [Ibn al-Jazari, al-Nashr fi al-Qiraʾat al-Ashr] So the man whose three conditions your teacher used did not require tawatur at all, and the reading is still excluded.

Nor does a sound chain by itself make something Quran. Makki ibn Abi Talib (Allah have mercy on him), quoted at length in al-Nashr, treats readings soundly transmitted by solitary chains and correct in their Arabic, and rules them accepted but not recited, “because it was not taken by consensus, it was only taken from solitary reports, and no Quran that is recited is established by a solitary report.” [Makki ibn Abi Talib, quoted in al-Nashr fi al-Qiraʾat al-Ashr]

The Commentaries Agree Against This Reading

The commentaries bear this out. Imam Tabari (Allah have mercy on him), the only one who supplies a chain for it, rules against it: “The correct reading here, in our view, and no other is permissible, is ghulibati l-Rum, with damma on the ghayn, because of the agreement of the authoritative body of the readers upon it.” [Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Jamiʿ al-Bayan] Ibn Atiyya (Allah have mercy on him) names four Companions who recited it, Ali ibn Abi Talib among them (Allah be pleased with him), then gives his verdict: “The first narration and the reading with damma on the ghayn is more sound.” [Ibn Atiyya, al-Muharrar al-Wajiz] Imam Baghawi (Allah have mercy on him) names five and closes the same way in Maʿalim al-Tanzil, calling the damma reading the more sound and the position of most commentators.

Imam Qurtubi (Allah have mercy on him) adds something that the others do not. He reports Abu Hatim’s claim, from ʿIsma, that the fatha form was the reading of the people of Sham, then undercuts it: “Ahmad ibn Hanbal says that this Isma is weak, and Abu Hatim reports a great deal from him, and the hadith indicates that the reading is ghulibat with damma on the ghayn.” [Qurtubi, al-Jamiʿ li-Ahkam al-Quran] The one attempt to widen it beyond a few people rests on a weak transmitter. Abu Hayyan (Allah have mercy on him) adds Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan al-Basri, and notes that those who read the first verb as active read the second as passive, sayughlabun, the form you quoted.

The Historical Problem Confirms the Verdict, It Does Not Create It

Now to the history. Read with fatha on the ghayn, the verse no longer says that the Romans were defeated and would afterward prevail. Imam Baydawi (Allah have mercy on him) sets out what forces the sense to become: “And it is read ghalabat with a fatha, and sayughlabun with a damma, meaning that the Romans had prevailed over the fertile country of Syria, and the Muslims would prevail over them.” [Baydawi, Anwar al-Tanzil] Imam Qurtubi then passes a verdict on the passive half of that pairing, narrated from Ibn Umar: “And it is narrated from Ibn Umar that he also read with damma on the ya in sayughlabun, and in this reading there is an inversion of the meaning that the transmitted reports have borne out.” [Qurtubi, al-Jamiʿ li-Ahkam al-Quran] The reports he means are the accounts of the Persian victory and the later Roman recovery, and a few lines earlier, he says the hadith indicates the damma. So the collision you noticed is not a problem for the tradition. It is one of the grounds on which the reading was set aside.

Imam Maturidi (Allah have mercy on him) registers the reading without passing judgment on it, as does Zamakhshari (Allah have mercy on him) in al-Kashshaf. Imam Razi (Allah have mercy on him) and Ibn Kathir (Allah have mercy on him), who both treat these verses at length, do not mention it at all; a reading the masters of recitation had received would not have been invisible to them.

The One Chain Rests on a Narrator the Critics Rejected

Now the chain itself. Imam Tabari transmits it thus: “Ibn Waki’ related to us, saying: my father related to us, from al-Hasan al-Jufri, from Salit, who said: I heard Ibn Umar reciting, Alif Lam Mim, ghalabati l-Rum. It was said to him, Abu Abd al-Rahman: “Over what did they prevail?” He said, over the fertile country of Syria.” [Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Jamiʿ al-Bayan] Its weight rests on al-Hasan ibn Abi Jaʿfar al-Jufri, whom the hadith critics did not treat gently. Imam Bukhari’s (Allah have mercy on him) entry reads: “al-Hasan ibn Abi Ja’far, al-Jufri, of Basra. He is al-Hasan ibn Ajlan. From Abu al-Zubayr. His hadith are denounced.” [Bukhari, al-Tarikh al-Kabir] A few lines later, he records that Imam Ahmad (Allah have mercy on him) declared him weak. Jawzajani (Allah have mercy on him) is blunter: “al-Hasan ibn Abi Ja’far al-Jufri, weak, feeble in hadith.” [Jawzajani, Ahwal al-Rijal] Salit, above him, cannot be securely identified: more than one man of that name reports from Ibn Umar, and the biographers disentangle them differently in Tahdhib al-Tahdhib.

What This Means When You Meet Such a Claim Again

So the honest state of your question is this. The reading is reported, it is named from Companions, and one weak chain carries it, so it fails the third condition on the narrow understanding and on the broad one alike. And the grade was never the decisive thing. Imam Tabari, who had the chain before him, excluded the reading not for weakness in its narrators but for the agreement of the qurraʾ against it, which is exactly the clause built into his third condition.

So when you meet a claim that a reading is Quran because it has a chain, the question is not whether the chain would satisfy a hadith scholar. It is whether the imams of recitation received it, taught it, and counted it among the readings rather than among the slips. If you want to go further, read the opening chapters of al-Nashr with a teacher.
references: Ibn al-Jazari, al-Nashr fi al-Qiraʾat al-Ashr
Makki ibn Abi Talib, quoted in al-Nashr fi al-Qiraʾat al-Ashr

records.title: Have I Committed Disbelief by Joking About the Hadith of the Prophet Eating Chicken?
records.question: I joked with a friend that an anticlimactic situation was like the hadith of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) eating chicken, since that report seems relatively unimportant. Now I fear I have committed disbelief by mocking, and if I have not, are jokes like these unlawful?
records.answer:
The fear in your message weighs more than the joke that caused it. You have not left Islam, and likening a flat, anticlimactic moment to a hadith that people find unremarkable is not disbelief (kufr). Contempt and fear do not live in the same heart.

What brought you here is not really a question of law. It is intrusive religious doubt (waswasa), and that is treated rather than argued away.

The Hanafi school’s caution runs in your favor. Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) states the rule: no one is judged an unbeliever on a mere possibility, and “no verdict of unbelief is issued against a Muslim whose words can be carried to a good construction.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar 4:224] Your words carry a good construction easily. They also carry an obvious one. And such a verdict is a qualified scholar’s to pass, never yours.

The grave case is mockery aimed at Allah, at His Messenger (Allah bless him and give him peace), or at the religion itself, as mockery; calling that a joke excuses nothing. Nobody arrives there by accident and then goes hunting for it in his memory. You were talking about a meme, not passing judgment on Revelation.

Your second question matters more. That report reads as slight only because we have stopped asking what it is doing there. Abu Musa (Allah be pleased with him) said, “I saw the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) eating chicken.” [Tirmidhi] A Companion watched what the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) ate and preserved it, so that Muslims who would never meet him could eat as he ate. The jokes live off missing that.

So this is manners, not creed. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) is spoken of with reverence, and his life need not be the material of jokes. Scroll past them, and do not be the friend who supplies the next one. [Quran 6:68]

Your Faith Stands, and the Checking Is Now the Injury

Nothing is owed here, so do not retake your testification of faith and do not hunt for an expiation. Regret the joke, ask Allah’s forgiveness, send blessings on the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), and put the question down. Stop reading about unbelief and takfir; every search feeds this. Sit with a teacher, and see a doctor for the checking. You have asked a version of this before, and the answer has not changed. Let this be the last time you open it. Fear like yours marks a heart that cares what it says about its Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace). Put that heart to better use.

records.title: Can I Own and Display a Framed Nad e Ali with Numeric Squares in a Sunni Home?
records.question: My father was given framed pictures said to be for protection, and he passed a couple on to me, one of them a Nad e Ali written in the shape of a lion, with writing underneath and numeric boxes in each corner, like a taweez. May I own and display such things in a Sunni Hanafi home?
records.answer:
Take it down. Relying on it for protection is what is not allowed, and hanging writing you cannot read is why it comes off the wall; owning it is neither, so wrap it, put it away, and find out what it says. Your father’s other pictures follow the same test.

Nothing in this touches Sayyiduna Ali (Allah ennoble his face). Love for the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) and his family is part of the religion. Asking Allah while mentioning a beloved servant of His is not associating partners with Allah; holding that a creature gives protection in his own right is another matter, and that is the line.

Nad e Ali itself is a question of transmission: it has no chain in Sunni hadith literature. Mulla Ali al-Qari (Allah have mercy on him), a Hanafi, placed it among fabricated reports and traced it to Shiʿi sources, and Imam Ajluni (Allah have mercy on him) transmits his verdict. [Ajluni, Kashf al-Khafaʾ 2:363]

Your corner boxes are numerical squares (awfaq), numbers laid into geometric figures in a particular form. [al-Mawsuʿa al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 24:261] “There is no disagreement among the jurists that an amulet is not permitted when it contains a name whose meaning is not known, because what is not understood cannot be secured against containing something of associating partners with Allah.” [al-Mawsuʿa al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 14:30] Numbers in boxes are not a name, but that reason is about what cannot be understood, and it reaches them. A thing that neither benefits nor harms is what the Quran warns against turning to. [Quran 10:106]

Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) draws the Hanafi line on the written amulet (tamima): there is no harm in one carrying the Quran or the Names of Allah, and the objection is to what is not known, since sorcery or disbelief may have entered it. [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar 6:363]

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Whoever attaches himself to a thing is entrusted to it.” [Abu Dawud] A thing the family walks past every day starts to be trusted, and nobody ever decides to trust it.

This is a ruling on an object, not a verdict on anyone in your family. Your father was handed these and told they would protect him, and nothing you have written puts his Islam in question. Ask him who gave them and what he was told, and keep it a question rather than an accusation. If anyone else asks why the wall is bare, you owe them no verdict on anybody.

Read the Words Before Anything Goes on Your Wall

Out of respect, wrap anything bearing the Name of Allah or a Quranic verse rather than throwing it away. If a picture contains only the Quran or the Names of Allah in Arabic, keep it as calligraphy; only the boxes remain problematic. If you want something on that wall, hang words you can read and would gladly say in your prayer. The protection your father was hoping for is real. It was never in the frame.

records.title: I Am a Software Developer on a Leveraged Forex and CFD Trading Platform. Is My Work Permissible?
records.question: I built a white-label trading platform that supports leveraged forex and contracts for difference. I never trade, take no share of the revenue, and earn a fixed salary. Is my work lawful, and does building the features that place these trades make me an assistant in unlawful transactions?
records.answer:
Your work is lawful in every part of the platform where no unlawful transaction occurs, and unlawful in any module that allows a user to open or finance a leveraged forex position or a contract for difference (CFD). That you never trade and take no cut of the revenue is honest, but the school draws its line at the thing built, not at your hands.

What Is Actually Wrong with These Two Products

The products do not share one defect. A leveraged position is bought with money the broker lends you, and the overnight swap fee you named is the charge on that loan. That is interest (riba), whatever the product sheet calls it. Currency exchange also requires a real taking of possession of both sides [al-Mawsuʿa al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 26:351], and a leveraged position takes possession of neither. A CFD is worse placed still: nothing is delivered, neither party owns what the price is quoted on, and the contract settles a movement in a number. That is excessive uncertainty (gharar), and, in many treatments, a wager rather than a sale.

Allah Most High commands mutual help in piety and godfearingness, “and do not aid one another in sin and transgression.” [Quran 5:2; Keller, The Quran Beheld] Ibn Nujaym (Allah have mercy on him) gives two rules side by side: “what is unlawful to take is unlawful to give,” and “what is unlawful to do is unlawful to ask for.” [Ibn Nujaym, al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair 1:132] Building the machinery of an unlawful transaction falls under the same principle, though degrees matter: writing that engine is not the same as fixing the company’s login screen.

The Hanafi test is whether the disobedience subsists in the thing itself [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar 6:391]. Timber sold to a man who will make musical instruments carries no dislike, “unlike the sale of a weapon to the people of sedition, because the disobedience subsists in the thing itself, and that is the aiding in sin.” [al-Mawsuʿa al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 9:212] Timber becomes a lute or a roof beam, and the man who sold it aided neither. A weapon handed to men already at war is the thing itself.

Your interfaces, account management, reporting, and the order flow for shares and ETFs are timber. An engine written so that a user can open or finance those positions is not a general facility that some customers misuse. It is the facility. Only you can say which of your tickets fall where, and by your own description, your work has been landing on both sides. That you could have written the same code for something lawful is an argument about your intention, not about what the module does. Cryptocurrencies, copy trading, funded accounts, and algorithmic execution need their own question.

Sort Your Tickets, Then Ask to Be Moved

Put your tickets in two columns: the leveraged forex engine, the CFD order and settlement path, and anything posting swap or financing charges in one; everything else in the other. Stop taking work from the first column now. Ask your lead in writing to be assigned off it, and keep earning on the second one in the meantime. Platform companies move developers between modules all the time, so this is an ordinary request.

If you are refused, set a horizon and not a mood: three months to be moved or to have another offer in hand. I know what that asks of a family that eats from this salary, and you do not sin by taking the time it needs. The money already paid to you is a separate question; this answer does not settle; send it on its own. If your visa is tied to this employer, say so, because that changes what is reasonable to ask of you. Take heart from where the line fell: most of this platform and all of your skill sit on the lawful side of it, and a developer who can build a trading engine has more doors open to him than he has time to walk through.

records.title: Is It Disbelief If I Sit More Respectfully at the Prophet’s Name Than I Do During Dhikr?
records.question: My legs are sometimes apart while I do the remembrance of Allah (dhikr) and I close them when I hear the name of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), so I fear I hold the Messenger in higher respect than Allah and have fallen into disbelief; then, to undo it, I deliberately spread my legs and said the blessings on the Prophet (salawat), and now I fear I have disrespected him.
records.answer:
You have been measuring your faith with your knees, and it has frightened you badly. A movement your body makes on its own carries no ruling at all. None of this is disbelief, and none of it is associating others with Allah (shirk). Nothing here comes near either. Your legs are not where your faith is kept. Faith is assent, something a person gives with his own will. [Taftazani, Sharh al-Maqasid 2:251]

What you are living with has a name: intrusive religious doubt (waswasa). It is a known condition, a symptom to be treated rather than a question of law to be answered.

Let me take that scale apart. You put Allah at one end and His Messenger (Allah bless him and give him peace) at the other, made your knees the needle, and read off a verdict on your own faith. Loving and honoring him is commanded, and he asked that love of us. [Mishkat al-Masabih] It does not compete with the love of Allah. Honor shown to him is honor to the One who sent him, and it comes out of nobody’s share.

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah.” [Quran 4:80; Keller, The Quran Beheld] Your body sitting up at his name is a sign of a sound heart, not a defect in it, and the same holds when the Companions (Allah be pleased with them) are mentioned.

Your second question, about spreading your legs on purpose, has the same answer. You were not making light of anything. You were trying to repair an offense you had convicted yourself of on no evidence.

Your Faith Sits in Your Assent, Not in Your Legs

Stop auditing your posture. Sit however you are sitting, and when the urge comes to fix it, or to fix the fix, let it pass unobeyed and carry on with your remembrance. An urge like this weakens when ignored and grows when answered. Keep sitting up at his blessed name if you like, as good manners (adab), never again as a measurement. Devise no more penances. The penance is what turned one fear into two.

Stop reading about disbelief and takfir; every search feeds the compulsion, and you do not need another ruling. Find a teacher you can sit with and be known by, and see a doctor about it. That is care for yourself, not a debt you owe Allah.

Hold on to one line from Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him): “Islam once established is not lifted by doubt.” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar 4:224] Your faith stands as you read this. That this frightens you at all tells you where your heart already is. A man careless of his Lord does not lie awake fearing he has slighted Him.

records.title: Is Someone Who Knowingly Lies about Being Descended from the Prophet Still a Muslim?
records.question: If someone knowingly lies about being descended from the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), does that make him a disbeliever? I accept that it is a major sin, but I want to know whether he remains a Muslim.
records.answer:
Someone who knowingly lies about being descended from the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) remains a Muslim, and the lie is a grave sin: a lie against him, and a false claim of lineage. It calls for rectification and sincere repentance. It is not outright disbelief (kufr), unless the person unequivocally deems it permissible.

You are asking about someone else. The ruling on a particular man is not yours to pass, and I cannot pass it from a description. Nothing here licenses calling another Muslim a disbeliever.

Two reports make this feel like a question about faith itself. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Do not turn away from your fathers; whoever turns away from his father has disbelieved.” [Mishkat al-Masabih 3315] He also said, “Whoever claims descent from someone other than his father, while knowing he is not his father, Paradise is forbidden to him.” [Mishkat al-Masabih 3314]

Both are texts of severe warning (wa id). The scholars leave such texts as they were said, neither softening them nor turning them into a verdict on the man’s faith. They name what the deed deserves, not where the doer stands. So “Paradise is forbidden to him” is read alongside the rule that keeps major sin and disbelief apart: whoever dies upon divine oneness (tawhid) does not abide in the Fire, even without repenting [al-Mawsuʿa al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 13:233]. That first report’s last word is printed more than one way, and nothing here turns on which.

Ibn al-Athir (Allah have mercy on him), in his dictionary of hadith vocabulary (al-Nihaya), draws the line your question turns on, quoted here by Mulla Ali al-Qari (Allah have mercy on him). Whoever holds such a claim to be lawful has disbelieved, for contradicting scholarly consensus. Whoever does not hold it lawful is said to have disbelieved in one of two senses: his act resembles the act of the disbelievers, or he is ungrateful for the blessing of Islam [Mulla Ali al-Qari, Mirqat al-Mafatih 5:2170]. Your word “knowingly” puts him on the second side, not the first. Nothing in your question puts him there.

That the lineage claimed is the Prophet’s own (Allah bless him and give him peace) makes this heavier than the general case. It is a lie told against his household, and it wrongs every family that carries that descent. It does not change the ruling. It deepens the sin.

Our Hanafi imams add one more check, addressed to the scholar and not to onlookers. Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) holds that nothing takes a man out of faith except denial of what brought him into it, and that where a case admits a construction that prevents a ruling of disbelief, the mufti must lean to it, thinking well of the Muslim, unless the man plainly says he intended what entails disbelief [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar 4:224]. The man in your question has said no such thing.

What He Owes Now

What he owes is more than private regret. He must undo the claim where he made it: correct the record with everyone who was told, stand down from any honor, position, or money it won him, and return what he took. Those are other people’s rights, and regret does not clear them.

As for you, hold him to be a Muslim who has fallen into a grave sin. If you know him, tell him privately what he owes, then carry it to no one else.

Allah Most High says:

ٱدۡعُوهُمۡ لِأٓبَآئِهِمۡ هُوَ أَقۡسَطُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِۚ فَإِن لَّمۡ تَعۡلَمُوٓاْ ءَابَآءَهُمۡ فَإِخۡوَٰنُكُمۡ فِي ٱلدِّينِ وَمَوَٰلِيكُمۡۚ وَلَيۡسَ عَلَيۡكُمۡ جُنَاحٞ فِيمَآ أَخۡطَأۡتُم بِهِۦ وَلَٰكِن مَّا تَعَمَّدَتۡ قُلُوبُكُمۡۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ غَفُورٗا رَّحِيمًا

“Call them by the names of their own fathers: it is more equitable in the sight of Allah; So if you do not know their fathers, they are and should be called your brothers and special friends in religion; And you bear no sin for an honest mistake in saying something else, but only what your hearts deliberately resolve on; And truly Allah was ever all-forgiving, all-compassionate.” [Quran 33:5; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

The verse that names the wrong closes on the mercy that meets it. A man who tells the truth about his father again and asks his Lord for pardon has a forgiven sin behind him.

records.title: Can Allah’s Attribute of al-Barr Resolve the Euthyphro Dilemma?
records.question: I heard the Euthyphro dilemma answered by saying that Allah is al-Barr, so that everything from Him is good: is that sound, and does it follow that it is rationally impossible for Allah to command lying, theft, or rape, since such a command would contradict al-Barr?
records.answer:
Yes to the first half of what you heard, and no to the second. Everything that comes from Allah Most High is good, and it is sound to answer the dilemma by saying so. It does not follow that a command to lie or steal is rationally impossible. He will never issue one, and the reason is His wisdom and His own word, not a shortfall in His power.

The dilemma comes from Plato: “Is the holy holy because it is loved by the gods, or do they love it because it is holy?” [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy] Either a thing is good only because Allah commanded it, and the good is arbitrary, or He commands it because it is good, and something stands above Him. Neither, and one answer disposes of both. I answer on the Maturidi road, the creed behind the Hanafi school.

What the Name Establishes, and What It Does Not

The All-Benevolent (al-Barr) is a revealed name: “Verily He is the All-graciously Kind, the Compassionate.” [Quran 52:28; Keller, The Quran Beheld] The name tells you what comes from Allah. Imam Maturidi (Allah have mercy on him) holds that every act Allah creates is at least wisdom and justice, or bounty and beneficence [Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, Kitab al-Tawhid 1:217]. No evil attaches to His act, which is not to deny that He creates evil.

A name will not carry a claim about what Allah can and cannot command, and your sentence folds two different impossibilities together. Rationally impossible means what could never be at all, like a second god; power does not relate to it. A command to lie is not in that class. When Imam Maturidi says an act of His cannot depart from wisdom [Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, Kitab al-Tawhid 1:125], he is not putting it beyond the reach of power. He is saying it cannot be ascribed to Allah, since it would ascribe folly to Him, and folly cannot be ascribed to the Lord.

Where the Two Sunni Schools Differ

Both schools of belief agree that reason knows some good and bad on its own, that knowledge is good and ignorance bad, with no disagreement recorded. They differ over good and bad as reward and punishment in the Law. The Asharis hold that the Law is the source, and that reason neither makes a thing good nor bad, nor obliges, nor forbids [al-Mawsuʿa al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 10:214]. The Maturidis hold that reason reaches the good and bad of some acts, not the Mutazili claim that reason grasps all of it, and even then the Law need not follow what we grasp [al-Mawsuʿa al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 16:248].

Imam Bayadi (Allah have mercy on him) states the position from within the school: reason is an instrument for knowing an obligation that Allah has established, not the thing that obligates, and not merely a way of understanding revelation and verifying that its reporter is truthful [Bayadi, Isharat al-Maram]. Hafiz al-Din al-Nasafi (Allah have mercy on him) reports that faith being obligatory by reason is narrated from Imam Abu Hanifa (Allah have mercy on him), and he puts the school’s answer in one line: “With us reason is an instrument for knowledge, and the one who obligates is Allah Most High.” [Hafiz al-Din al-Nasafi, al-Itimad fi al-Itiqad] Neither school sets the good above Allah, and neither leaves it to bare decree.

Put the Necessity in His Wisdom and in His Own Word

Abu Dharr (Allah be pleased with him) related that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, relating from his Lord Most High: “O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another.” [Mishkat al-Masabih] He forbade it upon Himself, by His own word, which is His report of what will never come from Him, not a law laid over Him. The wisdom and kindness you are grounding morality in are His own attributes, beginningless, not acquired, not standing over Him. To say that His act never departs from wisdom is to say something about Allah, not to raise a rule above Him.

So keep the first half of what you heard, and rewrite the second half. The necessity is real, and it is a necessity of wisdom and lordship rather than a shortfall in power.
references: Hafiz al-Din al-Nasafi, al-Itimad fi al-Itiqad

records.title: Do Blessings on the Prophet Sent Right After an Oath Fall Inside the Oath?
records.question: I swore an oath to keep away from a sin for a set period and then said, in Arabic, ‘and may Allah bless our master Muhammad,’ and I now fear that the word ‘and’ pulled those blessings inside the oath.
records.answer:
I can hear how heavily this has been sitting on you, and your own instinct about it is right. The blessings on the Prophet (salawat) that you sent are not part of your oath. Nothing you swore keeps you from sending blessings upon the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), and you should go on sending them freely.

An oath, in the Hanafi school, is defined as ‘… a contract by which the resolve of the one swearing is strengthened, upon doing or leaving something … and its pillar is the wording by which the oath is contracted.’ [Babarti, al-Inaya 5:59 (1)] Hold your own words against that. You bound yourself to leave a sin for a set period, and that is the whole of what you contracted. What you said next asked Allah to bless His Messenger. It binds you to no doing and to no leaving, so there is nothing in it for an oath to fasten upon.

Nor does the conjunction do the work you fear. Oaths are read here by what the words carry in ordinary usage, ‘because oaths are built upon customary usage … because an oath is contracted only to compel or to prevent.’ [Mulla Khusraw, Durar al-Hukkam 2:40] A Muslim closes what he says by asking blessings upon the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), and that is what your ‘and’ carried: a supplication, not a second undertaking. Your oath was over the sin, and it stayed there.

What is left in you is a fear rather than a fact, and the law does not act upon fears. Majallat al-Ahkam al-Adliyya, the Ottoman civil code that set down Hanafi rulings as numbered articles, states this in Article 74: ‘No weight is given to mere supposition.’ [Majallat al-Ahkam al-Adliyya 1:25]

So leave the wording alone. Replaying the moment is the whispering (waswasa) at work rather than fiqh, and every pass feeds it. When the thought comes that your blessings broke your oath, do not argue with it: send blessings upon the Prophet again, deliberately, and get on with your day.

Keep the Oath, and Keep Sending Blessings

Your oath itself stands, and it is worth keeping: what you swore over is turning away from a sin. Hold to it one day at a time. Know the rest of the rule as well, so it does not catch you by surprise later. The ruling of an oath is ‘fulfilment in that wherein fulfilment is obligatory, and expiation when that is missed.’ [Babarti, al-Inaya 5:59 (2)] If you do break this oath, two things fall due and they are separate: repentance for the sin, and the expiation of an oath (kaffarat al-yamin), which Allah Most High sets out in Sura al-Maida, verse 89, as feeding ten needy people, or clothing them, or freeing a slave, and three days of fasting for one who finds no means to do any of these. That is what breaking an oath obliges, and it has nothing to do with the blessings you sent, for which nothing at all is owed.

Then take those blessings as your help rather than your worry. Teaching his Companions to answer the call to prayer, the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, ‘… then send blessings upon me, for whoever sends a single blessing upon me, Allah sends ten blessings upon him …’ [Muslim] A man asking Allah’s blessings upon His Beloved through the whole of his day is not a man losing ground.

records.title: Is Raising the Index Finger in the Tashahhud a Sunna for Women Too?
records.question: Is raising the index finger in the tashahhud incumbent upon a woman the way it is incumbent upon a man?
records.answer:
In the Hanafi school, raising the index finger in the sitting (tashahhud) is a sunna for a woman exactly as it is for a man, and it is incumbent on neither.

Since you asked whether it is incumbent, the school counts the pointing (al-ishara) among the sunnas of the prayer [Shurunbulali, Maraqi al-Falah 1:101]. Imam Tahtawi (Allah have mercy on him) reports that the Hanafi transmissions agree on it, so it is a confirmed sunna [Tahtawi, Hashiyat Maraqi al-Falah 1:269]. Nothing in that ruling is restricted to men.

Our texts mark a woman’s difference exactly where it exists and leave the rest general. Imam Shurunbulali (Allah have mercy on him) marks her difference in the sitting, that she rests on her hip (tawarruk), then describes the tashahhud and the pointing without singling her out [Shurunbulali, Maraqi al-Falah 1:108]. Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) counts twenty-five points of difference between a woman and a man, and he explains the ones he names by a single concern, that they conceal her better [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar 1:504]. A raised finger changes nothing about how covered you are, so that reason does not reach it.

When you reach the testification of faith in the tashahhud, raise the index finger of your right hand as you say la ilaha, and lower it as you say illa Llah. The hand rests on your thigh before and after. Do this in both sittings: the first and the final. Hanafis differ on some details of the hand, and this is what the school settled on. Whichever detail is followed, women and men follow it alike.

Since the pointing is a sunna, your prayer is complete without it, and the forgetfulness prostration (sujud al-sahw) is only for leaving out an obligation [Shurunbulali, Maraqi al-Falah 1:178]. If you have been leaving it out, take it up from your next prayer, and you owe nothing for the prayers behind you. It is a sunna of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace), and it is yours exactly as it is his.

records.title: Is Worshipping Allah in Hope of a Reward in Paradise a Corrupt Intention?
records.question: Severe waswasa keeps telling me that my intention is corrupt, because I have come back to worship mainly in the hope of one particular thing I long for in Paradise. Is my intention sound?
records.answer:
May Allah Most High bless you and relieve you of such misgivings. Your intention is not corrupt. Worshipping Allah in hope of what He has promised is sound and praiseworthy; the Sacred Law asks this of you. The thought telling you that you have turned Allah into a bargaining tool is a baseless misgiving (waswasa).

What Spoils an Intention, and What Cannot

Let’s begin with what Islamic law says, as it clarifies the matter before considering various spiritual levels.

The great reference scholar of the Hanafi school, Imam Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him), states clearly: praying and seeking reward from Allah is an act of sincerity [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar].

What Does Sincerity Require?

Imam Birgivi (Allah have mercy on him) defines sincerity (ikhlas) in the Tariqa Muhammadiyya as stripping the intent to draw near to Allah of two things: (1) seeking worldly benefit, and (2) seeking people’s approval. [Birgivi, al-Tariqa al-Muhammadiyya]

His commentator, Imam Khadimi (Allah have mercy on him), transmits and expounds upon that definition [Khadimi, al-Bariqa al-Mahmudiyya]. The reward of the next life is neither of the two things that go against sincerity.

The Quran locates the fault in the same place. Allah Most High says of those He praises for feeding others, “We feed you but for Allah Himself; we want no requital from you, or any great gratitude.” [Quran 76:9; Keller, The Quran Beheld] Imam Nasafi (Allah have mercy on him) glosses “for Allah Himself” as seeking His reward [Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil].

The verse rules out wanting something back from people, and that is not what you are doing.

One verse describes your position exactly. “Whoever strives hard for the yield of the next world, we shall increase for him in his tillage.” [Quran 42:20] Allah does not rebuke the man who wants the harvest of the hereafter. He increases him [Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil].

Prophetic Clarity on Acting for Reward

The Sunna is plainer still: A man told the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) that his whole prayer was, “O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and I seek refuge with You from the Fire.” He admitted he could not manage the long murmured supplications of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) or of Muadh (Allah be pleased with him). He was not corrected. He was told, “It is around it that we murmur.” [Abu Dawud]

And Dhu al-Nun al-Misri (Allah have mercy on him) counts claiming the reward of the deed in the next life among the signs of sincerity, not among its defects [Khadimi, al-Bariqa al-Mahmudiyya].

Your Trouble Is Not Corrupt Worship

The scholars saw this concern coming up. Imam Khadimi opens his discussion of the matters that hover between showing off and sincerity by teaching how to repel the whispering of Shaytan, which is needed everywhere, “especially in the matter of sincerity.” [Khadimi, al-Bariqa al-Mahmudiyya]

Disregard the misgivings and whispers, and count them as nothing each time they come. Khadimi compares Shaytan to a barking dog: turn to face it, and it fastens on you; walk on, and it falls quiet [Khadimi, al-Bariqa al-Mahmudiyya].

The jurists say the same in their own idiom. Where a man means to pray or to recite the Quran and fears that showing off will enter, he must not leave it, because the fear is a thing of the imagination [Ibn Nujaym, al-Ashbah wa al-Naza’ir].

A man asked Imam Suhrawardi (Allah have mercy on him) whether it was better to stop working and sink into idleness, or to work and let self-regard in. He wrote back: work and seek Allah’s forgiveness [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar].

So do not examine this intention again. Do not renew it, do not test it, and do not check whether the hope is still the main one. That inspection is the illness, and every round of it costs you a prayer you could have prayed.

Hope Is the Prescription, Not the Problem

Imam Khadimi weighs the hardest questions in this field and gives his verdict in his own voice: the sound position is that a person carries out Allah’s commands in hope of His reward [Khadimi, al-Bariqa al-Mahmudiyya]. He prescribes your exact motive as the remedy for your exact worry. You have not fallen into something you must climb out of. You have been handed something to hold.

As for the thing you long for, ask Him for it. Allah Most High says of the people of Paradise, “They shall have anything they may wish therein: And with Us is unutterably more.” [Quran 50:35; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Say what you want, in your own words, and leave the how to Him. Bring the loneliness that began all of this to Him, too, and let a trusted friend or a qualified counselor help you carry it. Allah accepts your worship by His grace, not by the tidiness of your motives, and He is not waiting to catch you out.

records.title: Can I Accept a Group HR Role When One Client Company Runs a CFD Brokerage?
records.question: I have been offered a Group CHRO position at a company that provides HR services to several independent businesses. One of these businesses operates a Forex/CFD brokerage. I would not be involved in trading, selling, or marketing CFDs, but I would handle payroll, contracts, policies, employee relations, and recruitment for that company. Is this role and my salary considered halal? Would this count as indirect support or helping in something sinful? Is it allowed to recruit for that company, including for roles that sell CFDs or create incentives based on CFD sales? Can I accept the job if I avoid those specific tasks? I follow the Shafiʿi school, but can I follow a Hanafi opinion if it is different?
records.answer:
You can accept the job, and your salary is lawful, as long as you do not personally handle two things: recruiting people to sell, promote, or carry out CFD trades, and creating incentives tied to CFD sales or trading volumes. The regular HR work you would do for Company B, like payroll, contracts, benefits, employee relations, performance management, and hiring for support roles, is allowed in the Shafiʿi school. It is better to keep as much distance as possible from that company, but it is not required.

Why the Role and Salary Are Lawful

Your employer is Company A, which provides HR services. This work is halal, and the company earns money from several clients, most of whom have lawful businesses. A work contract (ijara) is valid if the job itself is allowed, and the salary is then halal. However, hiring someone for a forbidden job, such as playing instruments, wailing at funerals, or carrying wine, is not allowed, and payment for such work is not permitted. [Nawawi, Rawdat al-Talibin, 5.194; Shirbini, Mughni al-Muhtaj, 2.337]

As for the money itself, Imam Nawawi (Allah have mercy on him) rules that dealing with someone whose wealth is entirely unlawful is forbidden, and dealing with someone who holds both lawful and unlawful wealth is disliked. He cites the hadith of the clear and the doubtful for the second case. It becomes unlawful only when you know that the very money you receive is the unlawful money. [Nawawi, al-Majmu’, 9.343; Ansari, Asna al-Matalib, 2.41] He then gives a case close to yours: a man buys goods on credit and pays for them with grapes he sold to a known wine maker. Whoever later eats from those goods does something disliked, not unlawful. [Nawawi, al-Majmu’, 9.344] Company A pays you from pooled service income, so your salary is clean.

CFD trading is impermissible, as SeekersGuidance has already answered, because the trader never owns or takes possession of what he trades, and the contract is speculation on price alone. Company B’s core business is therefore unlawful. The question is how close your work may come to it.

Where the Shafiʿi School Draws the Line

The governing verse is, “Cooperate in righteousness and mindfulness of Allah, and do not cooperate in sin and transgression.” [Quran 5:2] The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) cursed the one who consumes usury, the one who pays it, the one who records it, and the two who witness it, and said, “They are all the same.” [Muslim] The scribe and the witnesses do not profit from the usury. They are cursed because their work is part of the transaction.

The Shafiʿi jurists work this out through the case of the grape seller. If you sell grapes to someone you know, or think likely, will press them into wine, the sale is unlawful, though it is valid. If that use is only a possibility, the sale is disliked. [Ansari, Asna al-Matalib, 2.41; Nawawi, al-Majmu’, 9.353] Ibn Hajar al-Haytami (Allah have mercy on him) takes from the hadith cursing ten people in connection with wine a general rule: every causal contribution to a sin and every assistance in it is unlawful, and so is every dealing that leads to a sin. He then explains why the grape sale is valid, though forbidden, while selling weapons to enemy combatants is void. In the second case, the harm lies with the buyer at the moment of sale. In the first, the sin is a later act of the buyer’s own choosing. [Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, Tuhfat al-Muhtaj, 4.316–317]

Ibn Hajar also gives the test that settles your case. He was asked why a man who is not obliged to attend Friday prayer may sell to someone who is obliged once the call is given, while a man who holds chess to be lawful may not play with one who holds it forbidden. He answered that in the sale, the seller’s purpose is profit, which is a sound purpose, and the sin lies in something outside the transaction. In the game, the sin is the shared act itself, so assisting in it cannot be avoided. [Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, al-Fatawa al-Fiqhiyya al-Kubra, 4.357–358]

So the rule is this. Assistance is unlawful when your work gives the sin its means, and you know or expect that this is what it will be used for. Assistance is disliked when your work is a general service that the business would need, whatever it trades in, and your part is at a distance from the unlawful act. Imam Ghazali (Allah have mercy on him) records that a tailor asked Ibn al-Mubarak (Allah have mercy on him) whether sewing for the rulers made him one of their helpers. Ibn al-Mubarak answered that their helpers were the people who sold the tailor his needle and thread; the tailor himself was one of the rulers. [Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, 2.13]

Applying This to Your Duties

Payroll, employment contracts, benefits, HR policies, employee relations, and performance management are general services. A brokerage needs them as much as a bakery does, and none of them is part of a CFD trade. They fall into the disliked category. Keep them routine, keep them as removed as your structure allows, and let Company B’s own management handle anything specific to its trading operation.

Recruiting for support roles at Company B, such as HR, finance, IT, and administration, is permissible on the same basis. Those jobs are lawful in themselves, and the person you place is answerable for their own decision to work there.

Recruiting for roles whose purpose is to sell, promote, or execute CFDs is different. You would be supplying the unlawful activity with the people who carry it out, knowing exactly what they are hired to do. That is the grape seller who knows what the grapes are for. The same applies to designing commission or bonus schemes tied to CFD sales or trading volumes, because there you are building the thing that drives the sin; that is, Ibn Hajar’s chess game rather than his sale. Both are unlawful in the Shafiʿi school, and any wage attached specifically to those tasks would be tainted.

Excluding Yourself From Those Tasks

You can accept the job if you make sure these tasks are not part of your responsibilities. Agree on this in writing before you sign the contract. Company B can handle its own hiring for sales and incentive design, or the group can give these tasks to someone you do not manage. It is not enough to delegate these tasks to your own team, because telling someone else to do them is still considered helping. [Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, Tuhfat al-Muhtaj, 4.317]

If the company will not agree to remove these tasks from your job and insists that you handle them yourself, then you should not accept the role. However, based on your description, this is unlikely for someone at your level.

On Following a Hanafi Position

The Hanafi school grades assistance based on how directly the act constitutes the sin. Where the sin is in the thing supplied itself, such as selling weapons to people known to be in rebellion, the assistance is prohibitively disliked. Where the sin only arises through a further free act of the other party, such as selling grapes to a wine maker, it is mildly disliked. [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar, 4.268] On your questions, this reaches the same place as the Shafiʿi position in everything that matters. Both schools permit lawful general services to a lawful employer, and both treat designing incentives for CFD trading as direct assistance. On recruiting people specifically to sell CFDs, the classical Hanafi texts leave a little more room than the Shafiʿi ones, since the sale is the recruit’s own act, but contemporary Hanafi muftis treat employment built around a forbidden product as direct assistance, and I would not advise you to rely on the narrower reading.

Following a sound position of another school in a specific matter is permissible when done on scholarly guidance rather than as a search for the easiest option, as SeekersGuidance has explained elsewhere. Here, it is not needed.

Your earnings are judged by the work you are hired for, and your accountability by how close your hand comes to the sin. The Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “The lawful is clear, and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters. Whoever guards against the doubtful matters has protected his religion and his honor.” [Bukhari; Muslim] Accept the role with the carve-out in place, keep your involvement with Company B to what its lawful operation requires, and ask Allah to put blessing in what you earn. If a comparable opportunity comes along without this entanglement, taking it would be the more scrupulous path.
references: Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, al-Fatawa al-Fiqhiyya al-Kubra, 4.357–358

records.title: Does Answering “Mhmm” to a Divorce Request Count as a Divorce?
records.question: I came across a fatwa on responding “okay” to a divorce request. Based on its reasoning, would a non-verbal affirmative sound, specifically “mhmm”, which in the UK commonly means “yes” or “I understand”, count as valid, explicit speech capable of constituting a response to a divorce request? Or would it fall short of the threshold of clear verbal articulation?
records.answer:
No. On the reasoning of that fatwa, and on the Hanafi texts it rests on, “mhmm” does not produce a divorce in either situation the fatwa describes. I will take the two situations in turn, because the reasons differ.

If She Asked Him to Divorce Her

The fatwa’s first point is that when a wife says “divorce me,” and the husband answers “yes” or “okay,” no divorce occurs, even if he intended one. She is asking him to do something, and “yes” is an agreement to do it, not the doing of it. Al-Fatawa al-Hindiyya puts it plainly: if she says “I am divorced” and he says “yes”, she is divorced; if he says “yes” in reply to “divorce me”, she is not divorced even if he intended it. [al-Fatawa al-Hindiyya, 1.356] A divorce here needs an actual formula from him, such as “I divorce you”.

If a clear “yes” does not count in this situation, a murmur cannot. So if what preceded the “mhmm” was a request, the question answers itself.

If She Asked Whether He Had Divorced Her

The fatwa’s second point is the one your question is really about. When the wife asks a factual question, “Have you divorced me?” or “Are we divorced?”, and the husband answers with a clear word of assent, one revocable divorce takes effect. Imam Haskafi (Allah have mercy on him): if he is asked, “Have you divorced your wife?” and says “yes” or “indeed”, one revocable divorce falls. [Haskafi, al-Durr al-Mukhtar, with Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar, 3.249]

In this situation, “mhmm” is not enough, and the Hanafi texts explain why. In this school, a divorce must be done with a clear statement, or something that counts as a statement, such as legible writing or sign language for someone who cannot speak. If a man can speak, gestures do not count. Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) gives an example: if a man argues with his wife and gives her three stones, meaning divorce, but says nothing, they are not divorced. [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar, 3.230] Al-Fatawa al-Hindiyya adds that if she says “divorce me” and he just raises three fingers to mean three divorces, nothing happens “until he says it with his tongue.” If he starts to say “you are di…” and stops, or someone covers his mouth, nothing happens, even if he meant it. [al-Fatawa al-Hindiyya, 1.357]

“Mhmm” is just a sound, not an actual word. It has no letters and is not part of any language. People understand it from tone and context, much like a nod. In this school, gestures from someone who can speak do not count in divorce matters. “Mhmm” does not meet the standard set by words like “yes” or “okay”.

A note of caution: Hanafi jurists look at how words are commonly used, not just their grammar. Ibn al-Humam (Allah have mercy on him) said that “naʿam” and “bala” should be treated the same in this context “because of usage” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar, 3.283]. Some might say that “mhmm” is now a word of agreement in British English. However, while common usage decides which words count as assent, it does not make a non-word into a word. The examples involving fingers and stones show that the school maintains this distinction, even when the intention is clear. If there is any doubt, the marriage continues, because certainty cannot be removed by doubt.

Two Practical Points

First, this answer assumes the husband said nothing else. If “mhmm” came before or after any clear or implied divorce wording, the ruling would depend on those words, not on the sound itself.

Second, if he answered a factual question but no divorce had actually happened, then even a clear “yes” would be a false statement. In the Hanafi school, this would be held against him in court, but it does not count as a divorce before Allah. So, a sound like “mhmm,” which is not even held against him in court, does not change the marriage status.

Husbands should avoid answering divorce questions with unclear sounds or incomplete words, and wives should not push for answers during arguments. If this question is about your own marriage, not just in theory, bring the exact words and sequence to a Hanafi mufti who can review the full conversation.
references: Haskafi, al-Durr al-Mukhtar, with Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar, 3.249

records.title: Can I Draw and Sell Stylized Human Characters with Eyes and Ears but No Nose or Mouth?
records.question: I am a Muslim digital artist opening art commissions for stylized human characters that have a head, hair, eyes, and ears, but no nose or mouth. Can I take payment for drawing them?
records.answer:
Taking commissions to draw these characters is not permitted. In the Hanafi school, an image of a living being is complete once the head is drawn, and by your own description, the head is there in full: hair, eyes, and ears, on a face that is still a face. Leaving out the nose and the mouth does not lift it out of the prohibition.

The exemption our books record is for the figure whose head was never drawn, or was drawn and then effaced, since “it is not worshipped without the head, ordinarily” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar 1:648]. Ibn Abidin (Allah have mercy on him) ties that exemption to the head alone: “He restricted it to the head, because removing the eyebrows or the eyes is of no account, since it is worshipped without them” [Ibn Abidin, Radd al-Muhtar 1:648]. The wording is Ibn Nujaym’s (Allah have mercy on him), and in al-Bahr al-Raiq it runs on: “… and likewise no account is taken of cutting off the two hands or the two feet. And in al-Khulasa: likewise, if he effaces the face of the image, that is like cutting off the head” [Ibn Nujaym, al-Bahr al-Raiq 2:31].

Read together, these settle your question. A face wiped out altogether is treated like a head cut off. A face that remains a face, with some features left out, is not the reason being that such a figure is still worshipped without them. If removing the eyes changes nothing, leaving out a nose and a mouth changes less, and stylization does not change it either, since the ruling turns on the head being there and not on how lifelike the drawing looks.

Payment follows the work. Hiring for an act of disobedience is not permitted [al-Mawsua al-Fiqhiyya al-Kuwaytiyya 38:217], and a commission does not become lawful because a client is willing to pay well for it.

The Head Is the Criterion, and It Leaves You a Wide Road

The same criterion shows you what is open to you: figures with no head, figures whose face is wiped out rather than merely simplified, and everything that is not an animate being. Landscape, architecture, plants, pattern, objects, lettering, and calligraphy are all commissionable, and there is beauty in that work and a living in it. Set your commission terms before you open, and let clients choose from what you can offer with a clear heart.

records.title: Is It Permissible to Weigh a Friend’s Bad Qualities?
records.question: Is it fine to deliberate between right and wrong? For example, when you’re considering whether a friend is good for you, you may think of their bad qualities too. Would that not be permissible?
records.answer:
Yes, it is permissible in such cases to consider the pros and cons of a friendship, or the good qualities or the bad qualities of a person. However, I advise you to choose a company that will benefit you in your relationship with Allah, and if you part ways with someone, do so with kindness. Sometimes it doesn’t even have to be said, and you just minimize contact until they’re not actively in your life.

Pray for Them, and an Angel Prays the Same for You

The most important thing in this, however, is to ensure that you pray for them, and for any negative quality you see in them, you ask Allah to replace it with something beloved to Him. We hope that Allah will answer this prayer, as an angel will be praying for you when you pray for something good for your brother in his absence. He will say, “Amin, may you be granted the like of it.” [Muslim]

records.title: Is It Disbelief to Say “Oh My God” in a Mocking or Sexual Joke?
records.question: My friends and I say “oh my God” in a sexual or mocking voice as a joke, sometimes with sexual gestures, sometimes imitating how we think a gay person speaks, or putting on an Indian accent. I am now frightened that this is disbelief, because we are using Allah’s name alongside such jokes.
records.answer:
Let the fear settle first: this is not disbelief (kufr), and you have not left Islam.

What you describe is sinful, in places gravely so. It is not kufr. Leaving Islam requires a knowing, willing rejection of what one knows the religion to be, and crude joking among friends, even joking that drags “God” into it, is not that. That reading your own words back frightened you tells you something true about where your heart stands.

The Line Falls at Mockery of Allah Himself

The Quran draws a parallel in the case of men who made light of the Prophet (Allah bless him and give him peace) and of the revelation itself, then excused themselves by saying they were only talking and amusing themselves. They were asked in reply whether it was at Allah, His verses, and His Messenger that they had been mocking [Quran 9:65], and then told: ‘Make no excuse: You have committed unbelief after this “believing” of yours.’ [Quran 9:66; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Notice what the mockery was aimed at. Derision (istihzaʾ) directed at Allah, His verses, or His Messenger is what the verse condemns. That is not what you and your friends are doing. You are being obscene, and the English word “God” is swept up in it as a piece of slang. That is a different thing, and a lesser one.

None of This Is Small

Do not walk away with only the relief. Attaching the Divine Name to sexual mockery is grave irreverence toward the One you worship, and the religion takes even frivolous use of that Name seriously. Set beside it the mocking of gay-coded speech and of Indian accents, which is contempt for people Allah made and provides for. None of this damns you. It hollows a man out slowly, which is worse than it sounds.

Change the Words, Not Only the Feeling

Sincere remorse suffices here: repent, and it is wiped away. You do not need to repeat your shahada or tell anyone. But remorse that changes nothing on Monday is not yet remorse. So make one concrete change. Drop “oh my God” and “omg” from your speech altogether, in every register, and tell your friends plainly that you are finished with that particular joke. You will be teased for a week.

After that, it will simply be who you are, and you will never have to be frightened like this again.

And strive to uphold this: The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should say the good or remain silent.” [Bukhari and Muslim]

records.title: How Great Is the Gap Between the Least of the Prophets and Sayyiduna Abu Bakr?
records.question: All prophets rank above all non-prophets. How great is that gap? Is the rank of the least of the prophets nearer to that of the Prophet Muhammad (Allah bless him and give him peace), or nearer to that of Sayyiduna Abu Bakr?
records.answer:
Your question rests on a picture that needs correcting, and once corrected, it largely answers itself. You are imagining one scale on which everyone stands, prophets higher and the friends of Allah lower, with a measurable distance between. That is not what prophethood is. Prophethood is a station (maqam), and its whole reality is the receipt of revelation (wahy). This is a station no one even approaches; nor can a non-prophet fathom the station of prophethood, as they lack true realization of what revelation is [Ghazali, Ihyaʾ Ulum al-Din].

Prophets and Prophethood

A prophet is a human being to whom revelation is given, with a sacred law he acts by, whether or not he is commanded to convey it [Bajuri, Tuhfat al-Murid ala Jawharat al-Tawhid]. No quantity of worship produces that. Nobody climbs to it.

Imam Laqani (Allah have mercy on him) puts it in a line of the Jawhara that the commentators have worked over for four centuries:

Prophethood is not acquired, even though a person ascends in goodness to the highest pass; Rather, it is Allah’s bounty, given to whom He wills

[Laqani, Jawharat al-Tawhid]

Imam Bajuri (Allah have mercy on him) explains that it is not earned by following any particular regimen of means, such as keeping to seclusion, and that “the highest pass” refers to the most arduous acts of worship [Bajuri, Tuhfat al-Murid]. He glosses the second line’s “Giver of gifts” as the One who gives without any counter-payment. The philosophers held the opposite, that prophethood is the fruit of ascetic training, and Bajuri observes that the whole disagreement is definitional: they differ over whether it can be earned because they differ over what it is.

The Comparison Asked About

That is why your comparison, natural as it is, has no measure. The gap between a prophet and Abu Bakr (Allah be pleased with him) is not a distance along one road. It is the difference between one who is given revelation and one who is not.

Imam Tahawi (Allah have mercy on him) fixes the ordering in the creed: no friend of Allah is preferred over any prophet, and a single prophet is better than all the friends of Allah together [Tahawi, al-Aqida al-Tahawiyya].

Imam Nasafi (Allah have mercy on him) reaches the same conclusion from the very hadith you would think of: that no sun has risen or set upon anyone after the prophets, better than Abu Bakr, which places him above everyone who is not a prophet and below anyone who is [Nasafi, al-Iʿtimad fi al-Iʿtiqad].

Ranking among the prophets themselves is affirmed in the Book, “Those are the messengers, We having preferred some above others” [Quran 2:253], but the Book affirms the fact without giving the measure, and the scholars decline to specify what revelation left unspecified. You asked to be told if this is one of those. It is, and that is a position rather than a gap in our knowledge.

What Is Ours to Know, and What Is Not

Prophethood is bestowed, not earned. Friendship with Allah is earned in following a prophet, and the follower does not overtake the one he follows. Hold the ordering with certainty, love them all, and leave the measure to the One who set it. Your Lord knows best all those in the heavens and the earth [Quran 17:55].
references: Bajuri, Tuhfat al-Murid ala Jawharat al-Tawhid

records.title: Can Beneficial Knowledge Learned From a Sinful Source Be a Gift From Allah?
records.question: I learned sound and useful things about the qualities of a good and a bad spouse from videos that also contained unlawful material. Can that understanding still be counted as a gift or guidance from Allah, and might it be Allah preparing me to choose well in marriage?
records.answer:
Yes. Every benefit comes from Allah, even when it reaches you through a place you wish it had not.

This is not just comfort. It is how Allah gives in this world. Allah Most High says, “He gives wisdom to act to whomever He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has been given immeasurable good.” [Quran 2:269; Keller, The Quran Beheld]

Allah gives wisdom as He wills. The source does not limit Him. If something true reached you and helped you, thank Allah for it and use it well.

Your sense that Allah may be preparing you to choose well in marriage is sound. Allah often turns a person’s heart toward what will help them before they know the reason.

Learn from Teachers You Can Trust

Let this lesson shape how you learn from now on. Seek knowledge from teachers who are qualified and whose practice you can trust.

This is not a small detail. Who you learn from shapes your heart and actions, not just your knowledge. When a teacher is not upright, truth and error come mixed. If a benefit once reached you through a bad source, do not keep returning to it.

Take the Good, but Change Where You Seek It

You may find benefit in many places, but the path you take matters. Now, take this same subject to a teacher, a course, or a book you trust. Let the next lesson about marriage reach you in a way you do not regret.

records.title: Kvass, Kombucha, and Kefir: Are They Permissible?
records.question: A friend offered me Kvass, a fermented bread drink with about 0.5% alcohol from natural fermentation, and I declined out of caution. In Hanafi sources, I read that the Imams of the school differed over drinks made from wheat and barley, and I also found a Hanafi fatwa permitting Kvass. Elsewhere, I found conflicting criteria: some look at the alcohol percentage, others at whether its taste or smell remains, and others at whether it intoxicates in large amounts. When my friend asked whether bread would then be unlawful too, I told him it is permissible because it does not intoxicate. Is Kvass permissible? What is the reliable criterion for fermented drinks like kombucha and kefir, and was I right about bread?
records.answer:
You did well to be cautious. You can set this worry aside.

Kvass at 0.5% alcohol is permissible. So are kombucha and kefir.

One Test: Does It Intoxicate?

The criterion you are asking for is one test: a drink is unlawful if it intoxicates when drunk in quantity, or if you drink it as an intoxicant. If so, a single sip of it is unlawful. If it does not intoxicate, it is lawful, no matter what trace of alcohol remains from fermentation or what the label says.

The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and give him peace) said, “Of whatever a large amount intoxicates, a small amount is unlawful.” [Abu Dawud; Tirmidhi; Ibn Maja] That is the relied-upon position of the Hanafi school, and it is the whole test.

The Disagreement Was About Drinks That Can Intoxicate
